articles.title: South Side Columbus Breaks Ground on 150-Unit Affordable Apartments
articles.excerpt: The NRP Group broke ground on Stone Ridge at High Street, 150 affordable apartments at 45 West Barthman Ave. on Columbus's South Side, set to open in 2028.
articles.body:
The NRP Group broke ground August 25, 2026 on Stone Ridge at High Street, a 150-unit affordable apartment community at 45 West Barthman Avenue on Columbus's South Side. Huntington Bank and Deutsche Bank are financing the project alongside the city and the Ohio Housing Finance Agency, with completion expected in April 2028.

## What Broke Ground on Barthman Avenue

Stone Ridge at High Street will consist of two five-story buildings on a 4.5-acre site, holding a mix of one-, two-, three-, and four-bedroom apartments, according to [The NRP Group's groundbreaking announcement](https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/news/nrp-group-breaks-ground-150-154700390.html), distributed via PR Newswire. The development will include a clubhouse with a multipurpose community room and kitchen, plus landscaped courtyards and a playground, [the announcement said](https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/news/nrp-group-breaks-ground-150-154700390.html).

The site sat empty for years before this groundbreaking. "For years, this property sat vacant, despite its proximity to downtown Columbus and some of the city's strongest employment centers," said Aaron Pechota, executive vice president of development at The NRP Group, in the announcement.

## Who the Apartments Are For

The units will be reserved for working professionals and families earning up to 60% of the area median income, [the release said](https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/news/nrp-group-breaks-ground-150-154700390.html), a tier aimed at renters priced out of market-rate housing but above the income limits some deeper-subsidy programs serve. [MultifamilyBiz.com's separate report](https://www.multifamilybiz.com/news/11455/the_nrp_group_breaks_ground_on_150unit_stone_ridge...) on the groundbreaking confirmed the same address, unit count, and site size independently.

## How the Deal Is Financed

Huntington Bank provided debt and equity financing, and Deutsche Bank is providing construction and permanent financing, with the City of Columbus and the Ohio Housing Finance Agency as public partners, according to the NRP Group announcement. Neither the release nor MultifamilyBiz.com's report disclosed a total project cost or the size of each financing piece.

Columbus Mayor Andrew Ginther framed the project as a model for the city's affordable-housing push: "Public-private partnerships are essential to the success of the Columbus Housing Strategy, and Stone Ridge at High Street demonstrates what can be accomplished when city leaders, financial institutions and private developers work together with a shared vision."

Andrew Hugger of Huntington Bank added: "We are proud to support Stone Ridge at High Street and help bring high-quality, affordable housing to the Southside of Columbus, creating new opportunities for residents."

## More South Side Housing in the Pipeline

Stone Ridge is one of several NRP Group projects along the South High Street corridor. According to [a Columbus Underground report](https://columbusunderground.com/two-projects-could-bring-over-400-affordable-apartments-to-south-side-bw1/) on city zoning and development records, a separate 245-unit NRP project called Dering Family Apartments near Fornof Road and South High Street has secured financing and neighborhood support and could break ground later this year, and a second NRP zoning application proposes roughly 200 more apartments on an 8-acre site nearby. CREN has not independently verified those two projects' records and is citing Columbus Underground's reporting on them.

## What to Watch Next

Construction on Stone Ridge at High Street is underway with an expected completion date of April 2028, roughly 20 months out. The next public milestones to watch are a building permit progress update from the City of Columbus and any zoning commission action on the second, 200-unit NRP proposal nearby. For more on how the South Side is changing, see CREN's [South Side area coverage](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/areas/south-side).

articles.title: Columbus Polaris: Permits Filed for Third Central Ohio Trader Joe's
articles.excerpt: Columbus’s first new Trader Joe’s in 20-plus years is planned for 2109 Ikea Way in Polaris, with permits for a 12,500-square-foot store under city review.
articles.body:
Columbus is set to receive its third Central Ohio Trader Joe's, with interior fit-out permits filed in July 2026 for a 12,500-square-foot store at 2109 Ikea Way in the Polaris corridor. A plumbing permit was issued July 21, and an interior build-out application remains under city review.

## What the City Filings Show

Plans filed with the City of Columbus on July 8, 2026 detail a full interior build-out of a newly constructed retail building at 2109 Ikea Way into Trader Joe's #889 — the company's internal store identifier — including new fixtures, millwork, flooring, and lighting, according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/plans-submitted-for-new-trader-joes-store-in-columbus-bw1/), which reviewed the permit filings. A plumbing permit was issued July 21, and a separate interior fit-out application was under city review as of late July 2026.

The shell building that will house the store was permitted separately in April 2026 and remains under construction. The site at 2109 Ikea Way is currently undeveloped.

The developer of the shell building is NP Limited Partnership, the firm behind Galaxy at Polaris — the mixed-use development at the intersection that includes apartments and a Puttshack — and much of the corridor's broader development since the late 1990s and early 2000s, according to Columbus Underground's review of city permit records. The Trader Joe's buildout application lists the parent as NP Limited Partnership, not a Trader Joe's subsidiary, consistent with a standard landlord-build-and-lease structure.

## Twenty-Two Years Without a New Central Ohio Store

Trader Joe's opened its first Central Ohio store on Sawmill Road in Dublin in 2002, and a second near Easton Town Center in 2004. No new location has followed in the more than two decades since.

The pause is ending as part of a broad national expansion wave. Trader Joe's has been expanding into new markets across the country, and Central Ohio is among the areas receiving new supply. A company spokesperson confirmed to [NBC4 WCMH-TV](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/trader-joes-is-planning-a-location-in-columbus-polaris-area/) that the company "is planning a new store in Columbus," but declined to provide a specific address or projected opening timeline. Trader Joe's typically does not announce new stores until shortly before opening.

## The Polaris Site

The 2109 Ikea Way location sits in the Polaris growth corridor near Delaware County's border, directly across the street from TopGolf Columbus and Galaxy at Polaris, according to [NBC4 WCMH-TV](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/trader-joes-is-planning-a-location-in-columbus-polaris-area/). The planned building measures 12,500 square feet with 132 parking spaces.

The Polaris corridor has served as one of Central Ohio's primary retail destinations since the late 1990s and straddles the Columbus and Delaware County boundary. This site sits within the Worthington City School District, which extends north into Delaware County along the U.S. 23 corridor.

NP Limited Partnership's dual role — as both the developer of the Trader Joe's shell building and the firm that developed Galaxy at Polaris and much of the surrounding retail footprint — suggests the company is filling a gap in its tenant mix at the intersection rather than bringing in an outside developer.

## What a New Grocery Anchor Means for the Corridor

A Trader Joe's is typically a neighborhood-format grocery store, smaller than a full-scale supermarket. The format draws frequent, dedicated shoppers and generates consistent midday traffic that differs from the big-box anchor stores that anchor most of the Polaris corridor's retail base.

For operators and investors tracking the corridor, a Trader Joe's commit signals that the trade area's demographics — household income, density, and purchasing patterns — clear the chain's site-selection threshold. Trader Joe's is known for deliberate market entry and does not open stores to experiment; the permit filing represents a durable location decision.

The surrounding Polaris market has continued to add apartment supply in recent years, bringing more rental households into the corridor's immediate trade area. The NRP Group's 336-unit OSU East community at 2575 West Dublin Granville Road, which broke ground in August 2026 about one mile west of the Ikea Way site, is among the most recent additions to that pipeline, as [CREN previously reported](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/blog/nrp-group-breaks-ground-on-336-unit-columbus-apartments).

## What Remains Unconfirmed

Trader Joe's has not announced a construction start date or opening timeline. Interior fit-out work on a store of this size typically runs several months after shell delivery, but that schedule depends on when shell construction completes and when the city issues a building permit for the interior buildout. As of late July, the interior fit-out application remained under review; no interior building permit had been issued.

The company has not released lease terms, rent per square foot, or whether it owns or leases the finished building. NP Limited Partnership has not issued a public statement about the project.

## What to Watch Next

The next public milestone is issuance of a building permit for the interior fit-out. City of Columbus Building and Zoning Services permit records are publicly searchable through the city's online permit portal. An issued permit would signal active interior work is authorized and provide a practical lower bound on the opening timeline. No opening date has been confirmed.

articles.title: Franklin County's Informal Property Value Review Closes Today
articles.excerpt: Today is the last day for Franklin County's informal property value review sessions before the county submits 2026 triennial values to the state.
articles.body:
Today, September 5, 2026, is the last day for Franklin County's informal property value review sessions, held ahead of the county's 2026 triennial value update. Owners who miss today's session can still challenge their value later through the county Board of Revision.

## What Closes Today

The Franklin County Auditor's Office has been holding in-person and virtual Property Value Review sessions since this summer, letting residential and commercial owners meet with appraisal staff about their tentative 2026 value. [Those sessions run through today, September 5](https://www.theclevelandamerican.com/franklin-county-opens-property-value-review-sessions-for-tentative-2026-appraisals/), according to a report on the Auditor's process.

## Why 2026 Is a Triennial Year, Not a Full Reappraisal

Ohio law requires county auditors to conduct a full reappraisal of every property every six years and a lighter-touch update at the three-year midpoint. Franklin County's [own real estate page confirms it completed its last full sexennial reappraisal in 2023](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/Real-Estate), with 2026 as the follow-up Triennial Update. A triennial update recalibrates values using recent sales data rather than a fresh physical inspection of every parcel.

## How Ohio Turns a Value Into a Tax Bill

Ohio does not tax a property's full appraised value. State law caps the taxable, or assessed, value at a share of true value that the state tax commissioner sets by rule — currently [35 percent, under Ohio Administrative Code 5703-25-05 and Ohio Revised Code 5715.01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5715.01). A property appraised at $300,000, for example, is taxed on an assessed value no higher than $105,000. That is the number the county applies local tax rates against, not the appraised figure itself.

## What Happens After Today

Once today's window closes, [updated values will be submitted to the Ohio Department of Taxation for evaluation before final appraised values are released](https://www.theclevelandamerican.com/franklin-county-opens-property-value-review-sessions-for-tentative-2026-appraisals/), which checks them for consistency across the county. County officials expect finalized property values to be issued in December, per that same report. The Auditor's office notes it is closed September 7 for Labor Day and again from 10 to 11 a.m. on September 14 for an all-staff meeting, so owners with follow-up questions about a value should plan around those windows.

## The Formal Appeal Path That Stays Open

Missing today's informal session does not end an owner's options. Once final 2026 values are certified, owners can still file a formal complaint with the county Board of Revision. [Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 sets that filing window at on or before March 31 of the following year](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5715.19), or the closing date of first-half tax collection for the current year, whichever is later — meaning complaints about 2026 values would be due by March 31, 2027 at the earliest cutoff. A Board of Revision complaint requires a formal filing and supporting evidence, such as a recent appraisal or comparable sales; the informal review does not.

## Why It Matters for Investors and Landlords

Franklin County does not use a separate tax rate for rental or commercial property — assessed value drives the bill under the same 35 percent framework regardless of use. An owner with several parcels who successfully lowers even one tentative value can see that saving repeat every tax cycle until the next update, which is part of why the informal review exists as a faster, no-filing-fee first step before the Board of Revision.

## What to Watch Next

Owners who want to weigh a formal Board of Revision complaint will have that final number, plus the March 31, 2027 filing deadline, to work from once it is issued.

articles.title: Columbus German Village Cedar Square Wins Contested 3-2 Vote
articles.excerpt: German Village commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 3 to approve Cedar Square's 52-unit concept at 251 E. Livingston, with opponents citing scale and a bylaws dispute.
articles.body:
The German Village Commission voted 3-2 on September 3 to give conceptual approval to Cedar Square, Mershad Development's 52-unit, three-story proposal at 251 East Livingston Avenue. The applicant must return for an exterior-materials review, and opponents contend the commission's own bylaws required four votes for passage, not three.

## What the Commission Approved — and What It Didn't

A conceptual approval from the German Village Commission means the body has accepted the building's basic footprint, massing, and design direction but has not signed off on the final materials palette, window details, signage, or lighting. Mershad Development must schedule a follow-up appearance before the commission with those specifics before receiving a final certificate of appropriateness. No demolition permit can be pulled on the existing office building at 251 E. Livingston until that second approval is granted.

The commission functions as an advisory body to the City of Columbus Building and Zoning Services division. Its recommendations on exterior design carry significant weight within the city's review process for the German Village Historic District, but the final legal authority to issue or deny building permits rests with the city.

## The Project, Scaled Back Over More Than a Year

Cedar Square is Mershad Development's third iteration on this site. The original 2025 proposal called for a four-story building with 96 apartments; community pressure and commission feedback prompted successive reductions. The version approved September 3 is three stories and 52 units — mostly studios and one-bedrooms with a handful of two-bedroom units on the top floor — plus 61 parking spaces on a ground-floor garage and a small retail component fronting Livingston Avenue, according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/controversial-german-village-development-gets-initial-approval-bw1/).

The building stretches approximately 327 feet east to west along East Blenkner Street, a span [614NOW](https://614now.com/2026/hot-topics/proposed-apartments-roughly-the-length-of-a-football-field-facing-pushback-in-german-village) compared to the length of a football field. That dimension anchors the opposition: German Village's streetscape is defined by shorter building faces and varied setbacks, and a 327-foot continuous wall at three stories is without precedent in the historic district.

## The Vote-Count Dispute

The approval came with a procedural wrinkle that opponents may pursue. The German Village Commission's own bylaws state that four votes are required to pass a motion. Wednesday's vote was 3-2 — three in the majority, two opposed.

Before the vote, city staff consulted with the city attorney's office, which concluded that Columbus City Code supersedes the commission's bylaws on the vote-threshold question: under city code, a majority of the quorum present is sufficient for approval. With five members present, a three-vote majority met that standard, according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/controversial-german-village-development-gets-initial-approval-bw1/).

The tension between the commission's written bylaws and the city attorney's interpretation is an unresolved procedural question. If opponents file a legal or administrative challenge arguing the bylaws govern, the status of the September 3 vote could become subject to review. No challenge had been announced as of publication.

## Community Opposition: 750 Signatures and Documented Concerns

A neighborhood petition opposing Cedar Square in its current form had topped 750 signatures ahead of the September 3 vote, according to [Hoodline](https://hoodline.com/2026/09/german-village-s-327-foot-cedar-square-plan-faces-final-vote-as-petition-tops-750-names/). Petition organizers asked the commission and the city to reject the proposal and require a version that more closely follows German Village's traditional development patterns.

The objections documented in prior commission proceedings go beyond aesthetics. Residents have raised concerns about pedestrian safety on the neighborhood's narrow brick streets and alleys, emergency-vehicle access, and traffic from 61 parking spaces with unclear egress points. None of those concerns produced a substantive developer response in the public commission record reviewed for this story. [NBC4 WCMH-TV](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/german-village-development-proposal-nears-vote-as-residents-raise-concerns/) reported on residents raising these issues in advance of the vote.

## A Project With a Long Prior Record

The Cedar Square proposal has been before the German Village Commission for more than a year. An earlier scaled-down version was denied approval, according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/scaled-down-german-village-proposal-denied-approval-again-bw1/), and Mershad Development revised the project again before the September 3 hearing. The current three-story, 52-unit version reflects two rounds of concessions since the 96-unit original.

The length of the review process is itself significant context: a project that has faced denial and required multiple revisions over 14-plus months carries a different procedural standing than one seeing its first commission vote. Opponents have had extensive opportunity to document objections; the September 3 approval reflects those objections remaining unresolved in the commission's final tally, not being considered for the first time.

## German Village Density in a Zone In Moment

Cedar Square's approval arrives while Columbus is running a 60-day public comment period on [Zone In Phase 2](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/blog/columbus-zone-in-phase-2-public-comment), the city's sweeping zoning overhaul that opened August 25 and runs through October 24. Zone In Phase 2 aims to add housing capacity across a wider portion of Columbus — but the German Village Historic District operates under separate historic preservation rules that govern exterior design regardless of underlying zoning.

The disconnect between citywide density goals and neighborhood-scale historic preservation is a structural feature of how Columbus regulates its historic districts, not a contradiction the commission has authority to resolve. Cedar Square is a live illustration: the city's housing-production goals support adding 52 units of infill close to downtown transit and employment; the community and two commission members contend the building's mass is incompatible with the district's established character. The September 3 vote moves the project one step closer to a building permit while leaving the procedural question, the materials review, and the community opposition unresolved.

## What Comes Next

Mershad Development must file a revised exterior-materials and design-details package and schedule a second German Village Commission hearing before a final certificate of appropriateness can be issued. The project cannot proceed to demolition or construction permits until that review is complete.

If a legal challenge to the September 3 vote is filed based on the bylaws dispute, it could pause or reset that timeline. No timeline for the follow-up commission hearing or for demolition has been released publicly. The office building currently at 251 E. Livingston Avenue and its parking lot would be razed before construction begins; no demolition permit has been pulled with Building and Zoning Services as of this writing.

German Village residents should expect at least one more commission proceeding on materials and design details before Cedar Square clears its final local approval gate.

articles.title: Columbus Diocese Plans to Demolish 1908 Gay St. Building
articles.excerpt: The Diocese of Columbus filed to demolish its 1908 building at 197 E. Gay St. for surface parking. The Downtown Commission votes September 22, 2026.
articles.body:
The Roman Catholic Diocese of Columbus filed a Certificate of Appropriateness with the city's Planning Division to demolish its 1908 five-story building at 197 East Gay Street and convert the site to surface parking. The Downtown Commission, which must approve demolition in the historic district, is scheduled to take up the application on September 22.

## What the Diocese Submitted

A Certificate of Appropriateness is the permit Columbus requires before anyone alters or demolishes a building within the Downtown Commission's jurisdiction, which covers exterior changes, new construction, and demolition in the downtown core. The application describes the project scope as demolition of the building and its "conversion to surface parking," according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/church-wants-to-tear-down-5-story-downtown-building-bw1/), which reported the filing on September 2. The filing was made with the Planning Division; no demolition permit has been pulled with the city's Building and Zoning Services as of publication.

The Diocese has not released a public statement on the application. CREN sought comment from the Diocese of Columbus; no response had been received by publication time.

## The Building and Its Tenants

The building at 197 East Gay Street was constructed in 1908 and is five stories. The Diocese has owned it since the 1960s, and it currently houses three occupants: the Diocese's administrative offices, Catholic Social Services of the Diocese of Columbus, and the Our Lady of Guadalupe Center, which provides pastoral and social services to Columbus's Latino Catholic community.

The Diocese has not announced relocation plans for any of the three tenants. No timeline for vacating the building has appeared in the public filing or in Diocese communications reviewed as of this writing. Catholic Social Services and the Our Lady of Guadalupe Center both provide programs whose continuity is relevant to the communities they serve, and where those programs would relocate is not addressed in the submitted application.

## Location in the Cathedral Block

The building sits in one of the more intact early-twentieth-century institutional blocks remaining in downtown Columbus. It stands behind [Saint Joseph Cathedral](https://www.stjosephcathedral.net/) at 212 E. Broad Street, next door to the [Columbus Athenaeum](https://www.columbusathenaeum.com/) at 32 N. 4th Street — a historic events venue still in active use — and across E. Gay Street from condominium units developed by Edwards Companies under its Neighborhood Launch initiative.

The [Catholic Diocese of Columbus](https://columbuscatholic.org/venue/197-e-gay-st-parking-lot/) lists a "197 E. Gay St. Parking Lot" as a venue on its website, indicating some existing parking use at the address. The relationship between that existing use and the building the Diocese seeks to demolish is not specified in publicly available documents.

## Why the Building Is in Trouble

An unsafe order was placed on the structure after a brick wall collapsed in January 2026. The Diocese has not released a structural assessment or estimates for repairs. The unsafe order is the disclosed precipitating event, though it does not by itself authorize demolition — the Certificate of Appropriateness process and Downtown Commission approval remain required regardless of building condition.

Historically, the Downtown Commission has weighed demolition applications against the applicant's documentation of condition and repair costs, the building's significance within the historic district, and whether adaptive reuse or rehabilitation is feasible. When owners have demonstrated that rehabilitation costs exceed a building's viable economic use, the Commission has sometimes permitted demolition to proceed. When the record is thin or alternatives appear viable, the Commission has requested additional documentation or required alternatives. The Diocese's case will likely turn on what condition evidence and cost estimates it presents at the hearing.

## The Surface Parking Tension

This application arrives while Columbus is running a 60-day public comment period on Zone In Phase 2, the city's comprehensive [zoning code modernization](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/blog/columbus-zone-in-phase-2-public-comment) that opened August 25 and extends through October 24. Zone In Phase 2 is specifically designed to add density and reduce surface parking's footprint in the city's urban core.

Replacing a five-story building with a surface lot would move counter to that direction on a block that sits within the walkable, transit-proximate downtown core that both Zone In and the city's long-range comprehensive plan identify as a priority for active-use development. That tension between an institutional property owner's decision and city planning goals is one the Downtown Commission will need to navigate. The Commission's mandate is historic preservation, not land-use planning, but surface parking conversion of a historic building is precisely the scenario that Columbus's Certificate of Appropriateness process was designed to give the Commission authority to weigh.

The Columbus Athenaeum, immediately adjacent, would be a logical party to weigh in; no public statement from the Athenaeum had been released as of publication. The Columbus Preservation Office advises the Commission on historic resource significance; its assessment of the property has not been made public.

## What to Watch

If the Diocese's application is on the agenda — which has not been formally published as of this writing — the Commission will take public comment before voting to approve, deny, or table the demolition request. An approval allows the Diocese to proceed to a demolition permit; a denial requires the Diocese to either appeal or revise its approach.

The building's fate after any Commission decision would depend on whether the Diocese pursues demolition, explores sale or adaptive reuse, or undertakes emergency stabilization of the structure pending a longer-term plan. None of those paths has been announced.

articles.title: Nationwide Children's Buys $7.6M East Main Street Block, No Plans Yet
articles.excerpt: Nationwide Children's paid $7.6M for a Near East Side block on E. Main St., closing Aug. 7. No plans announced for the 3.62-acre site north of I-70.
articles.body:
Nationwide Children's Hospital paid $7.6 million for a 3.62-acre block on East Main Street in Columbus's Near East Side on August 7, 2026, according to Franklin County property records. The hospital has not announced specific plans for the site, which sits just north of the interstate, adjacent to its growing main campus.

## What Was Purchased

The block at 818 E. Main Street sits on the south side of East Main between South 17th and South 18th streets, extending south to East Mound Street. The 3.62-acre parcel was previously owned by the Douglas Lula Foundation, a Columbus nonprofit associated with James "Buster" Douglas — the Columbus native who upset Mike Tyson for the world heavyweight boxing title in 1990. [Turner Construction Company](https://www.turnerconstruction.com/) had been leasing the site and using it for surface parking.

Nationwide Children's confirmed the acquisition in a brief statement but disclosed no specific development. "Acquiring the property allows Nationwide Children's to plan thoughtfully for both the short-term and long-term future of a site that is now adjacent to our growing campus," a hospital spokesperson said, declining to elaborate on timing or intended use.

At $7.6 million for 3.62 acres, the price works out to roughly $2.1 million per acre — a figure consistent with institutional land-banking on the Near East Side, where commercial land has traded between $500,000 and $4 million per acre over the past five years depending on improvements and proximity to anchor institutions.

## Why This Is a New Threshold for the Hospital's Footprint

The East Main Street acquisition puts a Nationwide Children's–owned parcel on the north side of the interstate, in contrast to the hospital's main campus and its other Near East Side facilities. The hospital's main campus at 700 Children's Drive sits south of I-70, as do the hospital's office buildings and research facilities on the Near East Side that have come online over the past decade.

The hospital's expansion activity has been sustained. In May 2025 it broke ground on a 14-story, 850,000-square-foot acute-care tower described as the largest single investment in Nationwide Children's history, at a cost of approximately $1.27 billion. That tower adds more than 430 beds — including an expanded neonatal intensive care unit, new surgical suites, and oncology services — and is expected to open in 2028. The City of Columbus approved an updated tax-incentive agreement in July 2025 extending the hospital's income-tax breaks through 2039 in exchange for adding 7,500 jobs over 15 years as part of its campus expansion plan.

The East Main Street block purchase follows a pattern of quiet pre-announcement land acquisition that healthcare systems typically use before committing to a specific program. Whether the intended use is clinical space, employee support facilities, housing, research, or a combination is not publicly known.

## The BRT Corridor Factor

The block sits directly along COTA's planned [LinkUS East Main Street Bus Rapid Transit corridor](https://www.cota.com/linkus/), a $340 million project projected to deliver dedicated BRT service along East Main Street around 2029. The BRT line is intended to run from downtown Columbus east toward the Bexley border, with dedicated lanes, stations, and frequent service that would substantially improve transit access along the corridor.

For a major employer and healthcare institution, high-frequency transit access carries operational weight: BRT proximity can improve employee recruitment and patient transportation options, factors that influence where hospitals locate clinical facilities and support services. The East Main Street block sits along the planned corridor, within the stretch of East Main Street the LinkUS project is designed to serve.

Neither COTA nor Nationwide Children's has announced any coordination between the BRT station design process and the hospital's plans for the acquired block.

## Near East Side Development Context

The Near East Side has become one of Columbus's most active development submarkets, partly because of Nationwide Children's own expansion and partly because OHFA and City of Columbus capital have followed the hospital's footprint into the neighborhood.

Other projects within roughly a half-mile of the new acquisition show the same pattern. [Kingsley + Co.](https://www.kingsleyandco.com/) received a 2026 Low Income Housing Tax Credit reservation from the Ohio Housing Finance Agency for Mercy on Main, a 65-unit affordable housing development one block west on East Main Street, backed by $3.25 million in City of Columbus HOME funds. Northstar Realty LLC and Schiff Capital Group began demolition in May 2026 for a 170-unit mixed-use development at 475 East Livingston Avenue, directly across from the hospital's main campus. Columbus State Community College and Woda Cooper Companies broke ground in August 2026 on a $51 million, 166-unit affordable housing complex two blocks northwest in the Discovery District.

Each of these projects draws demand, at least in part, from the worker and patient volumes generated by Nationwide Children's existing campus.

## What to Watch

As of publication, Nationwide Children's has not filed a permit application, rezoning request, or development plan for the site with the City of Columbus Department of Building and Zoning Services. No timeline for any announcement has been shared publicly.

The key signals to monitor: permit filings in Columbus's public building permit database, any rezoning application submitted to the City of Columbus Development Commission, a hospital press release, or a reference in Nationwide Children's next annual report. The LinkUS BRT station design and placement process is still underway and may influence what Nationwide Children's eventually proposes for the site, since station locations and pedestrian access points will shape the block's connectivity and development potential.

The Douglas Lula Foundation, the prior owner, did not appear to have any announcement about its plans for the proceeds from the sale.

articles.title: Downtown Columbus Office Tower Wins 2026 Redevelopment of the Year
articles.excerpt: Bernstein Cos. converted the former Continental Centre at 150 E. Gay St. into 409 apartments, earning CoStar's 2026 Redevelopment of the Year honor for Columbus.
articles.body:
Washington, D.C.-based The Bernstein Cos. has converted the former Continental Centre at 150 East Gay Street into Continental Tower, a 409-unit apartment building in downtown Columbus. CoStar recognized the project as its 2026 Redevelopment of the Year, citing more than $100 million invested in a 1970s-era office building.

## A 1970s Tower Gets a Residential Reboot

The Continental Centre was built in the 1970s at Gay and Third streets — one of the taller structures in the downtown Columbus skyline. Like many mid-century office towers in Midwest cities, it lost tenants steadily as employers moved to suburban campuses or newer buildings. By the time The Bernstein Cos. committed to a conversion, a substantial portion of the building was vacant.

The Bernstein Cos., headquartered in Washington, D.C., secured Ohio historic preservation tax credits in 2022 — part of the state's Historic Preservation Tax Credit program, which awards transferable credits to developers who rehabilitate historic income-producing properties in compliance with federal standards. Those credits provided a meaningful portion of the project's financing stack alongside private equity and debt. [HGC Construction](https://hgcconstruction.com/project/continental-tower/) managed the general contracting work, and Columbus-based [ArchAll Architects](https://www.archall.com/projects/continental-tower) handled the conversion's design.

## What 409 Units Look Like in This Building

The converted building holds 409 apartments — studios, one-bedrooms, and two-bedrooms — marketed as luxury rentals. Amenities include a fitness center with a spin studio, private co-working spaces, a residential lounge and clubroom on the 24th floor, an on-site market, a coffee shop, and a rooftop pool scheduled to open this month. Unit finishes, as described in the building's marketing materials, include floor-to-ceiling windows, quartz countertops, Samsung appliances, smart thermostats, soft-close cabinetry, and walk-in closets.

Continental Tower is a market-rate project — there are no income restrictions. Specific rent prices were not publicly available at publication time.

## CoStar's Recognition and What It Signals

[CoStar's Impact Awards](https://www.costar.com/article/2041876288/the-bernstein-cos-revives-1970s-office-building-as-mixed-use-residential-tower-in-midwest) are a commercial real estate industry competition that recognizes developers, owners, and projects across markets. The Redevelopment of the Year category focuses on projects that revived dormant or distressed buildings — the complexity of the conversion, the scale of investment, and the building's new role in its neighborhood all factor in.

Winning that award in Columbus carries meaning: an out-of-town developer put substantial capital into a downtown Ohio office building, not a coastal market. That is the kind of out-of-market capital deployment that tracks closely with a city's growing investment profile. For Columbus brokers, operators, and investors, the CoStar recognition is less a rubber stamp than a data point about how the city is being evaluated from outside.

## Downtown Columbus Context

Continental Tower sits in the Gay Street corridor, a stretch of downtown Columbus that has drawn several residential and mixed-use projects in recent years. The corridor runs adjacent to the Short North and connects the Arena District to the Broad and High Street core. [RealPage Analytics](https://www.realpage.com/analytics/office-to-apartment-conversions-ohio/) has identified Columbus as one of Ohio's most active markets for office-to-apartment conversions, alongside Cleveland and Cincinnati.

The project is part of a broader wave of downtown residential deliveries. The [Merchant Building renovation](/blog/downtown-columbus-merchant-building-fall-2026-opening) targeted a fall opening several blocks away, and the [Discovery District parking-lot apartment project](/blog/discovery-district-parking-lots-518-apartments-96-million) is adding several hundred units a few blocks east. Together, these projects are testing whether downtown Columbus can absorb a meaningful increase in residential inventory at market-rate price points.

A separate office-to-residential conversion — the Nationwide-owned tower, [tracked by Propmodo](https://propmodo.com/playbook/nationwide-is-converting-one-of-its-own-office-towers-into-apartments/) — would add another major residential count if it proceeds. Whether Continental Tower's lease-up pace provides confidence for that project's timing is a question the market will answer in the coming months.

## What Is Not Confirmed

CREN could not confirm current occupancy rate, a timeline to stabilization, or specific rent levels at Continental Tower from publicly available sources. The Ohio Historic Preservation Tax Credit award amount for this project was not identified in public summaries; the [Ohio Department of Development's tax credit project registry](https://development.ohio.gov/business/historic-preservation/ohio-historic-preservation-tax-credit) is the authoritative public record. The publication date of Columbus Underground's first-look coverage could not be confirmed precisely; CREN referenced it as recent based on the article's proximity to the rooftop pool opening.

## What to Watch Next

The next verifiable checkpoint is a lease-up announcement from The Bernstein Cos. indicating the building has reached or approached stabilization, the industry benchmark for a fully leased building. If and when that figure is disclosed, it will be the clearest signal of how much demand actually exists for the new market-rate apartments at Gay and Third streets.

Longer term, the city's office-to-residential conversion pipeline will determine how much existing office stock Columbus can redirect toward housing before new ground-up construction takes over the supply role. Continental Tower is the most visible data point in that pipeline right now.

articles.title: Old Hilliard Bank Building Becomes Lira Italian Kitchen
articles.excerpt: Westwood Collective will turn Old Hilliard's former Chase Bank building at 4056 East Main Street into Lira Italian Kitchen, with new apartments next door.
articles.body:
Hilliard developer Westwood Collective is converting the former Chase Bank building at 4056 East Main Street into Lira Italian Kitchen, a full-service restaurant from the owners of Clocktower Kitchen and Bar, with a new mixed-use building planned next door that will add ground-floor retail and luxury apartments above.

## A Historic Bank Building Gets New Life

Hilliard's Downtown Manager, Angela Zody, and Westwood Collective founder Andy Warnock announced the project through the City of Hilliard on June 5, 2026. The plan keeps the original Chase Bank building intact, repurposing its old vault as a wine cellar for the new restaurant, according to [the City of Hilliard](https://hilliardohio.gov/new-dining-retail-development-planned-for-downtown-hilliard/). Preserving the building's brick facade and teller-era details, rather than demolishing it, was part of what drew the developer to the site in the first place.

## Who Is Behind the New Restaurant

The restaurant is a project of Around the Clock Hospitality, the group behind Clocktower Kitchen and Bar in Plain City, according to [614NOW](https://614now.com/2026/food-drink/owners-of-the-clocktower-restaurant-bringing-new-italian-eatery-to-historic-bank-building). Owners Benjamyn Greig, Jenna Fisher, Shane Whitacre and Chelsea Whitacre are planning a menu built around handmade pasta and wood-fired dishes, along with European wines and craft cocktails served from the old vault. "Our goal is Lira to feel like the kind of restaurant that becomes part of the neighborhood," said Greig, one of the owners.

## New Apartments Planned Next Door

Westwood Collective also plans a new mixed-use building on the site's adjoining parking lot, with ground-floor dining and retail space and a limited number of luxury apartments above, according to [WhatNow](https://whatnow.com/columbus/restaurants/lira-italian-kitchen-set-to-fill-a-former-chase-bank-building-in-downtown-hilliard/). The project is expected to increase parking capacity compared with the current lot, addressing a common complaint about Old Hilliard's compact Main Street district.

## When Lira Could Open

WhatNow reports an opening target of 2028, though the City of Hilliard says exact timelines will be announced as plans move forward. Westwood Collective has led several other projects in Hilliard, plus developments in London and Plain City, Ohio, according to WhatNow, giving the firm a track record other Main Street property owners can point to when weighing their own renovation plans.

## Why Old Hilliard Keeps Its Landmarks

Downtown Manager Angela Zody called the project "a tremendous investment in the future of Downtown Hilliard," according to the City of Hilliard. The redevelopment follows a broader pattern in Old Hilliard, where developers have reused historic Main Street buildings rather than replacing them, betting that shoppers and diners are drawn to storefronts with visible history rather than new construction.

## What It Means for the District

Adding housing above ground-floor retail is also a small step toward the kind of walkable density that Central Ohio suburbs have been slower to build than the urban core. A restaurant that reuses a landmark, paired with new apartments next door, gives Old Hilliard both a dining draw and a few more residents within walking distance of it.

For more on Hilliard's ongoing redevelopment, see CREN's coverage of [Hilliard real estate](/areas/hilliard) and [Central Ohio dining and lifestyle news](/topics/events-lifestyle).

articles.title: Grove City, Columbus Add 240 Affordable Assisted Living Units
articles.excerpt: Evergreen Real Estate Group broke ground on 240 units of affordable senior housing in Grove City and Columbus, funded by $74 million in OHFA-approved bonds.
articles.body:
Chicago-based Evergreen Real Estate Group announced on August 27 that it broke ground on two affordable assisted living communities in the Columbus area — Green Oaks of Grove City and Green Oaks of Walnut Creek — each adding 120 units for seniors, including those eligible for Medicaid, with completion expected in fall or winter 2027.

## Where the Two Communities Are Rising

Green Oaks of Grove City sits at 3000 Holt Road, about 10 miles south of downtown Columbus. Green Oaks of Walnut Creek is planned for 4000 Westerville Road on Columbus's northeast side. Each building will hold 67 studio apartments and 53 one-bedroom apartments, for 120 units per site, according to [Fox 28 Columbus](https://myfox28columbus.com/news/local/3-new-affordable-assisted-living-communities-under-construction-in-ohio-chicago-based-evergreen-real-estate-group-grove-city-westerville-road-fairborn-dayton-medicaid-apartments-eldery-senior-citizens).

## What OHFA Approved in March

The Ohio Housing Finance Agency's board approved financing for both projects on March 19, 2026, according to [OHFA's own announcement](https://ohiohome.org/news/releases/2026/march-fundedprojects.aspx). For Grove City, the agency authorized the developer to issue up to $35 million in Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds. For Walnut Creek, it authorized up to $39 million in bonds. Both developments also received a 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit reservation, a federal subsidy that lets developers charge rents below what the local market would otherwise support.

## Who Will Live There

The apartments are reserved for seniors across a range of incomes, including residents who qualify for Medicaid, Fox 28 Columbus reported. Gardant Management Solutions, Evergreen's operating partner, will run both communities once they open. "Expanding senior living options in these areas of Ohio will have a positive and lasting impact both today and well into the future," said Steve Rappin, Evergreen's chief executive.

## Not Evergreen's First Central Ohio Project

Evergreen already has one assisted living community under construction in the region: Green Oaks of Canal Winchester, a 120-unit building at 3631 Gender Road that broke ground earlier this year, according to [REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/evergreen-real-estate-group-breaks-ground-on-120-unit-affordable-assisted-living-community-near-columbus/). That project is expected to open in March 2027, with Gardant also set to operate it.

## Inside the Walnut Creek Building

Plans for Green Oaks of Walnut Creek call for a four-story, 92,279-square-foot building, with a construction contract valued at $22 million, according to [The Douglas Company](https://www.douglascompany.com/green-oaks-of-walnut-creek/), the Holland, Ohio-based contractor building it. The design includes a dining room, a fitness room, a salon, and outdoor patios meant for residents who need daily help but not full nursing care.

For more on Franklin County development activity, see CREN's coverage of [Columbus development news](/topics/development) and [Grove City real estate](/areas/grove-city).

articles.title: Northwest Bank Plans New Dublin Headquarters at Bridge North
articles.excerpt: Dublin City Council approved incentives for Northwest Bank's new 75,000-square-foot Bridge North headquarters, targeting a 2029 move and 300 jobs by 2034.
articles.body:
Northwest Bank will build a new Dublin headquarters at Bridge North, moving out of its Easton-area offices into a 75,000-square-foot building by the first half of 2029. Dublin City Council approved economic incentives for the project on August 24, 2026.

## A New Anchor For Bridge North

The project sits inside Bridge North, a mixed-use development from Daimler Group and Indus Hotels in Dublin's Bridge Street District, according to [Dublin's city council announcement](https://dublinohiousa.gov/city-news/city-council-approves-economic-development-agreement-to-bring-northwest-bank-headquarters-to-dublins-bridge-street-district/). Moody Nolan, a Columbus-based architecture firm, is designing the office, and JLL is handling brokerage and project management, according to [Connect CRE](https://www.connectcre.com/stories/northwest-bank-to-open-75k-sf-corporate-headquarters-in-ohio/).

Bridge North already had a residential and hotel component in the pipeline before this office commitment became public; CREN covered [Dublin's approval of that plan](/blog/dublin-approves-bridge-north-296-homes-a-hotel-and-offices-near-bridge-park) in July. The bank's office lease fills in the commercial half of the same site.

## Council Ties Incentives To New Jobs

Dublin's economic development agreement does not pay out incentives upfront. Northwest Bank can earn a performance-based grant equal to 15% of new employee payroll withholding taxes generated from 2030 through 2034, capped at $460,000, according to the city's announcement. It can also receive a separate $50,000 grant once it signs the lease and obtains an occupancy permit.

That structure means Dublin only pays if the bank actually adds local payroll and completes the building, rather than committing money against a project that could still change.

## The Timeline: 2029 Move, 2034 Workforce Target

Northwest Bank expects to move into the new building in the first half of 2029 under an initial 15-year lease, according to Connect CRE. The bank's headquarters workforce is expected to more than double to 300 employees by 2034, according to Connect CRE and Dublin's announcement.

"This investment represents an important step in Northwest Bank's continued growth and transformation," said Louis J. Torchio, the bank's president and CEO, in the city's announcement.

## What The Space Says About Office Demand

Dividing the building's 75,000 square feet by the bank's 300-employee target works out to about 250 square feet per worker once the headquarters reaches full staffing. That is a denser build-to-suit than many downtown Columbus Class A towers, which is consistent with a suburban headquarters designed around collaborative space rather than a traditional floor plan.

The move adds a financial-services anchor tenant to Dublin's office market at a time when the [Bridge Street District](/areas/dublin) is still filling out its commercial mix alongside Bridge Park's residential and hospitality growth. Building permits, an occupancy certificate and Northwest Bank's actual move-in date will be the next verifiable checkpoints.

articles.title: Upper Arlington's Shops on Lane Avenue Splits Old Anchor Into Three Tenants
articles.excerpt: Upper Arlington's Shops on Lane Avenue is carving its former Bed Bath & Beyond box into three tenants while separately adding Anthropologie and CAVA.
articles.body:
The Shops on Lane Avenue in Upper Arlington is subdividing its former Bed Bath and Beyond space among three new tenants, Solidcore, Piccolo Buco and Pause, while separately adding Anthropologie, CAVA, goGLOW and a Weddings boutique, according to the property's own site and multiple retail-press reports published this month.

## A Landlord's Own Site Confirms Four Names

[The shopping center's own site](https://www.shopsonlaneavenue.com/), at West Lane Avenue and Beaumont Road and managed by an affiliate of Kimco Realty, lists Anthropologie, CAVA, goGLOW and Pause as "coming soon" on its store directory. The same page shows Warby Parker as already open. Anthropologie's own listing gives a specific suite, 1705 West Lane Avenue, Suite D7, in Upper Arlington.

That address detail matters because it comes from the landlord's own directory, not a secondhand account of an announcement. [WhatNow Columbus reported](https://whatnow.com/columbus/retail/anthropologie-bringing-new-store-to-upper-arlington/) on August 25, 2026, that the coming Anthropologie will span about 9,000 square feet and is expected to open in late spring 2027, combining the retailer's standard apparel and home-goods lines with Anthropologie Weddings, its bridal division that sells gowns, bridesmaid dresses and wedding decor.

## The Old Anchor Box Splits Three Ways

Separately, [WhatNow Columbus reported](https://whatnow.com/columbus/retail/solidcore-expands-to-upper-arlington-with-new-fitness-studio/) on August 27, 2026, that the boutique fitness chain Solidcore will occupy space inside the shopping center's former Bed Bath and Beyond box at 1675 West Lane Avenue, the same address where Piccolo Buco and the wellness center Pause are also opening. That means one vacated big-box anchor is being carved into at least three smaller storefronts instead of being re-let to a single retailer, a shift the Colliers Columbus [weekly commercial real estate review](https://www.yourresearchresource.com/post/the-weekly-review-august-28-2026) also flagged on August 28, 2026, describing renovations underway at a former anchor location being subdivided for new occupants.

No single source lays out that full three-way split. Combining the landlord's own listings with two separate retail-press stories and the Colliers review is what shows the pattern.

## Cooper's Hawk Brings a Rome Original to Ohio

The most distinctive of the new tenants is Piccolo Buco, a Neapolitan-style pizza concept that [WhatNow Columbus reported](https://whatnow.com/columbus/restaurants/piccolo-buco-by-coopers-hawk-to-make-ohio-debut-in-upper-arlington/) on July 23, 2026, will make its Ohio debut at the Upper Arlington plaza. The original Piccolo Buco opened in Rome in 1916. Cooper's Hawk Winery and Restaurants founder Tim McEnery visited that Rome location in 2019, then partnered with owner Luca Issa to bring the concept to the United States, and Upper Arlington would be its first location outside the Chicago area and Florida. WhatNow Columbus did not report a firm opening date, saying construction work was still ongoing at the site.

## What the Center Already Delivered

The shopping center's own directory lists Warby Parker as open now, alongside longer-standing tenants that are not part of this leasing wave. [The property's own site](https://www.shopsonlaneavenue.com/) describes the center as offering "the perfect balance of neighborhood feel and downtown appeal," positioning it as a mixed shopping and dining destination near Grandview Heights.

## What CREN Could Not Confirm

Neither the landlord's site nor any of the retail-press reports named a total redevelopment cost or how much retail square footage in total is changing hands across the five incoming tenants. WhatNow Columbus said Anthropologie did not respond to its requests for comment on opening details, and it reported the same about Solidcore. CREN could not independently verify a lease-signing date for any of the five incoming tenants beyond what each outlet or the property's own site disclosed.

## What to Watch Next

The clearest next checkpoint is Anthropologie's stated late-spring 2027 opening, since its size and address are already confirmed on the landlord's own directory. Whether Solidcore, Piccolo Buco and Pause open on a similar timeline, and whether the old anchor box's renovation stays on the schedule Colliers described, will show whether this becomes a full repositioning of the center or a slower, tenant-by-tenant fill-in. For more on how Franklin County retail corridors are being reused, CREN is tracking related [development](/topics/development) coverage, and readers can follow other [Upper Arlington](/areas/upper-arlington) stories as they publish.

articles.title: Columbus Rental Due Diligence Starts Before The Tour
articles.excerpt: Use Columbus rental due diligence before paying fees or signing a lease by checking ownership, code context, lease terms, campus rules, and maintenance.
articles.body:
Columbus rental due diligence should begin before a renter pays a fee, tours from photos, or signs a lease. The useful consumer checklist connects owner verification, code context, written terms, maintenance questions, and campus-area resources without turning public records into legal advice.

## Start With Who Controls The Unit

A renter should confirm that the person collecting money is the owner, the manager, or another authorized representative. That step matters because screenshots, portal listings, and payment requests can circulate separately from the actual owner record.

The [Franklin County property page](https://www.franklincountyohio.gov/Resident-Services/Property) gives residents a starting point for property, auditor, recorder, and tax resources. Those tools can help a renter compare the address and owner context with the name on the listing or lease materials.

This is not a claim that every mismatch is fraud. It is a practical way to slow down before sending money, especially when a listing asks for a fast deposit, an unusual payment method, or a decision before written terms are available.

## Public Records Are A Prompt, Not A Verdict

The [City of Columbus Code Enforcement page](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Building-Zoning-Services/Code-Enforcement) says code enforcement officers enforce housing, zoning, nuisance, health, sanitation, safety, and graphics codes. It also points users toward request, report, portal, and frequently asked question paths.

A code record should be handled carefully. It can raise a question about condition, timing, or management response, but it does not by itself prove what a renter will experience in a specific unit.

The stronger checklist asks the renter to document the tour, ask about maintenance response, compare recurring review patterns, and save written answers. That keeps the article useful without making unsupported allegations about a landlord or building.

## Ohio Law Sets A Baseline For Questions

The [Ohio landlord-obligation statute](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5321.04) says a landlord must comply with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes that materially affect health and safety. It also says a landlord must make repairs that are reasonably necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable.

The [Ohio tenant-remedy statute](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5321.07) describes written notice to the landlord and several possible court paths for qualifying tenants. The same remedies page says that section does not apply to a dwelling unit occupied by a student tenant.

Those sources are a starting point for consumer questions, not a substitute for a lawyer. A renter with a live dispute should get advice from a qualified source before withholding rent, ending a lease, or relying on a court process.

## Campus Renters Need A Separate Path

The [Ohio State Off-Campus Housing Network](https://offcampus.osu.edu/) is maintained for off-campus and commuter student engagement. Campus-area renters and parents often need a more specific checklist because lease timing, roommate rules, guarantors, packages, parking, utilities, and emergency maintenance can matter as much as advertised rent.

That is why CREN's OSU-area content should connect the rental checklist to area pages, not bury it in a generic apartment article. The campus version should separate legal questions, safety questions, daily routine, and payment obligations so students and parents can see what still needs verification.

The next checkpoint is to refresh the checklist when city record paths, Ohio tenant resources, or campus housing guidance changes, and to keep allegations out of the copy unless they are backed by records and fair response handling.

articles.title: Columbus Buyer Price Bands Need Monthly-Cost Checks
articles.excerpt: Use Columbus buyer price bands as a due-diligence tool, not a promise of available homes, by checking payment, records, permits, and substitutes.
articles.body:
Columbus buyer price bands are useful only when they are tied to payment, property records, permits, condition, and nearby substitutes. The safer CREN framing is to show buyers what to verify before touring, not to imply that a budget guarantees access to a neighborhood.

## Why The Band Is Only A Starting Point

A list price is a search filter, not the full housing decision. The same budget can describe a smaller renovated home, a larger property with repair exposure, a condo with association dues, or a location tradeoff that changes the daily routine.

[Columbus REALTORS Housing Reports](https://columbusrealtors.com/housing-reports) publishes monthly residential statistics with regional, county, city, and school-district report paths. That makes the reports useful for market direction, but a buyer still needs address-level checks before treating a band as realistic.

The better consumer product is not a generic affordability table. It is a pressure test: payment fit, cash to close, taxes, insurance, condition, permits, commute, school-context checks, and the closest substitute areas.

## Payment Comes Before The Search Map

The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Loan Estimate Explainer](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/loan-estimate/) tells borrowers to compare the form with the loan terms they discussed with the lender. It also points buyers to the estimated monthly payment, closing costs, cash to close, and escrow or insurance items.

That is why CREN should keep the buyer page focused on monthly cost before neighborhood preference. A home can appear to fit a list-price range and still fail the buyer's budget once taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance, association dues, repairs, or closing costs are included.

A useful page should make room for uncertainty. Rates, inventory, lender terms, property condition, and seller concessions can change the real answer. The page should push readers to verify the current deal structure rather than treating any band as fixed guidance.

## Records Change The Meaning Of A Listing

The [Franklin County property page](https://www.franklincountyohio.gov/Resident-Services/Property) routes residents to property, auditor, recorder, and tax resources. Those records can help a buyer compare parcel details, tax context, transfer history, and other public information before relying on listing copy.

The [City of Columbus permit page](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Get-a-Permit/Get-or-Track-a-Building-Permit?oc_lang=en-US) says the permitting process begins with an application and any plans required for review. It also says that after a record is created, application status can be tracked through the Citizen Access Portal.

Those checks do not replace inspection or professional advice. They help a buyer ask sharper questions when a listing claims major updates, converted space, additions, or recent work.

## Substitutes Are Part Of The Product

A buyer who cannot make one area work still may have a workable Columbus-area search. German Village might lead to Merion Village or the Brewery District. Dublin might lead to Hilliard, Worthington, or Westerville. A starter-home search might compare Grove City, Whitehall, Hilltop, and South Linden.

Those comparisons should not be framed as rankings. They should answer a practical consumer question: what changes when the buyer protects the payment, changes the commute, accepts an older home, or shifts the daily-life routine.

The next checkpoint is a monthly refresh tied to the latest regional housing report, current payment inputs, and spot checks that show whether the listed bands still describe realistic buyer tradeoffs.

articles.title: Dublin Ohio Christmas Market Opens Nov. 21 at Riverside Crossing Park
articles.excerpt: Dublin's free Christkindlmarkt runs Nov. 21 to Dec. 24 at Riverside Crossing Park, but the operator's name has already shifted between city announcements.
articles.body:
Dublin's Christkindlmarkt will run November 21 through December 24, 2026, at Riverside Crossing Park, the City of Dublin announced August 28. The free, German-inspired holiday market is operated by Christkindlmarkt Dublin LLC, led by CEO Maria Adele Rosenfeld, under an agreement Dublin City Council approved in November 2025.

## A Free Holiday Market at Riverside Crossing Park

The market will occupy Riverside Crossing Park at the base of the Dublin Link pedestrian bridge in Downtown Dublin, according to a [City of Dublin news release](https://dublinohiousa.gov/city-news/christkindlmarkt-dublin-to-launch-european-style-holiday-market-in-central-ohio/). Admission is free, and the market will run Wednesdays and Thursdays from 4 to 9 p.m., Fridays and Saturdays from noon to 9 p.m., and Sundays from noon to 8 p.m., closing Mondays and Tuesdays for most of the season.

## How Dublin Selected an Operator

Dublin City Council approved an agreement on November 19, 2025, to move the project forward after a feasibility study the city began in 2022, according to a [separate City of Dublin release](https://dublinohiousa.gov/city-news/city-council-advances-plan-for-european-style-market-in-dublin/). The city selected Maria Adele Rosenfeld, the former CEO of Carmel, Indiana's Christkindlmarkt, to lead the Dublin operation.

## A Detail That Changed Between Announcements

Dublin's November 2025 release named the operating company Christkindlmarkt Consulting LLC. The city's August 28, 2026, announcement instead credits a different corporate name for the same market, without explaining the change; both releases identify Rosenfeld as the person running it. Readers checking the market's own marketing should expect either name to show up on signage, invoices or vendor contracts.

## What Dublin Hasn't Said Yet

Neither city release nor [Columbus Navigator's write-up](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/dublin-christmas-market-2026/) specifies how many vendor chalets will open for the first season, and the city has not published a public budget or lease terms for the operator. Columbus Navigator reported the market plans limited-edition annual Glühwein mugs, a tradition borrowed from Rosenfeld's Carmel market. Shoppers weighing a trip should treat the chalet count and any vendor list as unconfirmed until Dublin or the operator publishes one, rather than assuming the market will match the scale of larger Midwest Christkindlmarkts.

## Why It's Landing Next to Bridge Park

Riverside Crossing Park sits inside the [Bridge Park entertainment district](/blog/2026-08-14-dublin-s-bridge-park-breaks-ground-on-89-condos-starting-at-400k) CREN has covered as it fills in with apartments, restaurants and shops, giving holiday visitors a reason to linger beyond the market itself. The market's run from November 21 through December 24 overlaps with the length of Dublin's shopping season at Bridge Park and Historic Dublin.

articles.title: Columbus State Breaks Ground on 166-Unit Housing in Discovery District
articles.excerpt: Columbus State and Woda Cooper broke ground on Opportunity Pointe, a 186-unit affordable housing project set to open in the Discovery District by 2027.
articles.body:
Columbus State Community College and Woda Cooper Companies broke ground August 25 on Opportunity Pointe, a 186-unit affordable and student housing project planned for a downtown Discovery District block. The development combines 166 income-restricted apartments with 20 units reserved for Columbus State students, with completion expected by the end of 2027.

## A Groundbreaking a Year Behind Schedule

Columbus State said in a May 2025 news release that construction on the project would begin in the second quarter of 2026. The actual groundbreaking came nearly a full quarter later, on Aug. 25, 2026, when [WSYX reported](https://myfox28columbus.com/news/local/columbus-state-woda-cooper-breaks-ground-on-51m-opportunity-pointe-with-166-affordable-units-downtown-discovery-district-housing-project) that city and college leaders gathered on site to mark the start of construction.

## What's Planned for the Discovery District Block

The project will fill a block bordered by Cleveland Avenue, North Grant Avenue, East Spring Street and East Long Street, according to [Columbus State](https://www.cscc.edu/about/news/2025/OpportunityPointeMay2025.shtml). Of the 186 planned units, 166 will be income-restricted workforce apartments and 20 will be set aside for Columbus State students, the same figures the college published when state tax credits were approved in 2025. The Discovery District takes its name from the cluster of Columbus State, Columbus College of Art & Design and other institutions east of Downtown, an area the city has targeted for infill housing for years.

## The Tax Credits Behind the Project

The Ohio Housing Finance Agency awarded Woda Cooper 9% federal low-income housing tax credits for each of the project's two construction phases on May 21, 2025, Columbus State said. That 9% credit is the federal program's largest annual subsidy, meant to cover most of a project's construction cost in exchange for keeping rents income-restricted for decades. Developer Jeffrey J. Woda said at the time, "We are excited to build Opportunity Pointe I and II, which will provide 166 much-needed affordable housing units."

## Rent Estimates Have Shifted Since 2025

When the tax credits were announced in 2025, Columbus State published planned rents of $365 to $995 for one-bedroom units, $410 to $1,175 for two-bedroom units and $440 to $1,295 for three-bedroom units, varying by tenant income. WSYX reported a different range at the Aug. 25 groundbreaking, describing rents of $480 to $1,400 across the project without breaking them out by unit size.

Neither outlet said what changed between the two estimates, so renters should treat the newer figures as the more current word until Woda Cooper publishes a formal rent schedule. Community land trust and income-restricted developments elsewhere in Columbus have seen similar gaps between early cost estimates and figures released at groundbreaking, underscoring why renters should wait for a signed lease before budgeting around either number.

## What's Next

Columbus State and Woda Cooper expect the project to open by the end of 2027, matching the timeline the college gave in 2025. It adds to a wave of downtown housing construction that has included the [Discovery District mixed-use conversion](/blog/2026-07-09-columbus-discovery-district-deal-turns-downtown-parking-lots-into-518-apartments) CREN reported in July, as developers keep reusing downtown surface lots and vacant office buildings for housing rather than building on greenfield sites. CREN will track whether the finished building matches the unit mix and rent figures Columbus State has published so far once leasing begins.

articles.title: Downtown Columbus's Preston Park Still Isn't Open, Developer Says
articles.excerpt: Edwards Companies promised Downtown Columbus's Preston Park would open to the public by October 2025. Ten months later, the gate still needs a key card.
articles.body:
Edwards Companies' Preston Park, an elevated public walkway planned above Fourth Street in Downtown Columbus, was supposed to open to the public in October 2025, [Columbus Underground reported](https://columbusunderground.com/promised-public-greenspace-still-not-open-to-the-public-bw1/). Ten months later, the walkway remains locked behind a key-card gate while an extension to Third Street is still under construction.

## What the Project Was Supposed to Be

The project reuses an enclosed skywalk built in the 1970s that spans Fourth Street, connecting two Edwards Companies properties on East Broad Street: the Pembroke at 195 East Broad Street and Preston Centre, the former PNC Tower, at 155 East Broad Street. [KEPHART](https://kephart.com/the-pembroke-a-journey-of-historic-preservation/), the architecture firm that worked on the Pembroke with Edwards Urban, describes the plan as removing the walkway's roof and glass walls and adding landscaping to create an open-air greenspace, with a further extension planned to Third Street. Columbus Underground has described the finished concept as similar in spirit to New York City's High Line, an elevated park built on a disused rail line.

## The Third Street Extension Isn't Finished

Columbus Underground reported that work continued through the summer of 2026 on extending the walkway to South Third Street, where a stairway and elevator are being built to serve as the project's main public entrance. Pedestrians who try to walk the existing pathway are met by a gate that requires a key card, according to that reporting. An Edwards Companies spokesperson told Columbus Underground, "We anticipate the elevated walkway to be open this fall," but declined to explain the delay. The spokesperson said the walkway would be open to the public daily from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. once it opens.

## Two Buildings That Already Opened

The buildings the project is meant to connect are both further along than the walkway itself. KEPHART's own account of the Pembroke, published June 24, 2025, says leasing was already underway there with final construction details wrapping up. [Preston Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Centre) has an even longer track record: Edwards Companies acquired the 27-story former PNC Bank Building in February 2024 and converted it into 105 residential apartments that year, according to Wikipedia's sourced entry on the building. Both private components of the project were delivered and generating rent well before the shared public amenity meant to link them.

## The Math on the Delay

If the park's public opening was originally promised for October 2025, as Columbus Underground reported, then as of August 27, 2026, roughly ten months have passed since that date without public access. Edwards Companies' new target of "this fall" would put the opening close to the one-year mark past the original promise.

## What CREN Could Not Confirm

CREN could not independently confirm the Downtown Commission's original review timeline for this concept; public references to that history vary across outlets, and Edwards Companies did not explain the reason for the delay. This account is limited to the walkway's current public-access status and the developer's stated timeline, not the full project history.

## What to Watch Next

The next verifiable checkpoint is whether the Third Street stairway and elevator are finished and whether Edwards Companies opens the walkway on its stated 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily schedule before the end of fall 2026. Until then, Preston Park remains a private amenity for tenants of the Pembroke and Preston Centre rather than the public greenspace it was promised to be. For more on how [Downtown Columbus](/areas/downtown-columbus) development projects have delivered on their public commitments, CREN is tracking related [development](/topics/development) coverage.
