articles.title: Sugar Opens Aug. 27 at 504 Park St. in Columbus Arena District
articles.excerpt: One Hospitality opens the Sugar restaurant at 504 Park St. on Aug. 27 — Latin-Mediterranean dining with a ticketed Grand Opening Party from 5 to 11 p.m.
articles.body:
One Hospitality opens Sugar, a Latin, Spanish, and Mediterranean restaurant, at 504 Park St. in Columbus on August 27, taking over a former Park Street bar space. The group behind Forno Kitchen + Bar, Astra Rooftop, and Standard Hall will host a ticketed Grand Opening Party from 5 to 11 p.m.

## A Park Street Name Returns

[Sugar](https://sugarcolumbus.com/) draws its name from a piece of the block's own history. Sugar Bar — a dance club that operated at 525 N. Park St. from 2005 to 2010 — was a fixture for that stretch of downtown nightlife before closing. One Hospitality revives the name on the same street, this time as a full-service restaurant at a different address and in a substantially different format: plated food, a full bar, and an outdoor patio rather than a cover-charge dance floor.

The 504 Park St. space was previously occupied by Howl at the Moon, the piano-dueling bar chain. [614NOW reported the reactivation](https://614now.com/2026/food-drink/former-nightlife-space-reintroduced-as-neighborhood-restaurant-concept-by-one-hospitality) of the address as a conversion from chain nightlife to a locally operated restaurant concept — a pattern that has played out at several similar Columbus venues over the past five years.

## Two Floors, an Outdoor Patio, and a Latin Kitchen

The interior spans two floors connected by a custom staircase, surrounded by custom-drawn wallpaper and lush greenery that leads to the outdoor patio. The patio features cabanas, fire pits, lounge seating, and photo booths.

[NBC4 first reported the concept details](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/owners-of-forno-astra-rooftop-opening-mediterranean-restaurant-on-park-street/amp/) when One Hospitality announced the opening. The menu centers on Latin American, Spanish, and Mediterranean flavors. Signature dishes include chipotle chicken tacos, pan-seared salmon, blackened garlic shrimp pasta, and cheese quesadillas. The cocktail program emphasizes agave spirits — tequila and mezcal-forward drinks.

One Hospitality, led by Chris Corso, already operates Forno Kitchen + Bar, Astra Rooftop, and Standard Hall. Sugar is the group's fourth active Columbus concept and its first with a full outdoor patio of this scale. The Park Street address puts it adjacent to Standard Hall, extending the group's footprint on the block.

## What Changes at 504 Park St.

The Howl at the Moon format relied on event-driven traffic — convention attendees, bachelorette parties, and the Nationwide Arena crowd. [Columbus Underground noted](https://columbusunderground.com/latin-and-mediterranean-restaurant-coming-to-park-street-ak1/) that Sugar introduces a neighborhood restaurant concept in its place: a format that can draw on foot traffic from the Scioto Mile, downtown office workers, and the growing residential population in and around the Arena District independently of arena event nights.

For the Park Street District, filling that address with a locally operated two-floor venue matters commercially. The block already anchors Nationwide Arena foot traffic. A permanent food-and-beverage destination with daytime and patio capacity adds a layer of activity that the prior concept didn't provide.

One limitation worth naming: Sugar has not yet opened. Review coverage and the sustained draw for a new concept in this location will determine whether the space translates from opening-party buzz to a reliable neighborhood stop.

## Grand Opening Party: August 27, 5 to 11 p.m.

One Hospitality will host a ticketed Grand Opening Party at Sugar on Thursday, August 27, from 5 to 11 p.m. The event transforms Park Street into a street party featuring live DJ sets, street food from local vendors, signature cocktails, light bites, and expanded outdoor seating with fire pits and cabanas activated.

Ticket and reservation information is at [sugarcolumbus.com](https://sugarcolumbus.com/). Feedback on the mixed-use corridor zoning that surrounds the Park Street District is open through October 24 at [columbus.gov/zoningupdate](https://www.columbus.gov/zoningupdate) as part of the Zone In Phase 2 public comment period, which opened August 25.

articles.title: Columbus July Home Sales Climb 6% as Inventory Hits Decade High
articles.excerpt: Columbus REALTORS: Central Ohio July sales up 6.3% to 3,083; median $350K (+2.3%); 6,193 listings — highest July inventory in more than 10 years.
articles.body:
Central Ohio logged 3,083 closed home sales in July 2026 — up 6.3% year over year — alongside a median price of $350,000 (+2.3%) and a July active listing count of 6,193, the highest in more than a decade. The 2.4-month supply still favors sellers even as inventory growth signals a market inching toward balance.

## July by the Numbers

[Columbus REALTORS](https://columbusrealtors.com/housing-reports) released the July 2026 Central Ohio housing report on August 12, covering single-family homes and condominiums across the metro. Closed sales came in at 3,083, a gain of 6.3% compared with July 2025. The median sale price landed at $350,000, up 2.3% from one year earlier. Year-to-date through July, closed sales are running 3.0% ahead of 2025, and the median price is up 4.4% for the year.

The inventory figure is the number that stands out. At 6,193 active listings, the metro recorded the highest July count in more than a decade, according to Columbus REALTORS. [The Columbus Team's monthly analysis of the July report](https://thecolumbusteam.com/central-ohio-housing-report/) places the year-over-year inventory growth at roughly 7% — a meaningful build in a market that spent most of the past five years in acute shortage.

## What Decade-High Inventory Actually Means

A decade-high July inventory figure sounds dramatic, but context matters. The 2.4-month supply — the number of months it would take to sell all current listings at July's pace of sales — remains well below the five to six months that housing economists generally use as the threshold for a balanced market. Buyers have more homes to choose from than in several years, but sellers are not facing anything resembling a buyers' market.

For scale: at the height of the pandemic-era shortage in 2021 and 2022, supply in Central Ohio regularly dropped below one month. The "decade-high" label reflects how compressed that comparison baseline was. The current build is meaningful — it represents real choices for buyers — but the market has not swung to the opposite extreme.

For property managers and multifamily operators, a 2.4-month for-sale supply implies the rent-versus-own calculation still tilts toward renting for many households. A $350,000 home purchased at the current 30-year mortgage rate requires roughly $2,300 per month in principal and interest with a standard 20% down payment — above what median rents command in most Columbus submarkets, which continues to support rental demand.

## Rising Sales and Rising Prices in the Same Month as Peak Inventory

The more analytically interesting combination is this: sales volume and prices both rose in July while inventory also rose. In a simplified supply-demand model, additional supply should dampen price pressure. The July data suggests that Central Ohio's underlying demand is absorbing the new supply without forcing concessions from sellers.

The Columbus REALTORS report characterized the month as reflecting "a healthy and active Central Ohio housing market, with sales increasing, prices appreciating, and inventory continuing to build." The consistent YTD median price gain of 4.4% — spread across seven months — supports the view that appreciation has been steady rather than concentrated in a single quarter.

One limitation worth naming: the Columbus REALTORS report covers the full metro (Franklin County and surrounding counties), meaning aggregate figures can obscure meaningful variation by price tier and submarket. A metro-wide median of $350,000 can coexist with softer conditions at the upper end and firm competition in entry-level brackets below $300,000, where inventory tends to be thinnest relative to demand.

## Mortgage Rates and What Buyers Are Actually Facing

For buyers weighing a purchase, the mortgage rate sets the affordability ceiling. [Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms) placed the 30-year fixed-rate average at 6.69% on August 6, moving to 6.67% on August 13 and 6.65% on August 20 — the most recent reads. ([GlobeNewswire, August 13, 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/08/13/3344775/0/en/mortgage-rates-average-6-67.html))

At 6.65%–6.69%, rates are approximately 0.1 percentage points above where they stood one year earlier, when the 30-year averaged approximately 6.58%. That marginal increase has not meaningfully shifted affordability in either direction. For buyers, the more consequential change is the inventory gain — the expanded selection of homes now on the market, not a rate swing, is what has made 2026 easier to navigate than 2023 or 2024 for households ready to purchase.

## What to Watch

The Columbus REALTORS August housing report will release in mid-September. The data point worth tracking is whether the months-of-supply figure continues moving upward from 2.4. A move toward 3.0 months or higher would represent a meaningful shift in negotiating leverage without yet signaling a buyers' market. Watch new listings too — if sellers continue bringing homes to market at a rate that outpaces buyer absorption, the multi-month trend toward equilibrium would accelerate.

Columbus is also collecting public comment on the next phase of its Zone In rezoning — the draft commercial and industrial code covered in [CREN's Zone In explainer](/blog/columbus-zone-in-phase-2-commercial-industrial-rezoning) — at [columbus.gov/zoningupdate](https://www.columbus.gov/zoningupdate). If the new districts enable housing development at scale on mixed-use corridors and industrial land, any resulting supply additions would appear in permit data over the coming years and affect the existing-home market beyond the current planning horizon.

articles.title: Columbus Zone In Phase 2 Draft Releases — Public Comment Opens Aug. 25
articles.excerpt: Columbus Zone In Phase 2 draft released Aug. 20: nine districts across 40% of the city. Public comment opens Aug. 25 through Oct. 24 at columbus.gov/zoningupdate.
articles.body:
The City of Columbus released its Phase 2 Zone In zoning draft on August 20, 2026, proposing nine new districts across roughly 40 percent of the city. A 60-day public comment period opens August 25 and runs through October 24 at [columbus.gov/zoningupdate](https://www.columbus.gov/zoningupdate).

## What Phase 2 Covers — and What Phase 1 Did Not

Zone In is Columbus's effort to modernize a zoning code written more than 70 years ago. [Phase 1, which City Council passed in summer 2024](https://www.columbus.gov/News-articles/Columbus-Introduces-Zoning-Code-Proposal-Capable-of-Creating-88000-Housing-Units), focused on approximately 140 miles of high-traffic corridors — unlocking taller buildings along High Street, Broad Street, and other major arteries without the need for variance approvals.

The new draft covers three categories of land that Phase 1 left untouched: mixed-use corridors outside the Phase 1 boundary, industrial and warehouse districts, and business and institutional campuses — a category that includes hospitals, universities, and major employment centers such as Tuttle Mall and Polaris. Together, these areas represent a little over 40 percent of the city's parcels, according to the city's August 20 announcement.

For background on the broader Zone In initiative and its citywide capacity claims, see CRE News's earlier coverage: [Zone In Adds Capacity, Not 88,000 Built Columbus Homes](/blog/columbus-zone-in-reform-could-open-room-for-88-000-new-homes).

## Which Corridors and Districts Are Now in Scope

Several corridors not reached by the first phase are specifically named in the new draft. Among them: Summit Street and Fourth Street running north from Downtown, and Whittier Street and Thurman Avenue on the South Side — areas that carry a mix of older commercial buildings, legacy industrial zoning, and residential edges where development pressure has been growing.

The Northland corridor along State Route 161 and East Dublin Granville Road was addressed earlier through a corridor-specific Council action: 160 parcels in Northland near the Worthington border were designated community activity centers in a prior Council vote. That action is part of the broader Zone In framework now entering public review.

The industrial and warehouse category is significant for Columbus real estate operators. Close-in industrial land — areas that have attracted adaptive-reuse interest from developers in other markets — currently carries legacy zoning written before modern warehouse, last-mile logistics, and light-manufacturing uses existed. The proposal creates nine new district types designed to separate incompatible uses while creating clearer pathways for mixed-use and transit-adjacent development in these areas.

## What Zone In Phase 2 Means for Property Owners

Zoning determines what can be built on a parcel, at what height, and at what density. A rezoning under Zone In does not automatically approve any specific project; it changes the baseline entitlement a property carries going forward. For owners of land in the newly covered corridors and districts, the new zoning districts could reduce the cost and time required to win approval for certain building types — or change what a neighboring owner can legally build.

City planners project that the areas covered in this phase could accommodate roughly 13,000 new homes over 10 years, in addition to commercial and industrial development. That figure is a capacity estimate under the new rules, not a construction forecast — actual production depends on financing conditions, demand, and market timing.

The [Columbus.gov announcement](https://www.columbus.gov/News-articles/Columbus-Introduces-Zoning-Code-Proposal-Capable-of-Creating-88000-Housing-Units) states the overall Zone In initiative — spanning all three phases — is capable of enabling up to 88,000 new housing units city-wide. That is a long-run theoretical capacity figure, not a near-term pipeline or city spending commitment.

## How to Participate Before October 24

The public comment window is the formal period for property owners, businesses, neighborhood groups, and city boards and commissions to submit input on the draft. Residents can review the draft changes and submit comments through an online survey at [columbus.gov/zoningupdate](https://www.columbus.gov/zoningupdate), or in person at the Zone In Gallery. A series of public meetings is scheduled during the comment period; specific meeting dates and locations were not listed in search results available at publication time — check the city's website for the current schedule.

Coverage from [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/new-zoning-changes-covering-nearly-half-of-city-unveiled-bw1/) confirms the same closing date for the comment window.

## What Comes After the Comment Period

The new proposal is a draft, not adopted code. City Council must vote on the final proposal after the comment period closes. A vote timeline was not specified in the city's announcement.

Phase 3, the final stage of Zone In, will address the remaining roughly 50 percent of city parcels — primarily traditional single-family residential neighborhoods, where the focus will be on infill housing and housing variety. City planners have described this final stage as the most complex portion of the overhaul, because it involves changing what can be built on parcels currently zoned exclusively for detached single-family homes. No timeline for the next phase has been set pending this draft's outcome.

articles.title: The Fitzgerald Opens 226 Apartments on Bexley's Main Street
articles.excerpt: The Fitzgerald Bexley apartments opened Aug. 14 with 226 units on a former seminary site, plus 11,000 sq ft of retail and 12,500 sq ft of office space.
articles.body:
The Fitzgerald, a mixed-use building by Continental Development Ventures, opened August 14 at 2200 E. Main St. in Bexley, delivering 226 apartments on a roughly three-acre former Trinity Lutheran Seminary site, along with about 23,500 square feet of restaurant, retail, and office space and a 300-space structured parking garage.

## From seminary apartments to 226 homes

The three-acre site at 2200 E. Main St. had previously held apartment buildings associated with Trinity Lutheran Seminary. Continental Development Ventures, a Columbus-based firm, acquired the site and secured approvals from the City of Bexley, which maintains an [official project page](https://bexley.org/2200-main/) documenting the development.

The new building holds studio through three-bedroom apartments across its residential floors. Coastal Ridge Real Estate—a Columbus-founded company managing more than 43,000 apartment and student housing units nationally—handles leasing and day-to-day operations, according to the company's public profile. Regional Manager Brittany Neff represented Coastal Ridge at the August 14 ribbon-cutting in the building's main courtyard.

Listing databases show rental pricing starting around $1,432 for smaller units and ranging higher for three-bedroom layouts, per [Redfin](https://www.redfin.com/OH/Bexley/The-Fitzgerald-Bexley/apartment/201677674).

## What 23,500 square feet of commercial space might bring

The building's ground floor holds roughly 11,000 square feet of restaurant and retail space facing E. Main St. An additional 12,500 square feet of office space occupies upper commercial floors. No tenants for that commercial portion have been announced publicly as of this writing, per the [PR Newswire grand-opening release](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/the-fitzgerald-officially-opens-in-the-heart-of-bexley-302853105.html).

That 23,500 square feet is among the larger additions to Bexley's retail and office inventory in recent years. E. Main St. through downtown Bexley already hosts an established strip of locally owned restaurants, specialty retailers, and service businesses. New ground-floor space at this scale creates room for uses that haven't found a foothold there before—or for expansions by existing tenants.

## 300 parking spaces in a walkable neighborhood

The Fitzgerald sits steps from Capital University, a private liberal arts college on E. Main St. The campus generates steady pedestrian traffic on the corridor during the academic year.

The 300-space structured garage is notable for a location that is walkable by Bexley standards. That capacity likely reflects the combined load: retail customers, office tenants, and residents all drawing from the same structure. For the ground-floor commercial spaces, on-site parking removes a common friction point for businesses that depend on customer arrivals by car.

## What more residents mean for the neighborhood

Adding 226 households to a compact, walkable neighborhood changes the arithmetic for nearby businesses. More residents walking to dinner on E. Main St., or stopping for coffee on the way to work, matters more to a neighborhood-scale retail district than the same number of households scattered across a suburb.

Whether that materializes depends on who occupies the commercial floors. A full-service restaurant or daily-needs retailer would plug directly into Bexley's existing pattern. Office tenants add daytime activity without the same evening foot traffic.

The Fitzgerald is the latest addition to [Bexley's development pipeline](/areas/bexley), which has attracted Columbus-area developers looking for established neighborhoods with room to add density near transit and walkable amenities.

## Developer and manager

Continental Development Ventures is a Columbus-based firm. Coastal Ridge Real Estate, the building's manager, was founded in Columbus in 2013 and describes its current portfolio as more than $6.1 billion in assets and over 43,000 units nationally, according to Coastal Ridge's public company profile. The firm is headquartered in Columbus.

articles.title: 959,579-SF Spec Warehouse Breaks Ground in Columbus's Rickenbacker Area
articles.excerpt: A partnership broke ground on a 959,579-square-foot speculative warehouse in Columbus's Rickenbacker area, due in early 2027 with no tenant signed and a 15-year tax break.
articles.body:
A partnership led by Trident Capital Group broke ground on a 959,579-square-foot speculative warehouse at 1669 Rohr Road in Columbus's Rickenbacker industrial corridor. The building is due in early 2027, is being built without a signed tenant, and carries a 15-year, 75% property tax break.

## What speculative means here

Most large warehouses used to be built only after a company signed a lease. A speculative, or spec, building flips that order — construction starts first, and the owner looks for tenants while the walls go up.

That choice is a bet. It says the owners expect demand to be there by the time the building is done. The group behind it — Trident Capital Group, O'Connor Capital Partners, and Clarion Partners — is making that bet in the Rickenbacker submarket south of the city, as reported by [Connect CRE](https://www.connectcre.com/stories/960k-sf-speculative-industrial-development-in-columbus-breaks-ground/) and [REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/partnership-breaks-ground-on-959579-sf-spec-industrial-facility-in-columbus-ohio/).

## The building's specs

The warehouse sits on 57.3 acres, and it will have 40-foot clear ceiling heights, 104 dock doors, 238 trailer parking stalls, and 336 car parking spaces, [according to REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/partnership-breaks-ground-on-959579-sf-spec-industrial-facility-in-columbus-ohio/). Delivery is targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

Those figures describe a distribution building — the kind used to move goods in and out by truck rather than store them for long. The high ceilings and heavy dock count are built for volume. JLL's Dan Wendorf, Brian Marsh, and Joseph Davis are marketing the building for lease.

## A second big building in a growing park

This is the newest phase of the Rickenbacker Industrial Center, a master-planned park designed to reach about 3.67 million square feet across roughly 230 acres, [according to CBRE](https://www.cbre.com/press-releases/cbre-phase-i-construction-completed-on-rickenbacker-industrial-center-in-columbus-ohio).

The park's first phase — a warehouse of about 1.06 million square feet — was fully leased to ODW Logistics and later sold to the investment firm AEW, per CBRE and [REJournals](https://rejournals.com/first-phase-of-construction-wraps-on-1-06-million-square-foot-industrial-building-in-columbus/). That the owners moved on to another large building after leasing and selling the first is its own signal about how the corridor is filling.

The site has rail access and sits near Rickenbacker International Airport, the Norfolk Southern Rickenbacker intermodal terminal, and Interstate 270. That mix of air, rail, and highway is why the area south of Columbus has drawn so much [warehouse and logistics development](/topics/development) in recent years.

## The tax break, in plain terms

The project sits in a Qualified Opportunity Zone and carries a 15-year, 75% property tax abatement, [according to Connect CRE](https://www.connectcre.com/stories/960k-sf-speculative-industrial-development-in-columbus-breaks-ground/).

The details matter. An Opportunity Zone is a federal designation that gives investors tax advantages for putting money into areas the government has flagged. The abatement is a separate, local deal: it lets the owner skip most of the property tax on the building's added value for the length of the term. Local governments offer these deals to attract big projects and the jobs they bring.

The trade-off is less public tax revenue in the near term — a live debate across central Ohio as [industrial and data-center projects](/areas/columbus-citywide) stack up.

## What to watch next

The real test for a spec building is leasing. An empty warehouse of nearly a million square feet is a large amount of space to fill, and how fast it signs a tenant will say more about Rickenbacker demand than the groundbreaking does.

CREN has tracked the corridor's activity, including a separate [Rickenbacker building sale](/blog/2026-07-28-columbus-rickenbacker-industrial-building-sells-for-49-million-to-boyd-watterson) in July. The next checkpoints here are a lease announcement and a confirmed completion date.

articles.title: ALDI Plans a Downtown Columbus Grocery Store to Open in 2028
articles.excerpt: ALDI plans a 20,000-square-foot store on 1.7 acres at Cleveland Avenue and Spring Street next to Columbus State, with construction in 2027 and a 2028 opening.
articles.body:
ALDI plans a 20,000-square-foot grocery store on 1.7 acres at the northwest corner of Cleveland Avenue and Spring Street, next to Columbus State Community College's downtown campus. Construction is set to start in spring 2027 and the store is expected to open in 2028.

## A Vacant Corner Gets a Grocery Anchor

Columbus State [announced the deal on August 18, 2026](https://www.cscc.edu/about/news/2026/ALDI.shtml). Its real estate affiliate, Columbus State Community Partners, will prepare the site and lease it to ALDI, which will build and own the finished store. The college describes the 1.7-acre parcel as largely vacant, and the structures still standing on it come down first.

## Why a Community College Is the Landlord

Columbus State treats groceries as a student-retention question, not only a real estate deal. The college says affordable, fresh groceries have been a priority because food insecurity is one of the key non-academic barriers that can affect student success. President David T. Harrison said the college focuses on making resources easy to access because "our students lead complicated lives," and that a grocer next door "will expand food options for Columbus State students while strengthening the broader community," [614NOW reported](https://614now.com/2026/food-drink/discount-grocery-store-chain-lands-first-downtown-columbus-location). That is why the college's own real estate arm, rather than a private developer, is assembling and leasing the ground.

## What the County Calls a Food Desert

Franklin County Board of Commissioners President John O'Grady was blunt in the announcement: "Downtown Columbus has been a food desert for decades. Today, we're changing that." The college says the store will be the first new grocery store by a national retailer in this part of the city in decades. CREN could not check that against a retail-history record, so treat it as the college's characterization.

ALDI framed the news around price. Laura Bauer, a regional vice president for the chain, said shoppers "can look forward to a convenient, affordable way to stock up on everyday essentials." Mayor Andrew J. Ginther said the added access "will benefit all downtown residents, and especially help Columbus State students to thrive." None of those statements mentions opening dates, hiring, or prices at this store.

## What Public Money Is Paying For

Franklin County is committing $900,000 for predevelopment, utility, and infrastructure work, and the Central Ohio Community Improvement Corporation is adding $100,000 toward demolition, [as WSYX reported](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/aldi-to-build-downtown-columbus-store-opening-2028-grocery-produce-cleveland-ave-spring-street-college-campus-students-faculty-staff-residents). Those commitments cover getting the ground ready. The building itself is ALDI's expense, because ALDI owns it when it is finished.

## What Nobody Has Announced Yet

The announcement covers a site, a size, and two years. It does not cover store hours, staffing, or whether any other retail will share the parcel. The build window is wide as well: a spring 2027 start and a 2028 opening span anywhere from roughly nine months to nearly two years, and neither the college nor the company has named a month.

## The Rest of the Block

Columbus State's downtown campus sits inside the Discovery District, where a separate venture between Pizzuti Companies and Encova Insurance holds a city economic development agreement for a phased $96 million redevelopment of surface parking lots, with roughly 518 apartments and up to 15,000 square feet of retail, [NBC4 reported](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/columbus-approves-economic-agreement-to-redevelop-discovery-district-parking-lots/amp/). The two projects are unrelated. Together they point at a downtown core adding housing and everyday retail at the same time. For more on the area, see our [Downtown Columbus guide](/areas/downtown-columbus).

articles.title: Columbus Opens Free Turf Hours at Kilbourne Run After Fee Fight
articles.excerpt: Northland's $34.4M Kilbourne Run Sports Park opened after Columbus dropped a $250 turf-rental minimum and posted free walk-up hours on named fields instead.
articles.body:
Columbus opened the $34.4 million Kilbourne Run Sports Park in Northland after residents objected to a $250 minimum charge for turf field time. The city now posts free walk-up hours on designated turf fields, and it held a ribbon-cutting and community day on July 29.

## A $250 Minimum, and a Child Told to Leave

Kilbourne Run covers 62.666 acres at 4625 Westerville Road on the city's northeast side, in Northland. Columbus Recreation and Parks priced turf rentals at $125 an hour with a two-hour minimum, so the smallest block a group could book cost $250. [WOSU reported in April](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-04-29/resident-frustrated-by-prices-at-kilbourne-fields-highlights-debate-about-use-of-columbus-parks) that Recreation and Parks employees had removed a neighborhood child from a turf field that was not in use.

City Council member Melissa Green described that to WOSU. A "neighborhood kid was out there trying to practice soccer and was removed by Rec and Park's employees out of concerns for making sure that the AstroTurf is preserved," she said.

## What City Hall Said About Access

Green told WOSU she was concerned with making sure "the communities where we have these facilities placed are also able to access them." Elon Simms, the mayor's chief of staff, defended the maintenance argument and then set it aside. The fields "need to be operated at a particular level to ensure their long-term viability to be used," he said, "but the bigger point here for us is that access matters." He added that no child or resident in Columbus should feel that something built in their neighborhood is not for them.

## The Free Hours the City Now Posts

The city's own [park listing](https://columbusrecparks.com/parks/kilbourne-run-sports-park/) is the clearest record of what changed, because it names the fields and the hours. Fields 3 and 4 were open for walk-up play daily from noon to 9 p.m. between July 1 and July 31, 2026. Field 2 carries the longer window, daily from noon to 9 p.m. from August 1, 2026 through May 31, 2027. The same listing sets the terms: fields "are to be shared fairly by all users," and "any coaching, guided instruction or organized competition is not permitted."

## What $34.4 Million Bought

Recreation and Parks' [capital project page](https://columbusrecparks.com/connect/about/capital-improvement-projects/kilbourne-run-sports-park/) puts the budget at about $34.4 million and reports that roughly that much work had been completed, about 97 percent of the budget. That is a spending figure, not a construction-progress figure. The scope it lists includes five lighted artificial turf soccer fields, a championship field with bleacher seating, a press box and a scoreboard, natural turf fields with irrigation controls, walking loops, playgrounds, restrooms, shelters, a new maintenance facility, a roundabout at the park entry drive, and a connector trail to the Alum Creek Greenway.

## Why This Park Exists at All

WOSU traced the park back to a 2018 effort to keep the Columbus Crew in Columbus. The project was first aimed at the Ohio State Fairgrounds before it landed on the Kilbourne Run site. That origin explains the specification: this is a tournament-grade soccer complex dropped into a residential neighborhood, which is exactly the tension the pricing fight exposed.

## Opening Day, and What Is Still Unsettled

The city held a [community day](https://columbusrecparks.com/calendar/kilbourne-run-sports-park-community-day/) at the park on July 29, 2026, from 1 to 3 p.m., with free activities, food, and giveaways, and cut the ribbon the same day. [Coverage of the opening](https://www.aol.com/articles/columbus-sports-park-opens-000000000.html) reported that the city dropped the planned $250 charge for community use and that the park now carries the city's first public-access turf field. Mayor Andrew Ginther said at the event that the city's kids are its top priority and that it has to keep investing in them.

One piece is still outstanding. WOSU reported in April that a grass field near the park's maintenance building would open for walk-up play in 2027, separate from the turf windows now posted. Neither city page CREN checked carries a date for it. For more on the surrounding area, see our [Northland guide](/areas/northland).

articles.title: CMHA Seeks 216 Affordable Apartments at Closed Garver YMCA Site
articles.excerpt: The YMCA agreed to sell its closed 1827 Livingston Ave. branch to CMHA, which is asking a Columbus area commission to back 216 income-restricted apartments.
articles.body:
The YMCA of Central Ohio has agreed to sell the closed Garver YMCA at 1827 Livingston Ave. to the Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority. CMHA has since asked a Columbus area commission to support 216 income-restricted apartments on the roughly nine-acre southeast side property.

## What the YMCA Agreed To, and What It Did Not

The Y is precise about the stage this deal has reached. Its [Jerry L. Garver YMCA closure FAQ](https://ymcacolumbus.org/garverfaq) says the branch would permanently close on Saturday, May 30, 2026, and that the YMCA "has agreed to sell the property to the Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority, building on a long-standing partnership." The Y adds that it is selling the site to CMHA "so the site can continue serving the community in a meaningful way." An agreement to sell is not a recorded transfer. The Y publishes no closing date and no price, and CREN could not check the parcel record because the Franklin County Auditor's property search was offline for maintenance on September 4.

The same FAQ gives the reason for the closure without softening it. The building could no longer be run sustainably, it says, because of "ongoing facility limitations, declining usage, and operational challenges."

## A Branch Cut From a 10-Year Plan

The closure was not a one-off. A [YMCA of Central Ohio release](https://ymcacolumbus.org/news/ymca-central-ohio-aligns-its-footprint-long-term-sustainability-part-10-year-vision) in February set out a 10-year plan to reshape the organization's footprint and reach more than half a million people by 2035, and it named Garver as the branch that would close. President and CEO Tony Collins framed the trade-off this way: "Every decision we make, no matter how complex or difficult, is grounded in responsibility and care." [614NOW reported](https://614now.com/2026/cancellations/after-30-years-southeast-columbus-ymca-closes-amid-sustainability-concerns) that the branch opened in 1996 and served the southeast side for three decades.

## The 216-Unit Plan CMHA Took to an Area Commission

By June, CMHA had a plan concrete enough to present in public. [NBC4 reported](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/former-columbus-ymca-targeted-for-apartment-development/amp/) that the authority proposed 216 affordable apartments on the roughly nine-acre site, in nine three-story walk-up buildings with a clubhouse and a pool, for households earning 70 to 76 percent of the area median income. CMHA also asked for variances covering building height, building setback, parking spaces, and first-floor residential units.

The Greater South East Area Commission did not settle it that night. NBC4 reported the vote was tabled to a July 15 committee meeting. Commission member Mark Harper put the case for the housing broadly, saying Columbus and central Ohio are facing a housing crisis like most of the country. Neighbor Jaimie Zydorczyk was unconvinced, telling NBC4 the complex "doesn't really fit that area."

## Who These Apartments Would Be For

That income band is workforce housing rather than deep subsidy. A household in it usually earns too much for the programs aimed at the lowest incomes and too little to absorb what new market-rate buildings in Columbus charge. Rents in an income-restricted building are set against a published income limit instead of against what the market will bear, which is what makes them predictable.

One thing the June presentation did not settle, at least in the account NBC4 published, is whether the units would carry project-based vouchers. That detail decides whether a resident with a deeper subsidy need can live in the same building.

## What the Neighborhood Lost First

Before any of this, Garver was the recreation anchor on this stretch of Livingston Avenue. When it closed, residents told [NBC4](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/residents-look-for-answers-as-ymca-building-closes-after-30-years/amp/) they had nothing comparable nearby. Lois Maier, who took exercise classes there, said she would now be traveling to Whitehall or Reynoldsburg. Mark Harper, from the same area commission that later reviewed CMHA's plan, said of the decision: "We have not been included in any of those conversations." The city's Recreation and Parks Department told NBC4 the building had significant water damage that made repairs financially irresponsible for the city to take on.

## Where CMHA's Money Has Been Going

CMHA is in an unusually active building period, which is the context for taking on a nine-acre site. [WSYX reported](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/cmha-columbus-housing-authority-mixed-income-investments-affordable-apartments-falls-demorest-townhomes-rosebrook-village-reynoldsburg-senior-vouchers-central-ohio) that in August 2025 the authority approved more than $100 million in housing investments, including 220 units at The Falls on Refugee Road, a $14.3 million acquisition of Demorest Townhomes in Grove City, and a $26 million purchase of the 244-unit Rosebrook Village in Reynoldsburg, backed by up to $64.3 million in tax-free municipal bonds. The Falls is also on the southeast side, so Garver would not be the authority's only bet in this quadrant.

## Three Records to Watch

A recorded deed at the Franklin County Auditor would confirm the sale actually closed, and at what price. A decision on the variance requests would show whether the buildings can be built at the height, setback, and parking counts CMHA asked for. A financing announcement would show how it gets paid for. Until those exist, this is an agreement and a proposal, not a project under construction. Our [affordable housing coverage](/topics/affordable-housing) tracks the same milestones on other Columbus sites.

articles.title: Chicago Firm Snaps Up Polaris Retail Center for $15.5 Million
articles.excerpt: Core Acquisitions (Chicago) paid $15.5M for Market at Polaris — 111,328 sq ft anchored by PetSmart, Big Sandy, and Slick City — per Delaware County Auditor records.
articles.body:
Core Acquisitions, a Chicago-based real estate investment firm, paid $15.5 million for the Market at Polaris shopping center — a 111,328-square-foot retail strip at 1170–1194 Polaris Pkwy. The deal, sourced from Delaware County Auditor records via the Colliers Columbus market digest, prices the center at roughly $139 per square foot.

## What's in the Center

The center is anchored by PetSmart, Big Sandy Furniture, and Slick City — an indoor slides and experiential entertainment concept that has expanded rapidly across the Midwest. Slick City signed a 10-year initial term at this property. Adjacent to the center sits a Cinemark theater that Colliers described as ranking in the top 20 percent of Cinemark locations nationally.

The tenant mix tells a story about where suburban retail is heading. PetSmart and Big Sandy are established national retailers that have held up in the e-commerce era by offering products people want to inspect or pick up in person. Slick City is different by design: it is a physical experience that cannot be replicated on a screen, and its long lease term here signals confidence in both the location and the concept's staying power.

## Where the Property Sits

Polaris Centers of Commerce is a sprawling commercial zone along the Columbus–Delaware County line, built around Polaris Fashion Place and extending north along Polaris Pkwy. The property sits adjacent to Polaris Fashion Place. O'Connor Capital Partners recently acquired full ownership of Polaris Fashion Place, the 1.3-million-square-foot enclosed mall, according to [REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/oconnor-capital-partners-acquires-full-ownership-of-1-3-msf-polaris-fashion-place-mall-in-columbus/).

The Polaris submarket has attracted real estate capital across multiple asset classes this year. Earlier this year, a Columbus investor paid roughly $60 million for two luxury apartment complexes in the area, as [Hoodline reported in May](https://hoodline.com/2026/05/polaris-power-play-as-columbus-investor-bags-two-luxe-apartment-complexes-for-60-million/). The retail purchase adds to that pattern — Polaris is drawing buyers across property types, not just retail.

## What the Price Says

Colliers did not disclose rental rates or full occupancy in its deal summary, so a precise capitalization rate cannot be determined from public records alone. What the per-square-foot price confirms: a Chicago firm found this suburban Columbus retail asset worth acquiring at that level, in this market, this year.

For context, Columbus' industrial market has priced modern, fully leased assets at comparable dollar-per-foot levels. Dogwood Industrial's purchase of the Gahanna Eastgate Business Center priced that fully leased industrial campus at a comparable per-square-foot level, [as CREN previously reported](/blog/gahanna-industrial-campus-near-airport-sells-for-42-million). The convergence of retail and industrial price points per square foot in Columbus — a gap that favored industrial heavily in past years — is a quiet but notable shift in how Central Ohio commercial real estate is pricing.

## Out-of-State Capital and the Columbus Retail Pattern

Core Acquisitions is Chicago-based, which places this deal inside a pattern that Columbus Business First noted this summer: out-of-state investors entering the Central Ohio market through retail acquisitions. Columbus' relative affordability compared to coastal and larger Sunbelt markets, combined with its stable employment base and population growth, has made it a consistent destination for mid-market commercial real estate capital.

For Columbus-based operators and investors, out-of-state buyers at measured price points generally signal market depth and exit liquidity. When institutional demand is excessive it inflates prices; buyers acquiring established properties at reasonable per-foot levels suggest genuine long-term conviction rather than speculative pressure.

## What Comes Next

Core Acquisitions has not announced plans for the center beyond the acquisition. With Slick City, PetSmart, and Big Sandy already in place, occupancy at the center appears stable. The most likely path for a new owner of this type of asset is active management — maintaining and leasing remaining space — rather than near-term repositioning or redevelopment.

The property is worth watching as a bellwether for suburban Columbus retail pricing. With Polaris Fashion Place under new ownership and the broader commercial corridor continuing to attract capital, lease renewals and any vacancy events in the next few years will help clarify where this submarket prices going forward.

---

articles.title: Central Ohio Inventory Rose 7% as June Prices Held Firm
articles.excerpt: Central Ohio had more homes for sale in June, but the regional median price still edged higher. The data describe a slower market, not a buyer takeover.
articles.body:
Central Ohio inventory reached 5,551 homes in June 2026, up 7% from a year earlier, while the median sale price rose 0.6% to $352,000. Buyers had more choices, but the regional MLS data do not establish a buyer’s market or broad price decline.

## June brought more listings and more closings

The [Columbus REALTORS market summary](https://columbusrealtors.com/) reported 3,100 home sales in June, compared with 2,951 one year earlier. That was a 5% increase, alongside the rise in active inventory from 5,188 homes to 5,551.

The combination matters. Inventory grew, but buyers also completed more purchases. A larger number of listings therefore did not translate automatically into falling prices or a collapse in demand.

The median sale price moved from $350,000 to $352,000 over the same year-over-year comparison. That 0.6% gain was modest, especially next to the inventory increase, but it was still an increase rather than evidence of a region-wide correction.

## Different sources answer different questions

[Redfin’s Columbus market page](https://www.redfin.com/city/4664/OH/Columbus/housing-market) covers Columbus proper and uses its own data definitions and rolling measurement periods. Columbus REALTORS reports the much broader Central Ohio regional multiple-listing service, which includes counties and communities outside the city.

Those boundaries should not be blended. A city-level days-on-market figure cannot be substituted for a regional MLS figure without labeling the difference, and an August commentary cannot establish what the official June dataset measured.

The previous version mixed June, July and August observations, then described them as one current market. This revision uses the dated June regional comparison for its central conclusion and treats other providers as context rather than interchangeable evidence.

## More inventory changes selection before price

An inventory gain can give a household more properties to compare and reduce the chance that every viable listing attracts immediate competition. It does not show that a particular buyer can obtain a discount, inspection credit or seller-paid closing costs.

Those outcomes depend on the property, price band, condition and competing offers. The available regional totals do not support neighborhood-specific advice about Upper Arlington, Grandview, Powell, Clintonville or any other submarket.

The trade association also represents real-estate professionals, so its description of market balance is not independent analysis. Readers can inspect the figures while treating promotional interpretations separately from the underlying counts.

## What the June evidence supports

The defensible takeaway is narrow: Central Ohio entered summer with more active listings, more completed sales and nearly flat year-over-year price growth. That is evidence of additional selection and slower appreciation, not proof that sellers lost control of pricing across the region.

The next checkpoint is a run of monthly reports using the same geography and definitions. Several consecutive months of rising inventory paired with flat or falling prices would provide stronger evidence of a durable shift than one month or a brokerage commentary.

articles.title: Hilliard Pickleball Club Still Says Coming Soon Before Target
articles.excerpt: Pickleball Kingdom’s Hilliard page still lists play as coming soon, so the reported late-August opening remains a target rather than a confirmed debut.
articles.body:
Pickleball Kingdom’s planned Hilliard club at 4500 Britton Parkway has 15 indoor courts, but the operator’s current page still lists reservations and open play as coming soon. A late-August opening reported in July remains a target, not confirmation that the Columbus-area facility is operating.

## The operator’s page confirms the address and courts

The [Hilliard club page](https://pickleballkingdom.com/clubs/hilliard-oh/) lists the address as 4500 Britton Parkway and describes 15 climate-controlled indoor courts. It also advertises locker rooms, showers, a pro shop, event space, coaching and organized play.

As of CREN’s August 15 review, the same page labels open-play times and court-reservation times as coming soon. That is the clearest current status signal available from the operator and is why this revision does not say the club has opened.

The prior version relied on a reported late-August target but wrote the headline in the present tense. A target can change, especially when the operator has not posted a first day of play or live reservation schedule.

## The timetable has already moved

Pickleball Kingdom’s [July 16, 2025 announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/pickleball-kingdom-to-open-in-hilliard-oh-302506744.html) said the approximately 36,000-square-foot facility was expected to open in early 2026. It identified the project as the chain’s third Ohio location after Cincinnati and Centerville.

[614NOW reported on July 18, 2026](https://614now.com/2026/culture/indoor-pickleball-club-to-open-later-this-month-in-hilliard) that the target had moved to late August. From the initial announcement to the revised target is roughly 13 months, but elapsed time is not the same as construction delay because the first release did not give a firm opening day or detailed project schedule.

The sources do not explain which permitting, construction, staffing or operational steps drove the changed timeline. CREN therefore does not assign a cause.

## Facility size does not equal court area

The original story divided 36,000 square feet by 15 courts and described about 2,400 square feet per court. That arithmetic is correct, but the interpretation is misleading because the total building also contains circulation, viewing, retail, locker and event areas.

Without a floor plan, the quotient is not the physical footprint of each playing court. This revision removes the comparison to a commercial storefront and reports the building and court counts separately.

The operator’s descriptions of programming and amenities are first-party marketing claims. They show what the business intends to offer, not utilization, membership demand or an effect on surrounding property values.

## What will confirm an opening

A live reservation calendar, posted hours or a dated opening notice from the Hilliard operator would establish that the club is serving customers. Local occupancy records could provide an additional public checkpoint.

Until one of those appears, the defensible status is that the 15-court facility is preparing to open and the late-August timetable remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: The Ellis Starts Construction After Dublin Approved Block J Plan
articles.excerpt: Construction has started on The Ellis at Bridge Park, but developer statements about pricing, pre-sales and completion remain forward-looking claims.
articles.body:
Crawford Hoying says construction has started on The Ellis, an 89-unit condominium building in Dublin’s Bridge Park, after the city approved Block J’s final development plan. Prices begin near $400,000, but the developer’s pre-sale count and late-2027 occupancy target remain claims rather than completed sales or guaranteed dates.

## The public record confirms an approved plan

The [City of Dublin’s case file](https://dublinohiousa.gov/pzc/25-055/) identifies Block J as a 5.37-acre mixed-use development southeast of Bridge Park Avenue and Dale Drive. Dublin’s Planning and Zoning Commission approved the final development plan on July 17, 2025.

That approval is stronger evidence than a rendering or sales announcement, but it does not show that every planned element has been built. The case file establishes zoning approval for the project and links the underlying plans, drawings and review history.

The city drawings identify an 89-unit condominium phase and a separate parking structure. The broader block plan also includes office and restaurant space, open space and a possible future condominium phase.

## Construction and sales claims come from the developer

[Crawford Hoying announced](https://www.crawfordhoying.com/news/theellisupdate) that work on The Ellis was underway and that prices started near $400,000. The company also said about 20% of the units were spoken for and projected initial occupancy in late 2027.

Applying 20% to 89 units produces 17.8, or about 18 units. CREN describes those units as reported reservations or contracts because the source is the seller; the available evidence does not include individual purchase records or closing statements.

The previous article multiplied the rounded count by the starting price and called the result at least $7.2 million in condos claimed. CREN has removed that estimate. A starting price does not reveal the contract price of each unit, and a pre-construction agreement is not a completed sale.

An [AOL report carrying local television coverage](https://www.aol.com/articles/construction-underway-89-unit-ellis-110000000.html) independently reported the construction announcement. However, its pricing, reservation and schedule details still trace primarily to the developer and its sales representatives.

## Block J adds more than housing

Crawford Hoying says the condominium building will offer one-, two- and three-bedroom flats, a connected garage, a pool deck and a fitness center. The same announcement describes more than 100,000 square feet of office space and about 7,000 square feet of restaurant and retail space elsewhere in Block J.

Those are planned program elements, not measurements of occupied space. The city file is the better source for approval status, while the developer’s update is the source for current construction, sales and leasing claims.

## What remains uncertain

Construction can change through permits, field conditions and later plan revisions. Prices may change, contracts can be canceled, and a projected occupancy date is not a guarantee.

The next verifiable checkpoints are building-permit milestones, certificates of occupancy and recorded condominium transfers. Those records will show whether the approved plan became completed housing and what buyers actually paid.

articles.title: Ohio Opens $45.6M Welcome Home Round for Columbus Nonprofits
articles.excerpt: Ohio opened a new $45.6M Welcome Home grant round today — $22.8M for foreclosure purchases and $22.8M for rehab and new construction — with Columbus nonprofits and Franklin County eligible to apply.
articles.body:
The Ohio Department of Development opened its latest Welcome Home Ohio grant round on August 13, making $45.6 million available to nonprofits and local governments — including the City of Columbus and Franklin County — to buy foreclosed homes or fund rehab and new construction for income-qualified buyers. The program was authorized by House Bill 96, the state biennium budget, and signed by Governor Mike DeWine in 2025.

## Two Pools, One Goal

The $45.6 million is split into two equal pieces of $22.8 million each.

The first pool covers **foreclosure purchases**: eligible entities can apply for grants to buy residential properties at foreclosure sales. The goal is to intercept foreclosed homes before they sit vacant or move to investors and keep them on a path to owner-occupancy.

The second pool covers **rehabilitation and new construction**: grants fund the cost of rehabbing existing homes or building new ones. Properties funded through either pool must ultimately be sold to qualifying homebuyers — the program is designed for permanent homeownership, not rentals or land banking.

"Welcome Home Ohio hasn't just opened doors for more communities to capitalize on Ohio's momentum, it has changed the lives of countless families who may have felt homeownership just wasn't possible," said Lydia Mihalik, director of the Ohio Department of Development, as reported by the [Ironton Tribune](https://irontontribune.com/2026/08/13/development-announces-availability-of-45-6m-to-improve-access-to-housing-across-ohio-2/) and [Logan Daily](https://www.logandaily.com/news/agency-announces-availability-of-45-6-million-to-improve-access-to-housing-across-ohio/article_c301b229-5bf3-4047-82a7-ece1d84ef30d.html).

## Who Can Apply

The program distinguishes between two categories of eligible entities:

**Qualified nonprofit developers** are Ohio nonprofit corporations engaged in community development activities, with community improvement as their primary purpose. Columbus's network of community development corporations — organizations active in neighborhoods like Franklinton, the Near East Side, Linden, and the South Side — fits this definition.

**Electing subdivisions** are local governments that have formally adopted the program's procedures by ordinance (municipalities) or resolution (townships and counties). The City of Columbus and Franklin County are both eligible to apply as electing subdivisions.

## Why the Columbus Market Makes This Round Timely

[Franklin County home sales cooled in early August](/blog/2026-08-12-franklin-county-home-sales-cool-as-mortgage-rates-hit-a-yearlong-high) as the 30-year mortgage rate climbed to 6.69% — a yearlong high. At that rate, fewer buyers can qualify for the metro's median-priced home, estimated at $329,900 in the most recent Franklin County Auditor weekly sales report.

That affordability gap is unlikely to close through rate movement alone. Programs that directly reduce the purchase price or rehabilitation cost — by layering a grant on top of a conventional mortgage — are among the few mechanisms available to move lower-income buyers into ownership in the current rate environment.

Welcome Home Ohio is not a down payment assistance program for individual buyers. It funds the intermediaries — nonprofits and local governments — who acquire, renovate, and sell properties at prices the market alone would not produce. That distinction matters: Columbus CDCs and city programs have to apply and win the grant before any individual buyer sees the benefit.

## Program History and Prior Rounds

Welcome Home Ohio has run multiple rounds since the program launched. The Ohio Department of Development previously announced a [$26.9 million round](https://governor.ohio.gov/media/news-and-media/governor-dewine-announces-26-9-million-in-grants-to-support-continued-housing-growth-across-ohio) and an earlier [$65.6 million round](https://www.eaglecountryonline.com/news/local-news/gov-dewine-announces-availability-of-65-6-million-to-improve-access-to-housing-across-ohio/) for the same program. The total biennium allocation through HB 96 is $91.2 million, according to [Ohio Department of Development program guidelines](https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/v1763144755/development.ohio.gov/community/Housing%20and%20Homelessness/Draft_26.27_Application_Instructions.pdf).

This $45.6 million round runs concurrent with the [Ohio Brownfield Remediation Program's $120 million application window](/blog/2026-08-11-ohio-s-120-million-brownfield-fund-opens-for-columbus-applications), which opened August 11 and runs through September 11. Columbus-area community development organizations are navigating both grant programs this month.

## How to Apply

Applications go through the Ohio Department of Development. Program guidelines and application materials are available at [development.ohio.gov](https://development.ohio.gov). Columbus nonprofits and city officials seeking program guidance can contact the Ohio Department of Development's Office of Community Development.

---

articles.title: Gahanna Industrial Campus Near Airport Sells for $42 Million
articles.excerpt: Dogwood Industrial (TPG Real Estate) paid $42M for Gahanna's fully leased Eastgate Business Center — 293,000 sq ft near John Glenn Airport in the East Columbus corridor.
articles.body:
Dogwood Industrial Properties, a TPG Real Estate platform, paid $42 million for Eastgate Business Center, a 292,594-square-foot industrial campus at 1800–1808 Deffenbaugh Court in Gahanna. The seller was a Scannell Properties and Manulife Investment Management joint venture, with Colliers brokering; the campus is fully leased to Wesco and Nuvik USA.

## Two Buildings, One Airport Corridor

The campus sits on Deffenbaugh Court in Gahanna, a city in eastern Franklin County just off I-270. The campus provides direct access to I-70 and I-71, sits about two miles from John Glenn Columbus International Airport, and is roughly 12 miles from the Intel semiconductor campus under construction in New Albany.

The buildings feature 32-foot clear heights and 30 dock doors — specifications consistent with modern regional distribution facilities that handle pallet freight rather than small-parcel e-commerce. Colliers, which represented the sellers, confirmed the sale in its [August 7, 2026 weekly market recap](https://www.yourresearchresource.com/post/the-weekly-review-august-7-2026). [REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/colliers-brokers-sale-of-292594-sf-industrial-property-in-gahanna-ohio/) and [CoStar](https://www.costar.com/article/1493261374/new-fully-leased-distribution-center-trades-outside-columbus) reported the deal; property records through Franklin County Auditor data, as indexed by [PropertyShark](https://www.propertyshark.com/cre/commercial-property/us/oh/gahanna/eastgate-business-center/), confirm the transfer.

## What $42 Million Tells You About East Columbus Industrial

At $42 million for 292,594 square feet, the implied price works out to approximately **$143 per square foot** — a premium relative to older industrial product in Columbus, but within range for a fully leased, modern-spec asset with creditworthy tenants and airport adjacency.

That fully leased status is the key detail. Dogwood didn't buy a bet on vacancy fill-up. It bought existing cash flow from two tenants: Wesco International (NYSE: WCC), a publicly traded electrical and industrial distributor, and Nuvik USA, a Canadian safety products company that uses Columbus for Midwest distribution. Both occupy the campus on full-building terms.

When institutional capital — a TPG Real Estate platform — writes a $42 million check for a fully leased East Columbus industrial asset, it signals that the submarket is performing well enough to justify premium pricing. Colliers' Columbus industrial market reports have flagged tight vacancy in key submarkets through the first half of 2026, and the East corridor has drawn steady demand from airport and Intel-campus proximity without the spec-supply wave seen in other parts of the metro.

## Who Dogwood Industrial Is, and Why They Chose Gahanna

Dogwood Industrial Properties is a [TPG Real Estate](https://dogwoodindustrial.com/about/) platform focused on acquiring and managing industrial and logistics assets across the U.S. TPG is one of the world's largest alternative asset managers. Dogwood targets modern logistics facilities in supply-constrained markets and has been expanding in Midwest cities as coastal industrial cap rates compress.

The Eastgate acquisition appears to be Dogwood's entry into the Columbus market. Central Ohio's logistics infrastructure — driven by Amazon, a growing Intel supplier base, and regional pharma and auto-parts distribution — has made it one of the more closely watched Midwest industrial markets, even as [CRE News has covered](/topics/development) the region's broader growth story.

Scannell Properties, the developer, and Manulife Investment Management, the institutional equity partner, were the sellers. Scannell has multiple industrial projects underway in Central Ohio and typically recycles capital from stabilized assets into new development — a pattern consistent with this transaction.

## What to Watch in East Columbus and Gahanna

For Gahanna and the East Columbus submarket, this transaction is a data point rather than a turning point. The East corridor has attracted institutional capital quietly — without the headline volume of spec parks in the southwest or southeast rings — because its fundamentals are durable: airport access, highway connectivity, and proximity to the Intel campus.

The next data point to watch: whether Dogwood or other core-plus buyers target additional East Columbus assets as Intel's New Albany campus moves toward its production phase. Construction and supplier activity along the New Albany–Gahanna ring has historically preceded a second wave of logistics investment. This acquisition suggests that wave may already be pricing in.

---

articles.title: Micro Center Sets Aug. 22 Debut for Remodeled Columbus Store
articles.excerpt: Micro Center plans to unveil its remodeled Bethel Road store on Aug. 22. The retailer says the location remained open during construction.
articles.body:
Micro Center plans an August 22 grand-reopening event for its remodeled store at 747 Bethel Road in Columbus. The company says the location stayed open during construction, so the event marks the debut of the finished retail layout rather than the reopening of a closed store.

## What the retailer says changed

Micro Center’s [official Columbus remodel announcement](https://www.microcenter.com/site/mc-news/article/micro-center-columbus-remodel.aspx?storeid=165) describes an expanded build-your-own computer department, a larger service area and new displays for networking equipment, artificial-intelligence hardware and three-dimensional printers.

Those descriptions come from the retailer, not an independent inspection of the finished work. The company has not disclosed the remodel budget, added floor area or a construction permit ledger in the materials CREN reviewed, so this article does not characterize the project as an expansion in size.

The store’s [current location page](https://www.microcenter.com/site/stores/columbus.aspx?storeid=131) lists more than 25,000 products in stock and confirms the Bethel Road address. That inventory figure is a company marketing claim and can change; it is not a count independently verified by CREN.

## Columbus is the chain’s starting point

Micro Center says its first store opened on Lane Avenue in Columbus in 1979. The current store is at 747 Bethel Road, while the company’s headquarters is in nearby Hilliard.

That history gives the remodel local significance beyond a routine merchandising update. It does not establish how the store performs financially or how the work will affect nearby retail property, traffic or employment. The company’s announcement supplied no local sales, staffing or economic-impact figures.

An [AOL report on the project](https://www.aol.com/articles/got-tech-micro-center-columbus-130059000.html) provides a second account of the reopening plans, but many of the feature details still originate with Micro Center. Readers should treat unverified operational claims accordingly.

## The event is promotional, not a closure recovery

The company’s location page schedules a ribbon cutting for 9:45 a.m. on August 22. It also advertises giveaways, including gift cards for the first 1,000 customers, with limits and availability conditions.

Those offers are included only to describe the announced event. CREN does not endorse the promotion, and readers should check the retailer’s current terms because quantities and schedules can change.

The distinction between a reopening and an unveiling matters. Micro Center says shoppers could continue using the store while crews remodeled it, so the event is not evidence that a vacant retail property returned to service.

## What remains to verify

The first checkpoint is whether the August event occurs on the published schedule. A later assessment would require public permit records or direct reporting on the work’s cost, scope and employment effects.

Until those records are available, the supported story is straightforward: a long-running Columbus electronics store is presenting a remodeled interior, while the commercial consequences remain unmeasured.

articles.title: Franklin County Weekly Sales Need Context as Rates Rise
articles.excerpt: A Franklin County weekly transfer report showed a $329,900 median, but it cannot by itself establish that the housing market cooled as mortgage rates rose.
articles.body:
Franklin County recorded a $329,900 median residential sale price for transfers reported from July 31 through August 6, 2026, while the national 30-year mortgage average reached 6.69%. The figures are useful snapshots, but they do not prove that higher rates caused county sales or prices to cool.

## What the county transfer report measured

The [Franklin County Auditor’s weekly report](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/News-articles/20260809-WHSR) listed 498 residential sales and an average sale price of $391,108 for the reporting week. Because the auditor compiles recorded transfers, the report describes closings that reached the public record rather than contracts newly signed during that week.

That lag is important when considering mortgage rates. Many purchasers whose deeds appeared in early August would have agreed to their transactions and arranged financing weeks earlier. A rate published during the closing week cannot automatically explain the price or number of those transfers.

The difference between the average and median also signals a wide price distribution. A relatively small number of expensive sales can pull the average upward, while the median identifies the midpoint of the reported transfers.

## The regional comparison is not like for like

The [Columbus REALTORS June statistics](https://columbusrealtors.com/) put the Central Ohio median at $352,000 and counted 3,100 home sales across its regional MLS. That geography extends beyond Franklin County, and the monthly window is much longer than the auditor’s weekly report.

The two medians differ by $22,100, but that subtraction is not a measure of month-to-month depreciation. It compares different places, periods and property mixes. Outer counties with more new construction can change the regional median, while a single week of Franklin County deeds can shift with the mix of homes closing.

The previous version treated the gap as evidence that Franklin County trailed the region. The records support only a descriptive comparison, not a trend or causal conclusion.

## Mortgage rates were higher, but causation is unproved

[Freddie Mac’s survey archive](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/pmms_archives) shows the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.69% on August 6, up from 6.66% on July 30. The rate eased to 6.67% on August 13.

Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey is a national measure based on conventional conforming purchase applications. It is not a count of Franklin County borrowers, and individual offers vary by credit, loan type, points and other terms.

Higher borrowing costs generally raise the monthly payment associated with the same principal, but this weekly evidence does not isolate how much local demand changed because of the rate movement.

## What would demonstrate cooling

A credible cooling claim would require several comparable periods showing changes in closed sales, prices, marketing time and inventory within the same geography. Contract dates or rate-lock dates would also be more informative than pairing a deed-recording week with the rate published that week.

The next useful checkpoint is the auditor’s subsequent weekly reports alongside the next monthly Franklin County series from the same provider. Until a consistent run develops, the August report is best read as a snapshot of recorded transactions, not proof of a turning market.

articles.title: Ohio's $120 Million Brownfield Fund Opens for Columbus Applications
articles.excerpt: Ohio opened a $120M brownfield cleanup fund round today through Sept. 11. Columbus has won nearly $30M in prior rounds — apply now at development.ohio.gov.
articles.body:
The Ohio Brownfield Remediation Program opened a new $120 million application round today, August 11, for cleanup of contaminated industrial, commercial, and institutional properties, with applications accepted through September 11 at development.ohio.gov. Columbus-area applicants have won nearly $30 million from the program's prior rounds.

## What the Program Covers

The Ohio Department of Development's Brownfield Remediation Program funds two types of work: assessment (identifying what contamination is present and estimating cleanup costs) and remediation (the actual cleanup, asbestos abatement, lead removal, demolition of hazardous structures, or some combination).

Eligible sites are industrial, commercial, or institutional properties where a known or potential release of hazardous substances or petroleum has left the property idle or underused. The program does not fund residential sites or cleanups already required under a court order or regulatory consent agreement.

One detail worth noting for private-sector readers: grants can cover the full cost of eligible project work. There is no required local match. For public-sector applicants working with tight capital budgets — land banks, townships, smaller municipalities — the no-match structure is a significant threshold to clear.

## Who Can Apply in Columbus

Eligible applicants include counties, townships, municipal corporations, port authorities, district parks, county land reutilization corporations, and for-profit organizations. Private developers whose sites qualify can apply directly without routing through a public entity, per the program's eligibility terms as published in state legislative summaries and Ohio House press releases.

In Franklin County, COCIC — the Central Ohio Community Improvement Corp. — serves as the county's lead entity coordinating brownfield grant applications. COCIC typically holds discovery meetings with potential sub-applicants before each round, helping Franklin County's submissions avoid overlap and cover more ground. Columbus-area applicants should check [cocic.org/grants](https://cocic.org/grants/) or contact COCIC to confirm whether Franklin County has reserved capacity in this round.

## What Columbus Has Won Before

Franklin County has built a consistent track record under this program.

In one earlier round, the Franklin County Land Bank received $3.75 million to remediate and demolish blighted structures across three sites: Eastland Mall, Gahanna's Creekside District, and a parcel in Weinland Park, according to a COCIC grant announcement.

In another round, Woda Cooper Companies received $1 million for the Lofts at 40 Long project — asbestos abatement, lead-based paint mitigation, and selective demolition inside the former downtown Columbus YMCA building at 40 Long Street, also per COCIC. The former YMCA building had sat vacant, and the grant made it possible to prepare the historic structure for residential reuse, part of a broader wave of [downtown Columbus reuse projects](/topics/development).

In 2024, COCIC submitted six Franklin County applications, and all six were funded for a total of nearly $29 million, according to Zimmer Development Co.

## The Statewide Picture

Since the program launched in 2021, it has awarded nearly $800 million to support 904 projects across 87 of Ohio's 88 counties, according to Ohio House press releases summarizing the program's track record.

Governor Mike DeWine announced the new round on August 6.

## Why This Round Matters for Columbus Operators

Columbus is a city with a long industrial history, and the legacy of that history shows up in the form of contaminated or blighted sites spread across older commercial corridors and neighborhoods. Brownfield grants address a specific and often decisive problem: who absorbs the cost and risk of what may be underground before a site changes hands.

A remediated site is a different asset than an unremediated one. Once the contamination risk has been documented, quantified, and paid for by a grant, the site can be bid out competitively, financed conventionally, or transferred to a developer who would not have touched it before. That's the reason the COCIC-funded Eastland Mall, Gahanna Creekside, and Weinland Park cleanups from prior rounds matter beyond the individual parcels: each one creates a cleared, lender-ready site that the private market can now absorb.

For Columbus operators working near older commercial corridors in [Franklinton](/areas/franklinton), the Near East Side, Linden, or the South Side, this application window is worth tracking. A site you've been holding because of contamination uncertainty may be exactly what this program is designed to address.

## How to Apply

Applications are submitted online. Navigate to development.ohio.gov → For Community → Redevelopment → Brownfield Remediation Program. The application requires site documentation, a project description, a budget, and confirmation of applicant eligibility. Assessment grants and remediation grants have separate tracks and different supporting documentation requirements.

For Franklin County coordination, contact COCIC at [cocic.org/grants](https://cocic.org/grants/).
