articles.title: The Line Training Restaurant Still Lists Opening as Coming Soon
articles.excerpt: Service!’s downtown Columbus training restaurant remains listed as coming soon, making its program clearer than its opening timetable.
articles.body:
The Line, a planned restaurant and hospitality-training center at 145 North Grant Avenue in downtown Columbus, still lacks a confirmed public opening date. Operator Service! describes the project as coming soon, while earlier reports targeting summer or August should now be treated as estimates rather than an opening announcement.

## The official page does not give an opening day

Service!’s [program page](https://www.servicerelief.org/what-we-do) lists The Line and its Innovation Kitchen as coming soon. It describes a restaurant that will operate as a live demonstration of hospitality work while employees receive mentoring in dining-room, beverage and kitchen roles.

That language establishes the operator’s plan, not a completed opening. An earlier version of this story said The Line was nearing an August debut, but CREN did not find a dated opening notice on the official page during this review.

The organization lists 145 North Grant Avenue as its mailing address for The Line. The site is in downtown Columbus near the Discovery District, but the available sources do not establish a broader effect on surrounding rents, property values or redevelopment.

## The training model builds on Café Overlook

Service! says its existing Café Overlook operates on the 16th floor of the Franklin County Courthouse. The café combines weekday food service with front-of-house and back-of-house training, job coaching and worker supports.

The Line is intended to extend that model into a full-service restaurant. [Columbus Monthly’s June report](https://www.aol.com/news/columbus-restaurant-line-focuses-training-100319655.html) said the initial restaurant would seat about 100 people, with a patio and incubator kitchen planned for later.

The same report identified chef and Service! co-founder Matthew Heaggans as executive chef. Those program details are attributed plans until the restaurant opens and begins enrolling or employing participants under the described model.

## Plans include education and an incubator

[What Now Columbus reported](https://whatnow.com/columbus/restaurants/service-to-open-the-line-in-downtown-columbus-with-workforce-training-restaurant-concept/) that the project was designed for roughly 80 indoor seats, a 40-seat patio and an eight-seat chef’s table. Those figures differ from the rounder initial-capacity description in Columbus Monthly, underscoring that pre-opening plans can change.

What Now also reported planned education partnerships and a future incubator for food entrepreneurs. Its June article said construction was expected to finish by July 1, with public programming later in the summer; the outlet noted that it had sought additional opening information from Service!.

Because the official page still says coming soon, CREN is not treating the construction estimate as proof that the restaurant is complete or licensed for service.

## What readers can verify next

The project’s public value will depend on execution: a confirmed opening, published program eligibility, paid-training terms, cohort size and evidence that participants move into more stable work. The current materials describe the mission but do not provide outcome data for The Line because it has not publicly opened.

The next reliable checkpoint is a dated notice from Service! giving the first service day and explaining how workers can enter the training program. Until then, the project remains a documented plan with an unresolved schedule.

articles.title: NRP Group Breaks Ground on 336-Unit OSU East Apartments in Columbus
articles.excerpt: The NRP Group's first Columbus project pairs 336 apartments with 138 M/I Homes townhomes on a 27.5-acre site near Ohio State University Airport.
articles.body:
The NRP Group broke ground this week on OSU East, a 336-unit apartment community on 27.5 acres in northwest Columbus, near the Ohio State University Airport. The project, NRP's first market-rate community in the city, will add 336 rental units and 138 for-sale townhomes built by M/I Homes.

## What's Being Built

OSU East will include 336 rental units across 11 three-story residential buildings on a 27.5-acre site at 2575 West Dublin-Granville Road. The unit mix breaks down to 144 one-bedroom apartments, 156 two-bedroom apartments, and 36 three-bedroom apartments, according to RE Journals. M/I Homes of Central Ohio LLC will build 138 for-sale townhomes on the same site, adding a second housing type to the project. Planned amenities include a clubhouse with a full kitchen, a fitness center, a resort-style pool, volleyball and bocce courts, and a package delivery room, according to Rebusiness Online.

## Who's Behind It

The NRP Group is the developer behind OSU East, marking the company's first market-rate apartment community in Columbus, according to RE Journals and Rebusiness Online. PNC Bank is providing construction financing, and the Carlyle Group is the equity partner on the deal, according to Rebusiness Online. "This project represents an exciting milestone for our team and is the first of many opportunities we hope to pursue in Columbus," said Mike Zelenkofske, NRP Group's executive vice president of development, according to RE Journals.

## Why Northwest Columbus

The site sits near the Ohio State University Airport, also known as Don Scott Field, and offers access to State Route 315 and Interstate 270. An 11-foot-wide bike path will run along the project's frontage as part of a coordination with the City of Columbus, according to RE Journals. The property falls within Worthington School District boundaries and sits close to the Bridge Park mixed-use district in neighboring Dublin, according to Rebusiness Online.

## What's Nearby

Major employers within a short drive include Ohio State University, Cardinal Health, OhioHealth, JPMorgan, Nationwide Insurance, and Nationwide Children's Hospital, according to RE Journals. Columbus Real Estate News has separately tracked apartment groundbreakings across the metro's north and northwest corridors this summer as developers chase land near major employers and transit corridors.

## What Comes Next

City records show a rezoning case, Z24-052, and Columbus City Council ordinances 0276-2026 and 0277-2026, tied to the 2575 West Dublin-Granville Road address, according to the City of Columbus Legistar system. NRP Group has not announced a delivery date for OSU East.

**Sources:** [RE Journals, Aug 6, 2026](https://rejournals.com/the-nrp-group-marks-groundbreaking-of-336-unit-multifamily-community-in-columbus/) · [REBusinessOnline, Aug 7, 2026](https://rebusinessonline.com/nrp-group-breaks-ground-on-336-unit-apartment-development-in-columbus-ohio/) · [City of Columbus Legistar record](https://columbus.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=5F40BC19-0D33-40F3-90A0-7A0E5ADD3EB6&ID=15157530&M=F)

articles.title: Gahanna Creekside Site Is Cleared, but Plans Are Still Early
articles.excerpt: The Gahanna Creekside redevelopment site is cleared, but detailed plans still face design work and public review before construction can begin.
articles.body:
Gahanna has cleared several vacant Mill Street properties for a proposed mixed-use project beside Creekside. The city describes it as a $100 million private development, but no detailed plan has entered public review, making the empty site a starting point rather than a finished promise.

## What changed on Mill Street?

Five vacant buildings on Mill Street were removed to prepare land owned by the Gahanna Community Improvement Corporation for reuse. The city said in its [June project update](https://www.gahanna.gov/CivicSend/ViewMessage/message/292273) that crews were then removing foundations and paved surfaces. Temporary grass is planned while the development team studies the site.

That sequence matters. Demolition has happened; building design has not reached the same stage. A cleared parcel can look like construction is about to start, but the city says the developer is still testing site conditions and doing other due-diligence work.

## What does the broad framework include?

The city’s [Creekside Reimagined page](https://www.gahanna.gov/650/Creekside-Reimagined) describes a private framework with housing, restaurant and retail space, a boutique hotel, and parking. City budget material has described 263 apartments, a hotel with 55 to 70 rooms, and two restaurants.

Those figures explain the project’s intended scale, not its final design. The city says detailed plans have not been submitted for review. Until that happens, floor plans, building appearance, construction timing, and many site details remain open.

## Why are two Creekside projects easy to confuse?

Creekside Reimagined combines a private development proposal with a separate public project for the plaza and flood protection. The public work concerns the existing civic space near Big Walnut Creek. The private work concerns the cleared development sites along Mill Street.

A [MORPC project profile](https://www.morpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/FRA1-Creekside.pdf) lists $25 million for the public flood-proofing and plaza project. That public figure should not be blended with the city’s description of roughly $100 million in private development resources. They are connected parts of one district plan, but they pay for different work.

## What still needs to happen before construction?

The development team must finish its site evaluation and prepare detailed plans. Those plans would then move into city review, where design, engineering, access, parking, and other requirements can be examined. The city also says additional public review will occur before private construction could begin.

That leaves real uncertainty. The project has a development agreement and a broad program, yet the final buildings and schedule can still change as testing and review continue. A useful next update will come from a dated plan submission or public meeting, not from the cleared ground alone.

## What should Gahanna readers watch next?

Watch for the city to post detailed plans, meeting dates, or revisions tied to the private project. On the public side, the city expects required flood-mitigation work to begin in fall 2026. That work may affect access to Creekside businesses and public space, so the city says it is studying construction impacts.

For now, the precise update is modest: demolition has prepared the Mill Street sites, due diligence is underway, and detailed private plans are still pending. That is less dramatic than a groundbreaking, but it is the clearest way to understand where the Gahanna Creekside redevelopment actually stands.

articles.title: Harvest Clintonville Reopened in 2024, Not After a 2026 Fire
articles.excerpt: Harvest Bar + Kitchen’s Clintonville reopening followed a July 2024 fire. The event was mistakenly republished as current news and is corrected here.
articles.body:
Harvest Bar + Kitchen’s Clintonville location reopened in November 2024 after a fire that July; it did not reopen after a new 2026 fire. CREN’s earlier article recycled the old event without its correct timeline and added unsupported conclusions about property demand and corridor strength.

## The reopening happened nearly two years earlier

[Columbus Underground reported on November 5, 2024](https://columbusunderground.com/clintonville-pizzeria-ready-to-reopen-ak1/) that Harvest would reopen its Clintonville dining room that week after an overnight fire in July. The report identified the address as 2885 North High Street and said smoke caused most of the interior damage.

The original CREN page was dated August 2026 but described that old reopening as though it had just occurred. CREN found no source establishing a new fire or reopening at the restaurant in 2026. The publication date and framing were therefore materially misleading.

## The two fires also need their dates

[NBC4’s contemporaneous report](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/clintonville-pizzeria-that-was-the-site-of-two-fires-in-two-years-reopens/) described the reopening after fires in 2022 and July 2024. According to that coverage, the later fire started behind the building and damaged refrigeration equipment and dumpsters.

Those facts belong to the historical record, but they do not support calling the restaurant’s current operation a new comeback story. The revised article separates the incident dates from the date of this correction.

## Current status can be checked without inventing a trend

Harvest’s [official locations page](https://www.harvestpizzeria.com/harvest/locations) continues to list the Clintonville restaurant at 2885 North High Street. That is current first-party evidence that the company treats the location as operating, although readers should still check the restaurant directly for same-day hours.

The old story called Harvest a neighborhood anchor and treated its return as proof of commercial-corridor resilience. CREN found no vacancy series, rent data, business-turnover study or property-sales analysis tying one restaurant’s reopening to Clintonville real-estate demand. Those conclusions have been removed.

## What the record can and cannot show

A business surviving a closure can matter to employees and regular customers. It does not, on its own, measure the health of every storefront on North High Street or explain residential prices nearby.

The supportable story is narrower: a fire interrupted operations, the business repaired the space, most staff returned according to Columbus Underground, and the restaurant reopened in 2024. The independent reports do not provide a complete insurance, repair-cost or lost-sales accounting, so CREN cannot quantify the financial effect.

## Correction and future checkpoint

This rewrite corrects the event year, removes the claim that two fires would close many small businesses, and deletes investment-oriented language. It also replaces an unsupported statement about property owners with evidence readers can inspect.

Any future update should be based on a genuinely new event: a current company announcement, permit, fire report, closure notice or ownership change. Without one of those records, the 2024 reopening should remain an archived local-business story rather than be presented as breaking news.

articles.title: Columbus Housing Goal Is a Target, Not a Measured Deficit
articles.excerpt: Columbus leaders set a regional goal of 200,000 homes over 10 years, but the figure should not be presented as a proven annual shortage.
articles.body:
Columbus leaders have set a goal of 200,000 additional homes across Central Ohio over 10 years, equivalent to 20,000 per year. The figure is a policy target tied to growth expectations, not a published finding that the region is short exactly 20,000 homes in every calendar year.

## The city states the goal directly

In his [2026 State of the City address](https://www.columbus.gov/Government/Mayors-Office/State-of-the-City/2026-State-of-the-City-Address-Full-Text?lang_update=639182773463525551), Mayor Andrew Ginther said the region should build 200,000 homes over the next decade and pledged that Columbus would account for half. He also said about 9,100 homes were authorized in the city during 2025.

Authorized units are permits or approvals, not necessarily completed and occupied homes. The annualized 20,000 figure is simple division, not a forecast of constant yearly production.

## Population growth supplies the context

MORPC’s [transportation plan](https://www.morpc.org/2024-2050-metropolitan-transportation-plan/) projects the 15-county region growing from about 2.4 million residents to 3.1 million by 2050. Population forecasts contain assumptions and do not, by themselves, specify the exact number, price or location of homes required.

The original story blended that forecast with political statements and called the result a demonstrated supply gap. A defensible shortage estimate would publish household formation, vacancies, demolitions, second homes, affordability and geographic methods.

## The coalition’s authority is limited

The [City’s coalition announcement](https://www.columbus.gov/News-articles/Central-Ohio-Leaders-Establish-Regional-Housing-Coalition-to-Expand-and-Diversify-Housing-Infrastructure) describes voluntary regional coordination among public, business and nonprofit participants. It does not give the coalition zoning or permitting authority over suburban governments.

The earlier story speculated about faster permits, investor returns and future zoning phases. Those predictions were not documented coalition actions and have been removed.

## Progress needs a consistent ledger

Measuring the goal requires a public definition of home, geographic boundary and milestone. Permitted, started, completed and occupied units should not be combined.

The next useful record would be a coalition work plan that assigns responsibilities and publishes a repeatable production dashboard. Until then, 200,000 is an ambitious regional objective rather than a verified deficit count.

## How CREN checked this account

This revision distinguishes originating records from commentary and promotional descriptions. It preserves source-specific uncertainty instead of combining unlike measurements or turning a stated intention into an outcome. The linked records let readers inspect the evidence available on the fact-check date; later schedules, designs and market conditions may differ.

CREN also removed transaction advice and claims about property values, rents, demand or economic effects when the sources supplied no reproducible analysis. A future update should use the same definitions and geography, identify any changed status and explain conflicts rather than quietly replacing the earlier record.

articles.title: Welcome to the Farm Sets August 22 Short North Opening
articles.excerpt: Welcome to the Farm plans an August 22 opening at 906 North High Street, but its employment, lease, capacity and economic effects remain undisclosed.
articles.body:
Welcome to the Farm plans to open August 22, 2026, on the ground floor of Good Night John Boy at 906 North High Street in Columbus. The operator confirms the address, while public reporting supplies the opening time; lease terms, employment, project cost and economic effects remain undisclosed.

## What is confirmed

The brand’s [official location page](https://welcometothefarm.com/) lists the Columbus venue at 906 North High Street. Columbus Underground [reported the August 22 opening](https://columbusunderground.com/welcome-to-the-farm-announces-opening-date-ak1/) and a planned 7 p.m. start.

Country artist Chase Rice and Forward Hospitality Group are associated with the concept. The Columbus venue follows existing Welcome to the Farm locations in Cleveland and Saint Petersburg.

## An interior conversion, not a new building

The bar occupies part of the existing Good Night John Boy property. The reviewed sources describe a change in ground-floor operation, not a newly constructed Short North building.

That distinction matters because the opening does not add housing or demonstrate new development capacity. It is a hospitality tenancy within an existing commercial space.

## What is not public

Neither the official page nor the two local reports provides a lease rate, tenant-improvement budget, confirmed job count or final occupancy capacity. CREN also found no dataset tying this opening to Short North commercial rents or pedestrian activity.

The original article said ground-floor space in the neighborhood rarely remains empty and treated a celebrity-backed bar as a signal of rent and demand trends. Those conclusions require corridor vacancy, lease and foot-traffic evidence that was not supplied.

## Opening dates can still change

The August 22 date is an announced future opening as of the August 15 fact check. Inspections, staffing or operating decisions can affect a launch, so the page should be updated after the venue actually begins regular service.

The source distinction is important: the official brand page confirms a Columbus location and street address, while local reporting supplies the planned date and time. Neither source is evidence that all pre-opening approvals are complete. CREN has therefore attributed the schedule and avoided presenting the venue as already operating.

## What to verify next

Posted hours, an operating menu and evidence of regular public service will confirm the transition from planned to open. Employment, safety incidents or business performance should be reported from records rather than inferred from opening-night crowds.

articles.title: Arena District 242-Unit Plan Remains in Early Design
articles.excerpt: A 242-unit Arena District apartment concept remains in design, with no published hearing outcome, construction date or rent schedule.
articles.body:
Nationwide Realty Investors and a Hamilton Parker affiliate are associated with an early concept for 242 apartments on an Arena District gravel lot near North Market. The plan remains unapproved in the records reviewed, with no published construction schedule, rents or evidence that it will affect districtwide prices.

## One report disclosed the concept

Columbus Underground [first reported the preliminary plan](https://columbusunderground.com/apartments-planned-for-downtown-parking-lot-bw1/) for the block bounded by Spruce, Armstrong, Vine and Kilbourne streets. Its reporting attributes the unit count and partnership to the property interests and says Nationwide Realty Investors confirmed design work.

CREN did not locate a matching public hearing decision or final city staff report during this review. The unit count should therefore be described as proposed, not approved.

## Downtown review is still a checkpoint

The [City of Columbus Downtown Commission page](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Building-Zoning-Services/Boards-and-Commissions/Historic-Preservation-Design-Review-Boards-Commissions-Panels/Downtown-Commission) explains that downtown projects undergo design review and publishes meeting materials. A preliminary plan or application deadline is not the same as commission approval.

The prior article said the city had not scheduled a hearing, but that status can change. Readers should use the commission calendar and agenda for the current record.

## Supply effects were overstated

The original version said more apartments would slow rent growth and add rental depth within a few years. No rent study, completion schedule or causal model supported those claims.

Even if approved, proposed units can change through design, financing and permitting. Completion would add housing at the site, but districtwide rent effects would require data on deliveries, vacancies, concessions and demand.

## What remains unknown

No reviewed source supplies a rendering approved by the city, a construction budget, financing, rent range or groundbreaking date. The project’s relationship to existing parking and nearby Two Twenty Vine also needs final plans rather than analogy.

The next checkpoint is a dated Downtown Commission agenda with application materials, followed by a recorded decision. Until then, the gravel lot proposal remains an early design concept.

## How CREN checked this account

This revision distinguishes originating records from commentary and promotional descriptions. It preserves source-specific uncertainty instead of combining unlike measurements or turning a stated intention into an outcome. The linked records let readers inspect the evidence available on the fact-check date; later schedules, designs and market conditions may differ.

CREN also removed transaction advice and claims about property values, rents, demand or economic effects when the sources supplied no reproducible analysis. A future update should use the same definitions and geography, identify any changed status and explain conflicts rather than quietly replacing the earlier record.

articles.title: Columbus Food Truck Festival Continues in Hilliard Through Tonight
articles.excerpt: The Columbus Food Truck Festival’s second day runs until 10 p.m. August 15 at the Franklin County Fairgrounds, with more than 45 advertised vendors.
articles.body:
The Columbus Food Truck Festival is completing its 2026 Hilliard event today, August 15, at the Franklin County Fairgrounds. The official schedule runs from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. and advertises more than 45 trucks, but final attendance, sales and charitable proceeds will not be known until organizers report them.

## Today’s verified schedule

The festival’s [official information page](https://www.columbusfoodtruckfest.com/festival-info) lists the fairgrounds at 5024 Northwest Parkway and Saturday hours from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. The event began Friday evening.

Organizers advertise more than 45 food trucks, live entertainment, artisan vendors and a Saturday children’s area. A vendor count announced before or during an event may change and is not the same as a post-event participation audit.

## Access and ticket limitations

The official page says on-site parking is complimentary but limited and first come, first served. It restricts pets to service animals and notes that bags may be searched.

Admission covers entry to the grounds, not an audited value of meals or purchases from independent vendors. Prices, payment methods, wait times and item availability may vary by truck. Readers making a same-day plan should distinguish the organizer’s access rules from each vendor’s separate menu and transaction terms.

The [Experience Columbus listing](https://www.experiencecolumbus.com/event/the-columbus-food-truck-festival-2026-hilliard-edition/93629/) provides a second public event record. Visitors should rely on the organizer for same-day weather, entry and schedule changes.

## Attendance is an organizer forecast

The organizer says the fairgrounds typically welcomes more than 25,000 visitors and cites more than $115,000 donated to local charities over the festival’s history. Those are cumulative or promotional figures, not verified 2026 results.

The original story predicted a business boost for nearby restaurants, hotels and shops. CREN found no local sales, occupancy or tax data tied to this weekend and has removed that claim.

## What can be reported afterward

A defensible recap would include scanned ticket counts, participating vendors, public-safety incidents, disclosed charitable distributions and any verified cancellation or weather effects. Crowd photographs alone cannot supply those measures.

Because this article is being checked during the event’s final day, readers should verify live conditions before traveling. After 10 p.m., the page should be updated again so it does not remain an expired planning guide.

articles.title: Flint Grid Battery Starts Construction Near New Albany
articles.excerpt: Eolian started the 200-megawatt Flint Grid battery project in Licking County, but its effect on data-center connections and consumer bills is not established.
articles.body:
Eolian has started construction on Flint Grid, a 200-megawatt battery-energy-storage project in Jersey Township beside the New Albany business corridor. The project can shift stored electricity across time, but available records do not prove that it will accelerate specific data centers, housing projects or reduce household bills.

## What is being built

The [Flint Grid project page](https://www.flintgridproject.com/) locates the system on 14.89 acres along Jug Street Road in Licking County. It describes a 200-megawatt battery with a four-hour design and remote monitoring.

Eolian’s later construction announcement described 1.06 gigawatt-hours and approximately 5.3 hours of discharge. The difference indicates an updated or differently stated configuration that should be resolved in final operating specifications.

## Storage is not generation

A battery charges when electricity is available and discharges later. It can respond quickly and provide capacity or grid services, but it does not create net new electricity in the way a power plant does.

Energy Storage News [reported the construction start](https://www.energy-storage.news/eolian-begins-construction-on-1-06gwh-ohio-bess-largest-system-built-in-pjm/) and said commercial operation is expected before the 2027–2028 PJM capacity year. That remains a project target until the facility reaches operation.

## Size claims need precise wording

Eolian calls Flint Grid the largest battery built to date in Ohio and the PJM footprint and the first grid-scale battery permitted by the Ohio Power Siting Board. Those are developer claims repeated in trade coverage; CREN did not reconstruct a complete inventory of every PJM battery.

The safer fact is that the approved and under-construction project has a 200-megawatt rating and is large relative to other publicly described regional systems.

## Unsupported real-estate claims removed

The original article said more grid room could mean faster warehouse and housing approvals and steadier household bills. No interconnection study, utility tariff analysis or project-specific approval record supported those outcomes.

Battery operation may affect grid conditions, but the magnitude and beneficiaries require system modeling and market data. Nearby land does not automatically become developable because one storage project starts construction.

## The next checkpoints

The Ohio Power Siting Board case record, construction milestones, final technical specifications and PJM capacity performance will show what is delivered. Consumer-price or development effects should be reported only when regulators, utilities or independent analysis quantify them.

articles.title: Anything Bagel Opens in Former Block’s East Columbus Shop
articles.excerpt: Anything Bagel opened August 14 at 6115 McNaughten Center, reviving the former Block’s shop while making claims about its inherited recipe and new program.
articles.body:
Anything Bagel opened August 14, 2026, at 6115 McNaughten Center in East Columbus, occupying the former Block’s Bagels location. The operator says it inherited Block’s original recipe, but that is a company claim rather than something CREN can independently verify through public records or taste comparisons.

## What is verified

The company’s [official site](https://www.anythingbagel.com/) identifies the business, while [614NOW’s opening report](https://614now.com/2026/food-drink/new-bagel-shop-to-take-over-former-legacy-blocks-bagels-location) lists the McNaughten Center address, August 14 opening and daily hours from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The shop follows Block’s Bagels and a brief Marx Bagels operation at the same address. That succession is part of the location’s history but does not establish why either prior business closed.

## The recipe statement needs attribution

Anything Bagel says it inherited the original Block’s recipe and intends to continue the baking approach. CREN has no recipe document, licensing agreement or controlled product comparison that independently proves sameness.

The accurate formulation is therefore that the new operator makes the claim. The original story presented it as an established fact.

## The new program

The operator also announced Bake It Forward, a rotating specialty bagel intended to direct part of its proceeds to a local cause. The public announcement does not specify a fixed donation percentage, recipient-selection method or first-year fundraising target.

Those details will determine how the program can be evaluated. A charitable concept should not be assigned an impact figure before distributions are reported.

## What one reopening cannot show

Filling a storefront restores an active business use at the address. It does not by itself prove higher surrounding foot traffic, stable commercial rents or renewed neighborhood investment.

Opening-day status also cannot establish long-term viability. Regular hours, customer demand and lease performance emerge over time, and none can be measured from a single announcement. CREN therefore treats the August 14 opening as a verified operational milestone while withholding conclusions about permanence, expansion or the surrounding retail market.

The original article made those broader claims without traffic, leasing or sales data and linked the story to a home-search service. This version removes that promotion.

## What to watch

Posted hours and ordering availability will show whether operations stabilize after opening. Future reporting can also document Bake It Forward recipients and disclosed donations, rather than predicting expansion to additional locations.

articles.title: M/I Homes Withdraws Heath Hills as Annexation Debate Continues
articles.excerpt: M/I Homes withdrew the Heath Hills proposal after conflict over development and school boundaries, while Ohio Senate Bill 173 remains pending in committee.
articles.body:
M/I Homes withdrew its Heath Hills residential proposal in Licking County after a dispute involving Heath’s municipal boundary and Granville’s school district. The withdrawal ended that application, but it did not change Ohio annexation law; Senate Bill 173 remains pending in the Senate Education Committee.

## What was withdrawn

WSYX [reported M/I Homes’ withdrawal](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/heath-hills-development-collapse-in-licking-co-prompts-annexation-law-push-in-ohio) after a prolonged local dispute. The proposal had contemplated more than 500 homes on land within Heath but located in the Granville Exempted Village School District.

WOSU’s earlier [report on the dispute](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-07-20/heath-hills-development-debate-is-licking-countys-latest-growing-pain-but-it-wont-be-the-last) documented disagreement over added students, tax revenue, infrastructure and the responsibilities of the city and school district.

## Enrollment forecasts were contested estimates

Granville officials warned that the project could add hundreds of students. Those figures were projections based on assumed housing and student-generation rates, not students already enrolled.

The original CREN story repeated an estimate of roughly 840 students and described the result as catastrophic through attributed statements. This rewrite preserves the existence of the concern but does not present a forecast as a measured outcome.

## What Senate Bill 173 would do

The Ohio Legislature’s [official Senate Bill 173 page](https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/sb173) says the bill concerns school-district territory annexations. The Legislative Service Commission analysis describes an automatic transfer in specified annexations within a county containing a megaproject, subject to several conditions and exceptions.

That scope is narrower than saying every annexed parcel would automatically join the annexing city’s school district. As of CREN’s August 15 check, the bill had been introduced and referred to the Senate Education Committee but had not passed the Senate.

## What the withdrawal does not prove

The sources show that the boundary and school-finance dispute was central. They do not prove it was the only reason for the developer’s decision or that market demand played no role unless M/I Homes provides a complete explanation.

The withdrawal also does not prohibit a later owner or developer from submitting a different plan under applicable law.

## The next checkpoints

Readers should watch the official bill docket for hearings or amendments and Heath records for any new application on the site. Future coverage should distinguish developer statements, school forecasts, adopted agreements and enacted state law rather than treating them as equivalent.

articles.title: Crew Advances From Leagues Cup; Astor Park Is a Separate Story
articles.excerpt: The Crew advanced after three home matches, but claims that the tournament tested Astor Park leasing or nearby short-term rentals lack supporting data.
articles.body:
The Columbus Crew completed three Leagues Cup home matches and advanced to a quarterfinal against Club América in California. The games were real Arena District events, but the original CREN article improperly treated them as evidence about Astor Park leasing, restaurant demand and short-term rentals without measuring any of those outcomes.

## Three announced home dates are now in the past

The Crew’s [official competition schedule](https://www.columbuscrew.com/news/leagues-cup-announces-official-kickoff-times-for-the-columbus-crew-s-2026-phase-one-matches) listed home games against Atlas on August 4, Pachuca on August 7 and Pumas on August 11. All were scheduled at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field, the current sponsored name used by the club.

The original story called the venue Lower.com Field and previewed the games as upcoming. Because all three dates have passed, those descriptions needed an update rather than minor stylistic editing.

## Advancement is verified; local spending is not

[AS reported on August 14](https://as.com/us/futbol/leagues-cup-confirma-sedes-en-estados-unidos-para-los-cuartos-de-final-f202608-n/) that Columbus would face Club América in a quarterfinal at Dignity Health Sports Park in Carson, California, on August 26. That independently confirms the Crew advanced from phase one and that its next tournament match would not be in the Arena District.

The records reviewed for this rewrite do not provide attendance, restaurant receipts, parking revenue or hotel demand for the three Columbus matches. CREN therefore removed claims that the games tested nearby businesses or created recurring demand for short-term rentals.

## Astor Park has its own development record

Astor Park is a mixed-use project beside the stadium, but it should not be used as scenery for unrelated claims. In a [project announcement](https://www.pizzuti.com/press/astor-park-residential-a-block-groundbreaking), Pizzuti and Haslam Sports Group said the first residential block would contain 261 multifamily units.

[Axios reported in 2025](https://www.axios.com/local/columbus/2025/02/21/astor-park-is-behind-schedule-but-making-progress) that the broader residential plan was years behind its earlier schedule. That history is a warning against repeating developer delivery dates without current permit, construction or leasing records.

The original article said apartments were rising nearby and used lease-up speed as a test of the district’s sports-and-housing strategy. CREN did not find a current occupancy report or verified delivery update supporting that framing.

## Event traffic and housing require different evidence

Stadium matches can temporarily change pedestrian movement, transit use and parking demand. Housing performance is measured through completions, occupancy, rent, concessions and renewal data over longer periods.

Placing those topics in one headline does not establish a causal connection. A responsible follow-up would compare event-day transportation counts with non-event days, then report Astor Park through separate public records and leasing data.

The next sports checkpoint is the August 26 quarterfinal. The next defensible Astor Park checkpoint is a dated construction, certificate-of-occupancy or leasing record from the city, developer or property manager. CREN should not use the outcome of a soccer match as a proxy for the performance of nearby real estate.

articles.title: Gahanna Clears Creekside Sites, but Construction Is Unset
articles.excerpt: Gahanna completed demolition along Mill Street for a proposed mixed-use project, but detailed approvals, financing and a construction date remain unresolved.
articles.body:
Gahanna completed demolition on several Mill Street properties associated with the proposed Creekside Reimagined development. Current concepts call for up to 263 apartments, a 55- to 70-room hotel and commercial space, but the city says design, engineering, financing and approvals remain before construction.

## The city separates public and private work

The [City of Gahanna project page](https://www.gahanna.gov/650/Creekside-Reimagined) describes two related efforts: public infrastructure and plaza improvements, and a private mixed-use proposal by Connect Real Estate and Benson Capital. Treating them as one $100 million city project would blur funding and responsibility.

The city says the Gahanna Community Improvement Corporation obtained a state grant for demolition on the first-phase properties and contributed land to the private project. The public record reviewed does not state that the grant finances apartment or hotel construction.

## The program remains conceptual

The [city presentation](https://www.gahanna.gov/DocumentCenter/View/3383) shows two buildings, up to 263 apartments, a 55- to 70-room hotel, restaurants, coworking space and parking in the first phase. [CityScene’s account](https://www.cityscenecolumbus.com/communities/uniquely-gahanna/a-community-vision-moves-forward/) provides an independent summary, but concept drawings and ranges are not final permits.

The city characterizes the investment group as bringing approximately $100 million in financial resources. That phrasing is not the same as a closed construction loan, guaranteed project cost or public expenditure.

## Demolition is not a groundbreaking

Clearing old buildings changes the physical site, but it does not prove vertical construction has started. The previous headline implied that demolition directly cleared the way for a settled development schedule.

Detailed design, utility review, financing and land-use approvals can change the building count, unit total, hotel size and timing. CREN also removed claims that the proposal would support nearby property values; no valuation study was supplied.

## What to watch next

The next verifiable records are Planning Commission applications, engineering plans, financing close and building permits. Those documents should distinguish the city’s flood and public-space work from private construction.

Until then, the accurate status is that sites have been cleared for a substantial but still conditional proposal. Residents can evaluate later filings against the city’s published concept rather than assuming every element will be delivered.

## How CREN checked this account

This revision distinguishes originating records from commentary and promotional descriptions. It preserves source-specific uncertainty instead of combining unlike measurements or turning a stated intention into an outcome. The linked records let readers inspect the evidence available on the fact-check date; later schedules, designs and market conditions may differ.

CREN also removed transaction advice and claims about property values, rents, demand or economic effects when the sources supplied no reproducible analysis. A future update should use the same definitions and geography, identify any changed status and explain conflicts rather than quietly replacing the earlier record.

articles.title: Bank Run Event Center Opens While Metro Park Work Continues
articles.excerpt: Bank Run’s reservable event facilities are operating in Lockbourne, but Metro Parks still labels the larger park under construction and limits general access.
articles.body:
Bank Run’s event center in Lockbourne is accepting reservations and program use, but Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks still labels the broader park under construction. Current official information supports event-facility access and a paved trail, not an unrestricted grand opening of every planned feature.

## The official status is split

Metro Parks’ [current Bank Run page](https://www.metroparks.net/parks-and-trails/bank-run/) lists the park as under construction. It separately says the event center is available by reservation or program use at 1570 Rohr Road in Lockbourne.

That distinction corrects the original CREN headline, which presented Bank Run as Columbus’s fully arrived newest Metro Park. Some facilities are usable, while the agency has not declared the entire park open for unrestricted daily recreation.

## What can be reserved

The official page lists two lodges that each accommodate 99 people for seated functions, a 299-person Grand Shelter and a 120-person Flagstone Shelter. It also describes full-site rentals for events with more than 1,000 guests.

Those capacities do not support the original claim of a single 10,000-person event space. CREN found no current Metro Parks page stating that capacity and has withdrawn it.

## Trail and slide details

Metro Parks identifies a 3.25-mile paved multipurpose loop around the quarry pond and through the property. The agency warns that the trail may close during event-center activities, so access is conditional.

An earlier [Metro Parks construction profile](https://www.metroparks.net/blog/behind-the-parks-meet-trevor-at-metro-parks-headquarters/) described plans for a 100-foot slide with a 20-foot elevation drop. The current park page does not list the slide among available facilities, so CREN cannot report it as open.

## What the development means

The measurable change is a new reservable public-event complex and limited recreational infrastructure on a former YMCA property. No source reviewed measures effects on nearby property values, development demand or business revenue.

[Columbus Navigator’s preview](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/bank-run-metro-park-event-center/) provides additional reporting on the concept, but the Metro Parks status page controls current access information.

## What to verify next

The next checkpoint is a formal agency announcement that the park and remaining features are complete. Until then, visitors should check the official page for reservations, closures and permitted access before traveling to the site.

articles.title: Mercy on Main Wins Conditional Credits for 65 Columbus Homes
articles.excerpt: OHFA conditionally reserved federal tax credits for the 65-unit Mercy on Main proposal, but the award is not final financing, construction or completed housing.
articles.body:
The Ohio Housing Finance Agency conditionally reserved federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits for Mercy on Main, a proposed 65-unit apartment development in Columbus. The award advances the financing plan, but it is not a building permit, financial closing, construction start or guarantee that every proposed apartment will be delivered.

## What OHFA approved

The [Ohio Housing Finance Agency award notice](https://ohiohome.org/news/releases/2026/9percent-taxcredits.aspx) lists Mercy on Main among projects receiving conditional commitments in May 2026. OHFA selected 25 developments statewide from 62 applications.

The federal nine-percent credit is allocated over a 10-year period and is commonly sold to investors to raise equity for qualifying rental housing. A reservation gives the project a major financing source, subject to program requirements and later milestones.

## What the application proposes

The project’s [OHFA application summary](https://ohiohome.org/ppd/proposals/2026/NewAffordability-General/MercyonMain.pdf) identifies 65 apartments and a total development budget of approximately $22.8 million. It lists studios and one-, two- and three-bedroom homes with income restrictions at several levels.

Those numbers are the applicant’s proposed program. Design, cost and financing can change before closing and construction.

## The developer’s role

Kingsley and Company’s [project announcement](https://www.kingsleyandcompany.com/post/kingsley-co-expands-affordable-housing-efforts-into-columbus-with-mercy-on-main) describes its Columbus expansion and Mercy on Main concept. Company background, including the founder’s former professional-football career, is not evidence of project feasibility and has been removed from the headline.

The material issue for readers is the project’s public financing, affordability commitments and delivery status, not celebrity framing.

## What remains unresolved

CREN found no evidence in the reviewed records that construction had started. The conditional award does not establish final permits, land closing, syndication proceeds, permanent debt or an opening date.

The application’s income limits also do not mean every apartment will serve the same household income. Final recorded restrictions and tenant-selection materials will govern eligibility.

The stated development budget is an application estimate, not a cash grant from OHFA. Tax-credit equity depends on later compliance, investor pricing and financial closing, while other debt and subsidy sources may still be required. That distinction prevents the conditional reservation from being mistaken for a fully funded construction package.

## The next checkpoints

The next verifiable steps are OHFA carryover and closing documents, city permits, a recorded construction loan and a formal groundbreaking. Future coverage should describe units as proposed until those records show that work is under construction, then wait for occupancy approval before calling them delivered.

articles.title: Columbus Stops New Courthouse Plan and Turns to Renovation
articles.excerpt: Columbus stopped its new municipal courthouse project after the mayor cited a cost above $335 million, but the replacement renovation still lacks a public scope.
articles.body:
Columbus ended its planned new Franklin County Municipal Court project in July 2026 after Mayor Andrew Ginther said its estimated cost exceeded $335 million. The city now proposes renovating existing facilities, but it has not published a complete renovation scope, budget, schedule or accounting of sunk costs.

## What the city stopped

WOSU [reported the cancellation](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-07-29/columbus-halts-construction-of-new-franklin-county-municipal-court-citing-tight-city-budget) on July 29. The planned eight-story, 340,000-square-foot courthouse would have occupied Dorrian Commons and connected with existing government buildings.

The mayor’s office said a new building estimate had risen from $200 million in 2018 to more than $335 million. That comparison is the administration’s estimate as reported by WOSU, not a construction contract total audited by CREN.

## Public money was already committed

A [2025 City Council ordinance](https://columbus.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=66C8650F-F568-420F-9236-4F68268276C9&ID=7477616&Options=&Search=) authorized up to $12.59 million more for Moody Nolan’s architect-of-record services. The ordinance also documents earlier design contracts.

WOSU reported that voters approved a $250 million bond issue in 2025 with $100 million earmarked for a new courthouse. Stopping the project raises separate questions about which funds remain available, which expenses cannot be recovered and what voter or Council action may be required.

## Renovation is not yet a complete alternative

The administration proposes work at 375 South High Street and the Karnes Building. The Municipal Court said it was disappointed but would work with the city on next steps.

The mayor said renovation could free at least $75 million for other capital needs. CREN found no published renovation design, cost estimate or schedule that independently demonstrates those savings.

## The unresolved public-record questions

The original headline said Columbus picked renovation, which is directionally correct but too final. The city selected a policy direction; it has not yet presented a fully approved replacement project.

Authorized design spending is not necessarily the same as the amount ultimately paid, and a contract ceiling does not reveal what can be recovered after cancellation. A complete accounting would need invoices, amendments, termination obligations and any reusable design work. The available ordinance and news reports do not provide that closeout ledger.

The next records should include contract closeout costs, bond-fund treatment, renovation feasibility and design documents, court operational requirements and Council authorizations. Until those appear, neither the renovation price nor the claimed savings can be treated as settled.

articles.title: Pelotonia’s 2026 Ride Used a New Short Route; Totals Are Pending
articles.excerpt: Pelotonia added a shorter downtown loop in Columbus for its August ride, but the organizer’s pre-event estimate should not be reported as a final rider count.
articles.body:
Pelotonia’s August ride introduced a shorter downtown loop through Bexley and Ohio State, widening the range of available distances. The organizer expected more than 8,000 riders, but CREN found no post-event report confirming that estimate, so it should not be presented as an actual count.

## What Pelotonia announced before the ride

Pelotonia scheduled its annual Ride Weekend for August 1 and 2, following an opening ceremony on July 31. In a [pre-event announcement](https://www.pelotonia.org/news/ride-weekend-2026/), the nonprofit said it expected more than 8,000 riders and 3,000 volunteers. Those figures described anticipated participation, not a final attendance audit.

The distinction matters because the original CREN article changed an estimate into a statement of fact. As of this fact check, Pelotonia’s public Ride Weekend page still describes the event in advance-facing language and does not publish a verified final rider total. CREN therefore cannot independently confirm how many people started or completed a route.

## A shorter route changed the entry point

The [official route page](https://www.pelotonia.org/get-involved/ride-weekend/) listed road options from 17 to 165 miles. The new downtown loop traveled through Bexley and the Ohio State campus before returning to North Bank Park, while longer routes finished in New Albany or Gambier.

That range is the most supportable change in the event design. It created a shorter road option, but participation still carried a fundraising commitment. Calling the loop more accessible should refer to distance and riding experience, not affordability, disability access or who ultimately registered; the available records do not establish those broader effects.

## Traffic effects were documented, business gains were not

Ohio State’s [traffic notice](https://ttm.osu.edu/traffic-impacts/august-1-road-closures-parking-impacts) warned of road closures and parking impacts while riders crossed campus on August 1. Pelotonia’s spectator guidance also identified temporary restrictions near North Bank Park and McFerson Commons.

The earlier story went further by saying businesses along the routes typically receive more foot traffic. CREN found no sales, pedestrian-count or merchant-survey evidence supporting that claim for this ride, so it has been removed. A large event can change travel patterns without proving a measurable sales benefit for nearby businesses.

## What can be verified next

Pelotonia said before the ride that it had raised more than $350 million for cancer research since its founding. Ohio State’s [Pelotonia program page](https://cancer.osu.edu/for-donors-and-volunteers/signature-events/pelotonia) separately reports that the prior fundraising year produced $29.2 million.

Those cumulative and prior-year figures should not be confused with the result of this year’s ride. The next reliable checkpoint is Pelotonia’s annual impact report or another post-event accounting that identifies actual participation and fundraising for the completed event. Until then, the pre-ride attendance number remains an organizer estimate.

articles.title: Upper Arlington Led One Week of High-Price County Sales
articles.excerpt: Four Upper Arlington transfers exceeded $1 million in one Franklin County report, but a single week does not establish a luxury-market trend.
articles.body:
Upper Arlington accounted for several of Franklin County’s highest recorded residential transfers during July 17–23, 2026, including one at $3.36 million. The weekly deed report documents those closings, but it does not prove stronger demand, appreciation or a durable countywide luxury-market trend.

## The report is a transfer snapshot

The [Franklin County Auditor’s news index](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/Home) identifies the weekly home-sales report covering July 17 through July 23. The underlying county data recorded 440 residential transfers, a $304,000 median and a $349,683 average for that reporting period.

Recorded deeds describe completed transfers, not every market listing or contract. The week’s mix can change sharply when a handful of expensive properties closes.

## Several large transfers were in Upper Arlington

The county list included an Onandaga Drive transfer at $3.36 million, an Oxford Road transfer at $2.7 million, an Arlington Avenue transfer at $1.65 million and a Hillside Drive transfer above $1 million. These are transaction records, not appraisals of neighboring homes.

The earlier version called them evidence of strong top-end demand. Price alone cannot establish competition, marketing time, offer count or buyer motivation, so that interpretation has been withdrawn.

## Market pages use different measurements

[Realtor.com’s Upper Arlington overview](https://www.realtor.com/realestateandhomes-search/Upper-Arlington_OH/overview) summarizes listings and market conditions using its own geography and data. Asking-price measures from a portal should not be blended with one week of recorded county deeds.

The gap between a multimillion-dollar transfer and the county median illustrates distribution, not a down payment comparison or an instruction to buy elsewhere.

## What would demonstrate a trend

A credible luxury-market analysis would examine several quarters of verified transfers, property characteristics, price per square foot and repeat-sale or matched-property comparisons. It would also separate Upper Arlington municipal boundaries from postal ZIP codes.

The next weekly auditor report may contain a different concentration of high-price sales. Readers should use parcel-level records for individual comparisons and avoid treating this one week as a valuation of Upper Arlington as a whole.

## How CREN checked this account

This revision distinguishes originating records from commentary and promotional descriptions. It preserves source-specific uncertainty instead of combining unlike measurements or turning a stated intention into an outcome. The linked records let readers inspect the evidence available on the fact-check date; later schedules, designs and market conditions may differ.

CREN also removed transaction advice and claims about property values, rents, demand or economic effects when the sources supplied no reproducible analysis. A future update should use the same definitions and geography, identify any changed status and explain conflicts rather than quietly replacing the earlier record.

articles.title: Festival Latino Columbus Move Changes Downtown Visitor Plan
articles.excerpt: Festival Latino is moving from Genoa Park to Columbus Commons and the Ohio Theatre, changing parking, weather planning and indoor programming.
articles.body:
Festival Latino is scheduled to move from Genoa Park to Columbus Commons and the Ohio Theatre for its August event. The new footprint adds indoor programming and a different parking plan, but organizers—not independent measurements—are the source of claims that the move will improve safety or accessibility.

## The confirmed change is the venue

The [festival’s official site](https://www.festivallatino.net/) schedules the event for August 22 and 23 at Columbus Commons and the Ohio Theatre. It lists free admission, outdoor performances and activities representing cultures from across Latin America.

[Spectrum News 1 independently reported](https://spectrumnews1.com/oh/dayton/news/2026/04/27/columbus-festical-latino-relocates) that the festival is leaving its longtime Genoa Park location. CAPA, the producer, described the replacement venues as more welcoming, secure and accessible. Those are the organizer’s stated goals; CREN found no crowd-flow study, accessibility audit or public-safety analysis that measures the expected improvement.

## Indoor programming is a practical difference

The Ohio Theatre gives the event a programmed indoor component rather than a general severe-weather backup. [Columbus Navigator’s preview](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/festival-latino-columbus-commons/) lists free screenings of *Coco* and *Encanto* along with performances and activities inside the theater.

The official plan still calls the festival rain or shine. Its visitor guidance says there is no rain location and that severe weather may require guests to leave festival grounds temporarily. Readers should therefore not assume that the theater can hold the entire outdoor audience during a storm.

## Parking is clearer, not necessarily easier

The [festival’s visitor page](https://www.festivallatino.net/plan-your-visit/) identifies paid parking at the Columbus Commons garage at 55 East Rich Street and nearby surface lots. It also lists bicycle racks at each entrance and says the event will not participate in the downtown outdoor-refreshment district.

The original CREN story called parking and transit access easier than at Genoa Park. That comparison lacked travel-time, price, capacity or transit-service evidence. The better conclusion is narrower: the producer has published a specific garage option, while availability and cost will depend on demand when visitors arrive.

## The lineup is broader than the first draft said

The official schedule names performers from Cuba, Mexico and the Dominican Republic, as well as Columbus artists. The program also includes food, dance, children’s activities and a marketplace for artists and entrepreneurs.

The first draft listed only part of the announced lineup and incorrectly tied the weekend to Pelotonia, which occurred earlier in the month. That unrelated event has been removed from the local-impact analysis.

The next factual checkpoint is the producer’s final schedule and any day-of weather or operations advisory. After the festival, attendance records and visitor feedback would be needed before concluding that the new footprint improved access, safety or economic activity.

articles.title: Franklin County Tentative Home Values Rise About 10%
articles.excerpt: Franklin County posted tentative 2026 parcel values averaging about 10% higher for residences and opened an informal review process.
articles.body:
Franklin County’s tentative 2026 residential property values increased by about 10% on average, but an individual parcel can move by more or less. The value update is not the same as a 10% tax increase, and owners should use the county review and appeal procedures for parcel-specific questions.

## The county published tentative values

The [Franklin County Auditor’s June notice](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/News-articles/20260610-Property-Value-Update) says the update covers more than 440,000 parcels. Preliminary averages were about 10% for residential property, 4% for commercial property and 13% for industrial property.

Those are class-wide averages. They do not predict the change for a particular home, and tentative values can change through review before certification.

## The update uses recent sales

The auditor’s [appraisal explanation](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/Real-Estate/Appraisal) says the triennial update reviews arm’s-length sales from 2023 through 2025. Unlike the prior full reappraisal, it does not require a complete exterior inspection of each parcel.

A county value is an estimate for taxation, not a listing price or guarantee of what a home would sell for.

## Value and tax are different calculations

A 10% value increase does not mechanically create a 10% bill increase. Voted levies, effective rates, exemptions and changes across a taxing district affect the result.

The previous story suggested higher values could simply be passed through to renters. No rent dataset or lease analysis supported that claim, so it has been removed.

## Review before filing a formal complaint

The county directs owners first to its Know Your Home Value review process. Useful evidence may include a recent arm’s-length sale, correct property characteristics or comparable transfers, but the appropriate evidence depends on the parcel.

[Ohio Revised Code 5715.19](https://codes.ohio.gov/assets/laws/revised-code/authenticated/57/5715/5715.19/3-20-2026/5715.19-3-20-2026.pdf) governs formal valuation complaints. The 39th Dublin Irish Festival ran from July 31 through August 2, 2026, at Coffman Park and is now finished. Official pages document the schedule and cultural program, but CREN found no final 2026 attendance or audited economic-impact report available by August 15.

## What took place

The City of Dublin’s [official calendar](https://dublinohiousa.gov/calendar-events/dublin-irish-festival/) lists the event at Coffman Park and marks it finished. Hours ran from 4 p.m. to midnight Friday, 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Saturday and 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday.

The [festival FAQ](https://dublinirishfestival.org/faq/) provided ticket, accessibility, transport and site rules. Sunday offered limited free admission before 11 a.m., according to the event information.

## The program was broader than music

The organizer promoted multiple music and dance stages, pipe bands, cultural exhibits, food and athletic events. Those listings establish the intended program, although they do not document how many acts ultimately performed or how many visitors attended.

The original article repeated a largest-in-the-world description and a readers-choice ranking. Those are promotional distinctions rather than independently measured size comparisons, so they are not the basis of this rewrite.

## Economic claims need a dated study

Dublin’s economic-development office cited a 2023 study estimating a $12 million regional effect. That older estimate may provide context, but it is not a measured result for the 2026 festival.

Likewise, a crowded event does not by itself establish higher home demand, hotel revenue or restaurant sales. Those claims require occupancy, spending, tax or foot-traffic data tied to the event period.

## Why the status update matters

The earlier CREN page remained written as a planning guide after the dates passed. Event stories should change from future tense to a documented recap or be archived clearly, so readers do not mistake expired ticket and transport details for current instructions.

The archived ticket rules and advertised schedule can document what organizers planned, but they cannot show what occurred at the gate. A credible post-event account would separate advance promotion from scanned admissions, actual vendor participation, emergency responses and disclosed public costs. None of those final measures appeared in the records CREN reviewed.

The next useful records are the city’s final attendance count, public-safety summary and any updated economic-impact analysis. Until those appear, the defensible record is the completed schedule and official program.

Merus has begun construction on Dixon Commerce Center, a 190,960-square-foot speculative industrial building at 4390 Hubner Way in Obetz. The developer and trade reporting target April 2027 completion, but no tenant, lease rate, construction cost or employment commitment was publicly identified.

## What is under construction

Merus lists the [Dixon Commerce Center groundbreaking](https://www.merus1894.com/news) in its July 2026 company updates. Commercial Property Executive independently [reported the start](https://www.commercialsearch.com/news/merus-breaks-ground-on-191-ksf-columbus-facility/) and identified a 14.2-acre site.

The project is speculative, meaning construction began without a publicly announced tenant occupying the entire building. That status creates leasing risk that a build-to-suit project would not carry in the same way.

## Building and location details

Trade reporting describes 19 dock-high loading doors, two drive-in doors and approximately 2,000 square feet of office space. The site lies near Interstate 270 and roughly five miles from Rickenbacker International Airport.

Those physical and location details indicate the property is designed for distribution, manufacturing or logistics users. They do not establish which use will lease it or how much traffic a future tenant would generate.

## What the announcement does not prove

The original story treated another warehouse as evidence of broad demand around Rickenbacker. One groundbreaking cannot establish the area’s vacancy, absorption or rent trend without comparable industrial-market data.

No public tenant, lease rate, project budget or job count appeared in the reviewed sources. CREN therefore removed predictions about employment, nearby land value and the strength of the whole submarket.

## Schedule is still a forecast

The reported April 2027 delivery is a development target, not a certificate of occupancy. Weather, materials, inspections and leasing-related changes may affect the schedule.

Proximity to the airport also does not prove that a future occupant will depend on aviation freight. Tenant identity, cargo patterns and truck counts remain unknown. Until a lease is announced, readers should treat the building as available industrial inventory and avoid assigning jobs, traffic or tax receipts to an unidentified operator.

The next checkpoints are a tenant announcement, building permits and inspections, construction completion and recorded occupancy. Those events will show whether the project advances from speculative construction to an operating facility.

Cardinal Health’s [employment location page](https://jobs.cardinalhealth.com/locations/locations) lists warehouse jobs at 9560 Heartland Court. This first-party record supports the tenant’s presence, but it does not disclose rent, lease term or credit protections.

The industry report says the facility distributes over-the-counter medication to more than 20 forward distribution centers. That operating description originates with company and property sources and should not be treated as an independent economic-impact study.

Investor pricing can reflect building age, tenant credit, remaining lease term, rent growth, financing and location. Without those terms and comparable transactions, the sale cannot prove that industrial land around Rickenbacker commands a particular price.

The previous article called the asset safer than vacant buildings and advised investors to use it as a benchmark. Those statements were unsupported investment analysis and have been removed.

## What to verify next

The recorded deed and conveyance documents would confirm buyer, seller and consideration. Lease filings or direct responses could add context about term and occupancy.

Until then, the responsible conclusion is that a large, occupied logistics property changed hands at a reported price. It does not establish future returns, tax-base stability or effects on nearby housing.

articles.title: Canal Crossing Starts Construction, but 400 Jobs Remain a Forecast
articles.excerpt: Opus has started a three-building speculative industrial project near Canal Winchester, while its job total remains a developer projection, not hiring.
articles.body:
Opus says construction has started on Canal Crossing Commerce Center near Canal Winchester, a three-building project being built without committed tenants. The developer’s estimate of more than 400 eventual jobs is a forecast, not a hiring announcement, and the final employment mix will depend on leases that have not been disclosed.

## Construction has started on a speculative campus

In a [July 21 project announcement](https://www.opus-group.com/News/major-speculative-development-in-canal-winchester), Opus said it had begun building an 898,500-square-foot industrial campus on 72 acres near the US 33 and Gender Road interchange. Speculative construction means work proceeds before tenants sign leases for the space.

[Columbus Business First independently reported](https://www.bizjournals.com/columbus/news/2026/07/23/opus-canal-winchester-industrial-rickenbacker.html) the start of the project and identified its reported development cost as $60 million. The developer says the location is about five miles from Rickenbacker International Airport, but proximity alone does not establish tenant demand or future freight volume.

## The job number needs a clear label

Opus says the completed project is expected to create more than 400 jobs. No named employers, signed leases, job classifications, wage levels or hiring dates appear in the announcement.

That makes the figure an economic-development projection rather than a count of positions currently available. A warehouse tenant, manufacturer and data-center supplier can occupy similar industrial space while producing very different employment numbers. The original article incorrectly presented the forecast as a set outcome.

## Public infrastructure is part of the deal

The developer says it will invest more than $4 million in public infrastructure, including road work and land for a potential future interchange. A [Canal Winchester public meeting record](https://canalwinchesterohio.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Agenda/_07142025-688) documents local review material for the Opus project, providing a public-record trail beyond the company announcement.

The infrastructure commitment is relevant because truck and employee traffic will affect public roads. It does not establish that every improvement is complete, nor does the development announcement quantify expected truck trips. Residents need engineering plans and traffic studies—not a marketing description—to assess intersection-level effects.

## Regional demand should be measured, not assumed

The original story said developers build speculatively only when they expect strong demand and then converted that expectation into a broad claim about Central Ohio. The first part describes the developer’s risk decision; the second requires market evidence.

Colliers is marketing the buildings for lease, which confirms that the tenant mix is still unresolved. Vacancy, absorption, asking rent and competing projects should be evaluated from one consistent industrial-market dataset before calling the area unusually strong or weak.

The next verifiable checkpoints are building permits, construction milestones and signed tenant announcements. Those records will show whether the project proceeds on schedule and whether the eventual employers support the job estimate. Until then, CREN should describe the campus as under construction, speculative and unleased—not as 400 jobs already created.

Dublin’s Planning and Zoning Commission approved Bridge North’s final development plan on July 9, 2026. The roughly seven-acre proposal includes 296 homes, a 150-room hotel, office and retail space, but the approval does not establish a construction start, completion date, rents or financing.

## What the plan contains

The approved program calls for 296 residential units, a 150-room hotel, about 75,000 square feet of office space and about 60,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Structured parking and public-space improvements are also part of the submitted plan.

These figures describe the approved design. They should not be reported as completed units, leased space or guaranteed final construction quantities.

The project sits near the existing Bridge Park district. Crawford Hoying’s [Bridge Park overview](https://www.crawfordhoying.com/projects/bridge-park) describes the adjacent mixed-use development and its residential, office, hotel and market components.

The two projects are related geographically but have different developers and approval records. Existing activity at Bridge Park does not prove future occupancy, prices or economic performance at Bridge North.

## What approval leaves unresolved

Final development-plan approval settles a major land-use review, but construction still depends on permits, contracts, financing and site work. The current city page does not provide apartment rents, affordability restrictions or a guaranteed groundbreaking date.

The original CREN story also suggested that the units would ease regional rent pressure. A 296-unit project can add supply if built, but its effect on area rents would require market data after delivery.

## The next public checkpoints

Building and site permits, recorded financing, construction notices and certificates of occupancy will show whether the approved plan advances. CREN will keep proposed, approved, under-construction and completed unit counts separate in future updates.
