articles.title: Columbus ADU Guide Clarifies Rules, but Sewer Question Remains
articles.excerpt: Columbus now permits ADUs by right and offers project guidance, while an independent study says separate sewer connections may still raise development costs.
articles.body:
Columbus now allows accessory dwelling units by right in residential and apartment-residential districts and provides a guide to the approval process. A Greater Ohio Policy Center study found that the city’s interpretation of sewer rules may require a separate connection, but it did not calculate one universal added cost.

## What the zoning change did

Columbus City Council approved [Ordinance 2526-2025](https://columbus.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=7743645&GUID=D87D9CFE-225B-4A5C-9015-3482794E8FFB&FullText=1) on November 24, 2025. It permits accessory dwelling units, commonly called ADUs, in the city’s residential and apartment-residential districts when a proposal meets the code.

An ADU is an independent second dwelling on the same lot as a principal home or apartment building. It may be internal, attached or detached and must have its own living, sleeping, cooking, sanitation and entrance provisions.

The ordinance record says Columbus approved 110 ADU variances but issued only 57 building permits between 2019 and September 2025. Removing the case-by-case Council variance does not remove building permits, zoning review or historic-district approvals.

## The city guide is a starting point

The city’s [residential zoning page](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Building-Zoning-Services/Zoning/Residential-Zoning-Clearance) links its ADU materials and preliminary-review information. The guidance helps owners identify dimensional and application requirements, but it is not a construction estimate or approval for a particular lot.

Site constraints, utilities, building code, easements and historic-review rules can change a project’s feasibility. Readers should not treat a general handbook as a substitute for parcel-specific review.

## What the sewer study found

The [Greater Ohio Policy Center investigation](https://www.greaterohio.org/publications/2026/6/5/investigation-of-adu-sewer-requirements-in-columbus-oh) compared Columbus with Austin, Ann Arbor, Portland and Boston. It found that a shared sewer configuration commonly allowed in those peer cities is not permitted in Columbus under the city’s code and its interpretation of Ohio plumbing rules.

The report says a separate lateral is likely to increase costs and that savings from another configuration could be significant. It does not provide a single dollar amount applicable to every Columbus lot, so the original story’s broad cost framing has been narrowed.

## What has not changed

The reform creates legal capacity for more small homes; it does not guarantee that owners can finance or construct them. Nor does an ADU automatically produce affordable rent or positive investment returns.

The next verifiable checkpoints are permit counts after the rule change, any written utility-policy revision and actual project-cost data. Those records will show whether legalization translates into completed homes.

The [Columbus Recreation and Parks calendar](https://columbusrecparks.com/calendar/jazz-rib-fest/2026-07-24/) identifies the festival as a city-presented event with free music and barbecue vendors. Friday and Saturday hours run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.; Sunday runs from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The [festival’s event page](https://www.hotribscooljazz.org/about-the-event/) separately confirms West Bank Park and Bicentennial Park as the principal venues. Because schedules can change, visitors should use that page for weather, accessibility and last-minute programming notices rather than relying on an archived article.

## Three stages divide the program

The official lineup assigns national and regional acts to the West Bank and Bicentennial stages and adds a brass-band stage near the Main Street Bridge. That layout spreads performances across both sides of the river and means visitors should allow time to move between venues.

The earlier article called the lineup the strongest in years. CREN found no published comparison or scoring method that could support that superlative, so it has been removed.

## Admission is free, food is not

The city describes admission and music as free. Barbecue, drinks and other vendor purchases carry separate prices, and CREN did not find an official standardized food-price list.

The festival site says the organizers provide accessible routes and services. Visitors who need a specific accommodation should confirm the current procedure with the event because a general accessibility statement does not guarantee that every viewing position or vendor line will meet every need.

## Housing claims were unsupported

The previous version claimed festival visitors would consider moving downtown and that free events helped sustain housing demand. Attendance, residential inquiries and transaction data were not supplied, so those causal claims have been withdrawn.

The event may generate foot traffic, but measuring economic or real-estate effects would require attendance counts, visitor spending research and a method that separates the festival from other downtown activity. The next verifiable checkpoint is the city’s post-event reporting, if it publishes attendance or operating results.

## How CREN checked this account

This revision distinguishes originating records from commentary and promotional descriptions. It preserves source-specific uncertainty instead of combining unlike measurements or turning a stated intention into an outcome. The linked records let readers inspect the evidence available on the fact-check date; later schedules, designs and market conditions may differ.

CREN also removed transaction advice and claims about property values, rents, demand or economic effects when the sources supplied no reproducible analysis. A future update should use the same definitions and geography, identify any changed status and explain conflicts rather than quietly replacing the earlier record.

articles.title: Columbus Discovery District Deal Authorizes Talks, Not Construction
articles.excerpt: Columbus authorized an agreement for a proposed 518-unit Discovery District project, while separate votes, designs and financing remain necessary.
articles.body:
Columbus authorized an economic development agreement for a proposed Discovery District redevelopment with approximately 518 homes. The ordinance did not appropriate project funding, approve final buildings or start construction; later votes and development records remain necessary.

## The ordinance authorized an agreement

Columbus [Ordinance 1707-2026](https://columbus.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=380E7AC4-FBDE-4006-AC1A-F62E69AEC9ED&ID=8117731&Options=&Search=) authorizes an agreement with Pizzuti and an Encova affiliate for surface lots near Oak Street and Washington Avenue. The record describes approximately 518 homes, up to 15,000 square feet of retail and an estimated $96 million investment.

The fiscal-impact section says the ordinance itself requires $0 in funding. That directly contradicts language implying the city had already committed and spent infrastructure money.

## Future public contributions need later action

The city record contemplates a later request of up to $1.65 million for design and utility work, later construction funding, and a 575-space public garage. Each item needs its own budget and legislative process.

Describing those steps as planned commitments is more accurate than saying the city is already putting money into the project. Timing, final cost and approval can change.

## Design remains incomplete

[Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/96-million-development-planned-for-downtown-parking-lots-bw1/) and [Columbus Business First](https://www.bizjournals.com/columbus/news/2026/07/06/encova-pizzuti-downtown-columbus-development.html) reported the proposal, but detailed building locations, heights and phasing were not final.

CREN has removed statements that apartments are headed to the lots as a certainty. The approved agreement supports negotiation and coordination; zoning, commission review, financing and permits will determine what proceeds.

## No basis for investment advice

The old article predicted nearby land appreciation and directed readers toward an investment service. No appraisal, parcel-sales study or completed project result supported that advice.

The next checkpoints are capital-budget legislation, garage design, site plans, zoning, financing and permits. Until then, this is a city-authorized development framework for a proposed 518-unit project—not a completed transfer from parking lots to housing.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the development agreement separately from future public spending and physical delivery. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. CREN will revisit the question when a comparable record adds facts, rather than converting possibility into certainty or transaction advice.

articles.title: Great Southern Opens as Central Ohio’s 21st Metro Park
articles.excerpt: Great Southern Metro Park opened April 1 on the Scioto River in south Columbus, adding 70 acres of trails, prairie, play areas and fitness features.
articles.body:
Great Southern Metro Park opened April 1, 2026, becoming the 21st park in the Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks system. The 70-acre south Columbus site offers trails, prairie, play and fitness areas, while a planned Scioto Greenway connection remains a future project.

## What is open now

The [official park page](https://www.metroparks.net/parks-and-trails/great-southern/) places Great Southern at 125 Williams Road along the Scioto River. It lists a playground, recreation field, fitness stations, obstacle course, picnic areas and a combination of paved and natural-surface trails.

Metro Parks says the property covers 70 acres. Its April opening made Great Southern the system’s 21st park, a status also reported by [WOSU](https://www.wosu.org/2026-03-30/new-metro-park-to-open-in-south-columbus).

## Trail details matter

The park page identifies the paved Heer Park Loop and Lookout Loop, along with the gravel Canal Trail. Trail lengths and permitted uses vary, so visitors should use the official map rather than assume every route is paved or bicycle-accessible.

The site’s prairie occupies about 3 acres, according to Metro Parks. The agency describes a mix of native grasses and wildflowers intended to bloom through much of the growing season.

Metro Parks marks the Heer Park and Lookout loops as accessible paved routes, while the Canal Trail is gravel and includes a steep section. Those distinctions help visitors choose a route that matches their mobility and equipment.

## The river connection is incomplete

Early coverage emphasized the park’s Scioto River location. The official page says the Scioto Greenway Trail will eventually extend from Scioto Audubon to Great Southern, but it does not give a completion date on the current park page.

That distinction is important: the park is open, while the continuous trail connection to downtown is not yet presented as completed. CREN found no current construction schedule for the extension in the sources reviewed.

## What the opening means locally

The measurable change is expanded public access to recreation on the south side. The available records do not quantify effects on nearby home prices, business revenue or development demand, so CREN does not infer those outcomes.

The next checkpoints are any Metro Parks board action or capital plan that funds the greenway extension, plus updates to trail maps as the site develops. Visitors can already verify hours, rules, accessibility notes and route conditions through the park’s official page.

articles.title: Columbus Oktoberfest Returns, but It Does Not Prove Home Demand
articles.excerpt: Columbus Oktoberfest is scheduled for Sept. 11–13 at the Ohio Expo Center, while claims that the event raises German Village demand lack evidence.
articles.body:
Columbus Oktoberfest is scheduled for September 11 through 13 at the Ohio Expo Center, with free admission and paid parking. Its German Village history is documented, but the festival does not by itself prove stronger housing demand, higher values or a reason to buy in the neighborhood.

## The schedule and venue are confirmed

The [organizer’s event page](https://columbusoktoberfest.com/about/) lists September 11–13, 2026, at the Ohio Expo Center and State Fairgrounds. [Experience Columbus](https://www.experiencecolumbus.com/event/columbus-oktoberfest/80168/) independently lists the same dates and free admission.

The organizer lists $15 parking and different operating hours for each day. Readers should recheck those first-party details before traveling because event schedules and policies can change.

## The German Village connection is historical

The [Schmidt’s history](https://schmidthaus.com/oktoberfest) says the Columbus event began in Schiller Park and was revived with the Expo Center and partners in 2009. The current festival occurs at the fairgrounds, not in German Village.

That history is worth reporting, but it should not blur the current geography. Visitors do not automatically pass through German Village, and the sources do not measure event-day traffic there.

## Culture is not a housing-price model

The previous article said the festival gives buyers reasons to move into German Village and helps homes hold value. CREN found no attendance-to-sales study, buyer survey or price analysis supporting those statements.

Neighborhood culture can matter to individual preferences, but a yearly event at another venue cannot be isolated from housing supply, property condition, financing and other location factors.

## What responsible event coverage includes

Useful coverage should provide dates, hours, location, admission, parking, accessibility and weather policies. It should separate organizer claims from independently confirmed operations and avoid turning a public event into a home-search advertisement.

The next checkpoint is the final organizer schedule. Post-event attendance or economic effects would require documented counts or a stated method; CREN has removed the sales link and all unsupported real-estate conclusions.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the current festival venue separately from its German Village history and housing demand. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: COTA Line 30 Will Serve Hilliard, Not Dublin, in September
articles.excerpt: COTA’s finalized Line 30 will connect Hilliard, Upper Arlington, Ohio State and downtown in September; Dublin service will use an extended Line 1 instead.
articles.body:
COTA’s finalized September 2026 service plan puts Hilliard, Upper Arlington, Ohio State and downtown on the new Line 30, with buses every 30 minutes seven days a week. Contrary to the earlier CREN headline, Dublin is not on Line 30; it receives a separate extended Line 1 connection.

## The final route differs from the early concept

COTA’s [current service-change page](https://prodwww.cota.com/servicechanges/) says Line 30 will begin in September 2026. The route is planned to serve Hilliard, Kingsdale Shopping Center in Upper Arlington, Ohio State’s Wexner Medical Center and Carmenton Innovation District, then continue downtown.

The agency describes all-day service every 30 minutes, seven days a week. Exact trip times and stops should be checked against the final timetable when COTA publishes it.

## Dublin uses another line

Early planning materials described a possible Line 30 connection involving Dublin. COTA’s finalized information instead extends Line 1 to Ohio State Outpatient Care Dublin and downtown.

That correction materially changes the original article. Dublin riders may gain a direct connection, but it is not provided by Line 30 under the September plan.

## The budget is larger than one route

The [COTA 2026 budget announcement](https://cota.com/blog/cota-board-adopts-2026-budget-advancing-linkus-and-improving-transit-service-for-central-ohio/) funded approximately 94,000 additional service hours, 42 new operators, 38 buses and 30 COTA Plus vans. It also described 37 sidewalk and bikeway projects connected with the LinkUS program.

Those are budgeted resources and planned projects, not a guarantee that every service-hour or infrastructure target has already been delivered.

## Transit does not prove a property-value effect

A new route changes access for people whose origins, destinations and schedules match it. The available COTA materials do not measure Line 30’s effect on rents, home values or car ownership.

[WOSU’s LinkUS reporting](https://www.wosu.org/news/2026-05-27/cota-says-timeline-for-west-broad-street-bus-rapid-transit-line-construction-remains-fluid) also shows that separate rapid-transit projects have their own schedules and uncertainties. Line 30 should not be treated as proof that every LinkUS component is on the same timetable.

## What to verify next

The next checkpoints are the final Line 30 map and timetable, the first day of service and COTA’s ridership and on-time-performance reports after launch. Those records will show how the route operates in practice and whether later adjustments are needed.

articles.title: Amara Brings Mediterranean Dining Back to the Scioto Mile
articles.excerpt: Amara has replaced Milestone 229 on the Scioto Mile, but the riverfront restaurant’s opening history is more complicated than the original announcement suggested.
articles.body:
Amara has brought a new Mediterranean restaurant to the former Milestone 229 space at 229 South Civic Center Drive, restoring food service beside Bicentennial Park. Public records verify the lease and operating plans, although the restaurant’s published opening dates shifted during 2026.

## What the records establish

The [restaurant’s official site](https://www.eatamara.com/) lists the Civic Center Drive address, dinner service from Tuesday through Saturday and a menu built around dips, vegetables, seafood and grilled meats. A [Columbus City Council record](https://columbus.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=525BE8A3-542F-44BF-A628-08ABBD4001C9&ID=8007697&Options=&Search=) identifies BICHHU LLC as the operator and chef Joshua Dalton as a principal party.

That legislation says Amara entered its lease in March 2026. It authorized a temporary extension of the restaurant’s liquor permit onto Bicentennial Park property for as many as 19 city and Downtown Columbus Inc. events during 2026. The agreement does not establish customer traffic, sales or any effect on nearby property values.

## The opening date moved

The first public descriptions pointed to spring. [WOSU reported](https://www.wosu.org/2025-10-03/former-milestone-229-in-downtown-columbus-slated-to-be-riverside-mediterranean-restaurant) in October 2025 that Dalton planned a spring 2026 debut in the space Milestone 229 vacated after closing in late 2024. Amara’s own site later displayed July 2026 while also carrying a coming-soon message.

Those records support a narrower conclusion than the original story: the operator, lease and concept were real, but the launch schedule changed. CREN could not verify one definitive first day of regular public service from the available records.

## What diners can expect

Amara describes its cooking as Mediterranean, drawing from Southern Europe, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean. The current menu provides more reliable evidence than the early publicity: it includes hummus, labneh, muhammara, salads, grilled fish, chicken, lamb and beef dishes.

The location places the restaurant directly beside the Scioto Mile Fountain and within the Center City designated outdoor refreshment area. That setting may make Amara useful during park programming, but no available dataset measures whether one restaurant materially changes downtown housing demand.

## What remains to watch

The next verifiable checkpoints are stable posted hours, confirmation that the patio and park-event service are operating, and any later city filings that amend the 2026 agreement. Those facts will show how the restaurant uses its unusually public riverfront location without requiring claims about future development or real-estate prices.

articles.title: Columbus Begins Deploying $500 Million Housing Bond
articles.excerpt: Columbus voters approved a $500 million affordable-housing bond in 2025. The city has begun funding rounds, but the authorization is not 500 million new construction.
articles.body:
Columbus voters authorized a $500 million affordable-housing bond in November 2025, and the city began outlining and opening funding programs in 2026. The authorization covers new housing, preservation and housing stability over time; it is not evidence that $500 million has already been spent or that every dollar builds new homes.

## What voters approved

The [city’s housing-bond page](https://www.columbus.gov/Services/Housing-Assistance-Programs/Housing-Programs/Affordable-Housing-Bond-Investments) says voters approved the $500 million authorization in November 2025. It describes the package as the city’s largest local housing investment and says prior bond programs helped create or preserve more than 7,000 housing units since 2019.

An authorization allows the city to issue debt and allocate proceeds under applicable budgets and program rules. It does not mean the full amount was borrowed or disbursed on election day.

## The proposed uses are broader than construction

In the [2026 State of the City plan](https://www.columbus.gov/Government/Mayors-Office/State-of-the-City/2026-State-of-the-City-Address-Full-Text), Mayor Andrew Ginther proposed $150 million for new affordable homes and $125 million for housing stability, including transitional and permanent supportive housing. Other portions address preservation and homeownership.

[WOSU reported](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-02-11/columbus-leaders-lay-out-plans-for-500-million-affordable-housing-bond-package) on the rollout and the public discussion surrounding allocations. The mayor’s plan is a policy framework; individual projects still require applications, underwriting, contracts and public approvals.

## Funding rounds create the auditable record

The city opened a 2026 rental housing production and preservation application period from June 15 through July 17. Its program guidelines capped a standard request at $5 million in total and $50,000 per unit, subject to stated discretion and evaluation.

Those awards, rather than the headline authorization, will show which projects receive money, how many income-restricted homes result and when they reach construction or completion.

## What remains uncertain

Bond spending alone does not establish that Columbus rents will fall. Outcomes depend on project delivery, affordability periods, household eligibility, construction costs and the amount of other financing each award secures.

The public pages reviewed do not provide one consolidated disbursement schedule for the full authorization. Timing matters because bond proceeds, project commitments and completed housing can appear in different fiscal years.

The next checkpoints are published award lists, City Council ordinances, bond-issuance records and project completion reports. CREN will distinguish authorized, allocated, contracted and spent dollars in future coverage.

articles.title: Zone In Adds Capacity, Not 88,000 Built Columbus Homes
articles.excerpt: Columbus says the first Zone In rezoning could support up to 88,000 homes, but that figure measures theoretical capacity rather than approvals or construction.
articles.body:
Columbus’s first Zone In rezoning expanded theoretical capacity on more than 12,300 corridor parcels from about 6,000 homes to as many as 88,000. That estimate describes what zoning could allow over time, not approved projects, financed construction or homes that are guaranteed to be built.

## What City Council changed

The [City of Columbus proposal](https://www.columbus.gov/News-articles/Columbus-Introduces-Zoning-Code-Proposal-Capable-of-Creating-88000-Housing-Units) created six mixed-use districts for major corridors. The first application covered more than 12,300 parcels and replaced rules that city officials said were based on a decades-old code.

City Council approved the first corridor package in July 2024. The districts allow combinations of housing and commercial uses with different height and design standards tied to their locations.

## How the 88,000 figure works

The city said the affected parcels previously had capacity for approximately 6,000 additional homes. Its analysis estimated that the new rules could add capacity for 82,000 more, producing a total potential of 88,000.

That is a zoning-capacity calculation. It does not account for whether each owner wants to redevelop, whether financing is available, whether utilities can serve a proposal or whether a project receives every required approval.

## Later phases cover different questions

Columbus Underground’s [council preview](https://columbusunderground.com/zoning-updates-heading-to-city-council-on-monday-we1/) documented subsequent code work, while [10TV reported](https://www.10tv.com/article/news/local/columbus-city-council-approves-phase-two-zone-in-initiative/530-777ab85d-46d5-4974-89fa-ad20ee8f27fd) on a later phase affecting a much broader set of parcels.

Those actions should not be collapsed into the original 88,000-home estimate. Phase one corridor capacity and later citywide code changes have different geographies and policy functions.

## What the reform may change

The code can remove a regulatory barrier by allowing denser housing without a project-specific rezoning. It cannot by itself reduce construction costs, set rents or guarantee affordable units.

The city framed the capacity estimate over a 10-year period. Even on that horizon, actual production will depend on many independent property decisions rather than a single municipal construction program.

Claims that an individual parcel became more valuable also require a sale, appraisal or income analysis. CREN found no citywide dataset proving a uniform land-value effect.

## The next measurable checkpoint

Permit applications, approved unit counts and completed homes along the rezoned corridors will provide the practical test. Future coverage should compare those outcomes with the city’s capacity model while keeping proposed, approved, under-construction and completed units separate.

articles.title: Ohio Pauses New Data Center Tax Deals, Not Existing Benefits
articles.excerpt: Ohio paused consideration of new data-center tax exemption requests while lawmakers study the industry; previously approved benefits remain in place.
articles.body:
Ohio paused consideration of new data-center sales-tax exemption requests while lawmakers study the industry’s effects. The action does not revoke previously approved benefits, permanently end the program or prove that Central Ohio land values and development plans will decline.

## The pause applies to new requests

The [Associated Press reported](https://apnews.com/article/4d56561a14f9b0d00553001e8c2757a3) that Governor Mike DeWine paused new exemption offers on May 27, 2026. Previously approved incentives were not cancelled.

Ohio’s [administrative rules](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/122%3A28) continue to describe the exemption program. A pause in consideration is therefore different from repeal, a statutory moratorium or retroactive removal.

## The fiscal estimate needs precise language

AP reported that the state projected $136 million in fiscal-year 2025 exemptions but later reported nearly $1.6 billion. Those figures describe tax revenue not collected under the program, not a cash payment from the state to operators.

The original headline said costs exploded and the body dated the announcement June 2. This revision uses the May 27 action date and describes the measure without implying that every prior estimate used the same accounting basis.

## Lawmakers are studying more than taxes

The [Ohio House announcement](https://house.ohio.gov/news/republican/holmes-chavez-announce-joint-data-center-committee-144038) says a joint committee was formed to examine economic, environmental, energy and security effects. That inquiry had not produced a final policy when CREN checked.

A study process can lead to legislation, recommendations or no change. The old article incorrectly described an open-ended review as a clear signal that projects and industrial land prices would cool.

## Local real-estate effects remain unknown

CREN found no parcel-sales model, cancelled-project list or counterfactual analysis showing the pause changed Central Ohio land values. Existing approvals, local abatements, utility access and construction schedules differ by project.

The next checkpoints are committee findings, formal Tax Credit Authority actions, enacted legislation and project-level changes. Until those exist, the accurate story is a policy pause for new requests—not the end of Ohio’s data-center development market.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the committee pause separately from existing exemptions and later tax-policy decisions. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Columbus Mortgage Rate Story Went Stale Within One Week
articles.excerpt: Freddie Mac recorded a seven-week low on July 2, but rates rose the following week, showing why one national survey should not be framed as a buying window.
articles.body:
Freddie Mac’s national mortgage average fell to a seven-week low on July 2, 2026, then rose the following week. CREN’s earlier article treated one observation as a durable opportunity for Columbus buyers and gave transaction advice that the national survey could not support.

## The low was accurate and temporary

Freddie Mac’s [archive](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/pmms_archives) shows a 6.43% average for a 30-year fixed loan on July 2, 2026, and 5.79% for a 15-year loan. The [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/29c907cc408cf7f88a8fcb3292150b1f) reported the 30-year average rose to 6.49% on July 9.

A one-week reversal does not make the first number wrong. It shows that a weekly rate should be timestamped and not presented as a lasting window.

## The survey is national, not a Columbus quote

Freddie Mac says its [survey methodology](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms?sf230874538=1) uses loan applications submitted by lenders across the country. It is a market benchmark, not an offer to every borrower.

Actual pricing varies with credit, down payment, property, loan type, points, lender and lock period. The old article used the national average to tell Columbus readers when to shop and lock, which exceeded what the dataset could establish.

## The payment example omitted important costs

The earlier calculation compared principal and interest on a $300,000 loan at two rates. It omitted taxes, insurance, association charges, mortgage insurance, points and closing costs, so it was not a complete housing payment.

Even a correct principal-and-interest calculation should state its assumptions and should not imply that a small average-rate move makes a particular purchase affordable.

## A better reader takeaway

Readers can use PMMS to understand direction, then obtain standardized loan estimates from lenders for their own scenario. Comparing annual percentage rate, fees, cash to close and lock terms is more useful than trying to identify one national weekly bottom.

CREN has removed commands to buy now, seek preapproval immediately or stop waiting for lower rates. The next report should pair a dated national benchmark with current Central Ohio prices and clearly disclosed payment assumptions.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats a national weekly survey separately from local lender quotes and borrower qualifications. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. CREN will revisit the question when a comparable record adds facts, rather than converting possibility into certainty or transaction advice.

articles.title: Central Ohio Added Listings While May Home Prices Rose
articles.excerpt: Central Ohio posted more sales and inventory in May 2026 while its median price reached $350,000, a combination that requires more context than a seller-market label.
articles.body:
Central Ohio’s median sale price reached $350,000 in May 2026 as closed sales and available inventory both increased from a year earlier. The regional figures show more selection without a broad price decline, but they do not describe every county, school district or price tier.

## Sales and inventory moved together

The [May report from Columbus REALTORS](https://columbusrealtors.com/news/central-ohio-housing-report---may-2026) recorded a 4.3% year-over-year increase in the regional median sale price. Closed sales rose 7.8%, while active inventory increased 8.2% to 5,223 homes and condominiums.

New listings totaled 4,044, and homes spent an average of 29 days on market, one day longer than in May 2025. These measures describe a busier spring market with more homes available, not a uniform change in negotiating power.

## Supply remained limited by the MLS measure

The report calculated 2.0 months of inventory. Months of inventory estimates how long the available listings would last at the recent sales pace if no additional homes entered the market.

That measure increased alongside listings, but a single month cannot establish a lasting move toward balance. Seasonal listing patterns and the mix of closed properties can change both supply and price statistics.

## Local outcomes varied

The same MLS report placed Olentangy Local School District’s median at $587,000 and Union County’s at $487,500. Marion County’s median was $212,500. These are separate transaction pools, so their medians should not be used as direct estimates for individual homes.

For a broader inventory check, the Federal Reserve Bank’s [Columbus active-listing series](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ACTLISCOU18140) republishes Realtor.com data for the metropolitan area. It uses a different geography and methodology from the regional MLS, making direction more useful than exact cross-source comparisons.

## What the data cannot answer

The May release does not report concessions, inspection terms or bidding-war frequency. It therefore cannot support claims that all buyers had more leverage or that all sellers retained an advantage.

CREN’s source comparison also found that promotional summaries often call four to six months a balanced market without identifying the local historical baseline. The safer conclusion is that inventory expanded while prices continued to rise.

## The next checkpoint

The most informative follow-up will compare several consecutive months from the same MLS series. Inventory, price, closed sales, days on market and price reductions should be evaluated together before labeling the change a new market regime.

articles.title: Bexley Spring Sales Rose, but One Month Is Not a Trend
articles.excerpt: Bexley’s spring sales data show a sharp median-price increase, but the small local sample and changing mix of homes make broad value claims unreliable.
articles.body:
Bexley’s spring 2026 sales were expensive and competitive, but the latest data do not support a simple claim that every home gained the same amount. Redfin’s three-month measure showed a higher median price, while its marketing-time measure was slightly slower than a year earlier.

## What the latest snapshot shows

For the three months ending May 2026, [Redfin’s Bexley dataset](https://www.redfin.com/city/1663/OH/Bexley/housing-market) reported a median sale price of $749,302, up 18.0% from the comparable period a year earlier. It counted 46 May sales, down 16.2% year over year, and an average of 33 days on market compared with 31 days.

Those figures contradict the original article’s claim that homes were selling faster based on an earlier snapshot. They also show why a live market page needs a clear measurement date: the values change as transactions enter the reporting window.

## Median price is not home appreciation

A median sale price is the midpoint of homes sold during a period. It can rise because more large or renovated homes sold, even if no individual property appreciated by the same percentage. Bexley’s limited transaction count makes that mix effect especially important.

Zillow publishes a different measure. Its [Bexley home-value page](https://www.zillow.com/home-values/3663/bexley-oh/) uses a modeled typical value rather than only the prices of homes that closed during one month. The two products answer different questions and should not be combined as if they use the same sample or method.

## The longer baseline

The [Columbus REALTORS 2025 annual report](https://cms.columbusrealtors.com/api/media/file/CBR_ANN_2025_Revised.pdf) provides a separate full-year community view derived from the regional multiple-listing service. A yearly series is less sensitive to one unusual month, although its coverage and definitions still differ from Redfin and Zillow.

CREN’s comparison of the three sources is the main finding: Bexley remained a high-price, active market, but the size and direction of the reported change depend on the time window and metric. None of the sources proves that school reputation, walkability or scarce land caused a particular price movement.

## What to watch next

The next useful comparison is another rolling three-month period using the same Redfin geography, paired with the full-year MLS series when it becomes available. Sales count, median price, days on market and sale-to-list ratio should be read together.

Readers evaluating a particular house still need comparable sales matched for location, size, condition and date. Citywide medians describe the transactions in the dataset, not the value of every Bexley property.

articles.title: Upper Arlington Ballot Combines $273.5M Bond and 4.9 Mills
articles.excerpt: Upper Arlington’s Nov. 3 ballot combines a $273.5 million facilities bond with a 4.9-mill operating levy and a district-estimated tax impact.
articles.body:
Upper Arlington voters will decide a combined school bond and operating levy on November 3, 2026. The final measure is a $273.5 million bond plus 4.9 mills for operations—not a single $285 million building plan—and its tax estimate uses county-appraised value.

## The final ballot package has two parts

The district’s [June 30 resolution summary](https://www.uaschools.org/our-district/district-news/district-news/~board/upper-arlington-schools-news-1/post/board-of-education-takes-final-step-to-place-bond-levy-on-fall-ballot) says the November 3, 2026, ballot includes a $273.5 million bond and a 4.9-mill operating levy. The estimated bond increase is 2.25 mills above current collections.

The prior headline rounded the package into a $285 million building plan. That obscured the separate operating levy and did not match the final bond amount.

## The tax estimate uses appraised value

[Dispatch coverage](https://www.aol.com/articles/upper-arlington-schools-seek-tax-174448000.html) reports the district estimate that the combined measure would add about $1,250 a year, or $105 a month, for property valued at $500,000 by the Franklin County Auditor. That is an example, not every owner’s bill.

Market price and county appraised value are not interchangeable. Owners should use their parcel valuation and final ballot materials rather than applying the example to a listing price.

## Bond and levy dollars serve different purposes

The [facilities plan](https://www.uaschools.org/our-district/facilities-master-planning) identifies middle-school and early-childhood projects for the bond. The operating levy is intended for programs, services and daily operations.

CREN has removed language calling the tax a direct investment in property value. School facilities and taxes can both matter to buyers, but the cited records do not quantify a net home-price effect.

## What voters should verify

The authoritative checkpoints are final ballot language, county tax calculations, project scopes, debt schedules and district financial reports. Voters should distinguish estimated construction costs from the amount borrowed and from annual operating revenue.

The article also withdraws sales-timing advice and unsupported market statistics. The defensible conclusion is about the decision itself: voters will choose whether to authorize both long-term borrowing and additional operating millage.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the facilities borrowing question separately from the operating levy and parcel-level tax effects. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. CREN will revisit the question when a comparable record adds facts, rather than converting possibility into certainty or transaction advice.

articles.title: German Village Data Show Higher Prices but Slower Sales in 2026
articles.excerpt: Redfin’s rolling German Village data show a higher median price and longer marketing time, contradicting the earlier claim that prices were simply flat.
articles.body:
German Village’s rolling sales data do not support CREN’s earlier claim that prices were flat in mid-2026. Redfin reported a higher median sale price alongside longer marketing times, a combination that requires attention to sample size, geography and property mix.

## The rolling median was not flat

Redfin’s [German Village market page](https://www.redfin.com/neighborhood/153655/OH/Columbus/German-Village/housing-market) reported a $616,793 median sale price for the three months ending May 2026, up 15.7% from the comparable period. It also reported 49 median days on market, 16 days longer than a year earlier.

Those measures can move in different directions. A higher median can reflect which homes sold, while longer marketing time can reflect pricing, condition, financing or buyer choice.

## Listing and sale measures answer different questions

The old article combined a [Movoto listing snapshot](https://www.movoto.com/columbus-oh/german-village/) with Redfin closed-sale data and called the market steady. Listing price describes seller expectations; sale price describes completed transactions.

CREN has withdrawn the flat-price conclusion because the figures used different periods and measures. A valid comparison needs the same geography, property types and time window.

## Historic review is a rule, not a price guarantee

The [German Village Commission](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Building-Zoning-Services/Boards-and-Commissions/Historic-Preservation-Design-Review-Boards-Commissions-Panels/German-Village-Commission) reviews exterior alterations and issues certificates under city code and district guidelines. Owners should verify whether planned work requires review.

The earlier article said those rules protect an owner’s investment over time. CREN found no causal study in the cited sources linking commission review to a defined price premium, so that assurance has been removed.

## A better next comparison

Future updates should use a rolling period and report sale count, median price, price per square foot, days on market and property-type mix together. Property-level comparisons can help distinguish market movement from a changing mix of houses and condominiums.

The supported takeaway is cautious: recent transactions produced a higher median while taking longer to sell. That does not prove historic charm caused demand or that every German Village property appreciated by the same percentage.

## How to use this correction

That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Clintonville Market Reports Disagree on May Sales Pace
articles.excerpt: One broker report said Clintonville homes sold in 10 days, while a broader Redfin measure showed 30 days. Geography and time windows explain much of the gap.
articles.body:
Two May 2026 reports gave sharply different pictures of Clintonville’s sales pace: a broker snapshot reported a 10-day median, while Redfin’s broader three-month measure showed 30 days. The difference reflects incompatible boundaries and time windows, so neither number should be presented without its method.

## The original claim used a narrow snapshot

A [local broker’s May report](https://www.searchcolumbushomesonline.com/blog/may-2026-clintonville-real-estate-market-report/) grouped Clintonville and Beechwold transactions and reported a $415,000 median sale price, 65 sales and a 10-day median marketing time. It compared those figures with the same month a year earlier.

That source is useful as a defined snapshot, but it is secondary promotional material and its public page does not provide a downloadable transaction file. CREN could not reproduce the calculation property by property.

## A broader source gives different results

Redfin’s [Clintonville market page](https://www.redfin.com/neighborhood/152473/OH/Columbus/Clintonville/housing-market) uses a rolling three-month period ending in May. It reported a $436,053 median sale price, up 0.2% year over year, with 121 May sales and 30 average days on market compared with 32 days a year earlier.

The 10-day and 30-day figures are not necessarily errors. One is a monthly median for a broker-defined Clintonville and Beechwold area; the other is a three-month average for Redfin’s mapped neighborhood. Median and average also respond differently to unusually fast or slow sales.

## The annual baseline adds context

The [Columbus REALTORS 2025 annual report](https://cms.columbusrealtors.com/api/media/file/CBR_ANN_2025_Revised.pdf) groups Beechwold and Clintonville using ZIP codes 43214 and 43202. It counted 487 closed sales in 2025, nearly unchanged from 485 in 2024.

That stable full-year count does not prove that May 2026 was weak or strong. It shows why a one-month jump should be checked against a longer series before it is called a trend.

## What readers can conclude

All three sources support that homes continued to trade actively in the area. They do not support a blanket instruction to rush, nor do they establish that every segment cooled because one median price fell.

The next reliable checkpoint is a same-boundary, same-method comparison across several months. CREN will treat neighborhood market claims as provisional unless the underlying geography, statistic and observation period are disclosed.

articles.title: Hilliard Selects Mixed-Use Concept for Former Chase Site
articles.excerpt: Hilliard selected a restaurant-and-apartment concept for the former Chase site on Main Street, but negotiations, approvals and final design remain ahead.
articles.body:
Hilliard has selected The Westwood Collective’s mixed-use concept for the former Chase branch at 4056 East Main Street, including a proposed Italian restaurant and apartments. The selection begins negotiations; it is not a completed sale, final development approval or construction start.

## How the site reached this point

The [Hilliard Development Corporation request for proposals](https://hilliardohio.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/4056-Main-RFP.pdf) covers approximately 0.836 acre at 4056 E. Main St. The corporation owns the former bank property and sought a development team to buy and redevelop it in line with the city’s plans for Old Hilliard.

Proposals were due in March 2026. The RFP reserved the corporation’s right to reject proposals, request more information or pursue another approach if no submission met its requirements.

## What the selected concept contains

The [city’s June announcement](https://hilliardohio.gov/new-dining-retail-development-planned-for-downtown-hilliard/) identifies The Westwood Collective as the selected developer. The concept preserves the former bank for an Italian restaurant called La Volta and proposes a new building with ground-floor commercial space and apartments above.

The announcement says the bank vault would become a wine display. It does not give a final apartment count, rents, construction cost or opening date.

## Selection is not final approval

The city described the next step as negotiation of a purchase agreement with the Hilliard Development Corporation. The corporation’s board would still need to approve an agreement, and the project would remain subject to land-use, design, building and other applicable reviews.

[Hoodline’s summary](https://hoodline.com/2026/06/old-hilliard-bank-vault-poised-to-become-italian-hot-spot-with-luxe-flats/) correctly notes that the drawings were conceptual. Calling the restaurant and apartments set for construction would overstate their status.

## What the record does not prove

A mixed-use proposal may add activity to the district, but the available sources do not measure its effect on nearby sales, rents or commercial performance. The developer’s selection also does not guarantee that negotiations will produce a closing.

Because the Hilliard Development Corporation owns the property, the purchase agreement will be the key record for price, conditions and public obligations. None of those terms appears in the concept announcement.

## The next checkpoints

Readers should watch for a public purchase agreement, Hilliard Development Corporation board action, a final site plan and building permits. Those records will provide the apartment count, financial terms and development schedule that the current concept lacks.

articles.title: Canal Winchester Lock Pointe Advances With 120-Unit Limit
articles.excerpt: Canal Winchester records cap Lock Pointe Village at 120 apartments and show infrastructure work advancing, correcting earlier 122-unit language.
articles.body:
Canal Winchester records show Lock Pointe Village advancing after final development review, with approved plans capping the project at 120 apartments. Earlier 122-unit language came from the preliminary hearing, and the available records do not establish rents, lease-up speed or effects on nearby land.

## Final review reduced the count

The preliminary public hearing discussed [122 apartments](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/canal-winchester/company-proposes-122-unit-apartment-development-in-canal-winchester/). Later [commission minutes](https://www.canalwinchesterohio.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Minutes/_08112025-694) say the approved plan set a maximum density of 120 units in two-unit and four-unit buildings.

CREN now uses the later approved maximum. The discrepancy reflects plan evolution, not two separate projects.

## Infrastructure records show continuing work

A [June 2026 council record](https://www.canalwinchesterohio.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Agenda/_06012026-764) says the developer had closed on the property and received approval for civil-engineering drawings. The city was considering right-of-way for turn-lane improvements.

Those steps show advancement but do not establish that every home is under construction or provide a verified first delivery date.

## Rents and demand were not established

[REBusinessOnline](https://rebusinessonline.com/stark-enterprises-to-break-ground-on-120-unit-build-to-rent-community-in-metro-columbus/) described the planned amenities and a construction schedule. The reviewed sources did not document the $1,600-to-$2,100 rent range used in CREN’s earlier article.

CREN also removed claims that build-to-rent is one of the fastest-growing sectors and that nearby landowners should interpret the plan as proof of outward demand. Those conclusions require defined market data.

## What to verify next

The next records are building permits, construction starts, completed turn-lane work, published rents, certificates of occupancy and actual leasing. They will show timing, price position and market response.

For now, Lock Pointe is an advancing 120-unit rental plan with approved development parameters. It is not evidence that local rents, school enrollment, road performance or property values will move in a particular direction.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the later local plan record separately from an earlier project count and market forecasts. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Hilltop RISE Purchase Is Funded; Renovation Outcomes Need Proof
articles.excerpt: Columbus funded Hilltop RISE’s acquisition of two West Broad Street properties, but affordability, renovation and corridor effects need later records.
articles.body:
Columbus approved acquisition funding for Hilltop RISE to purchase two mixed-use West Broad Street properties near the planned bus-rapid-transit corridor. The public record confirms the grant and redevelopment purpose, but not completed renovations, permanent affordability or rising corridor values.

## The ordinance funded acquisition

Columbus [Ordinance 2059-2025](https://columbus.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?FullText=1&GUID=77853171-0BC8-4F37-9F28-3A7112306FB2&ID=7647757) authorized a $1.2 million agreement for acquisition and related costs at approximately 3085–3099 West Broad Street. Council approved it on September 8, 2025.

The ordinance assigned Hilltop RISE responsibility for redeveloping, operating and maintaining the properties. It did not state that rehabilitation had been completed or certify future rents.

## The renovation plan remains a reported intention

[Columbus Underground reported](https://columbusunderground.com/renovation-plans-for-historic-hilltop-buildings-moving-forward-bw1/) plans for apartments and ground-floor commercial space while retaining existing residents. Those commitments should be checked against leases, construction scopes and affordability covenants after work proceeds.

Calling apartments naturally affordable describes their current unsubsidized rent position; it does not by itself guarantee long-term restrictions. CREN has narrowed the language until recorded requirements or program documents establish duration and eligibility.

## Transit proximity does not prove appreciation

The properties sit along the planned LinkUS West Broad Street bus-rapid-transit corridor. The previous story said better transit tends to raise land values and presented the project as protection from future displacement.

CREN found no corridor-specific valuation or displacement analysis in the cited records. Transit, rehabilitation and affordability may interact, but the direction and size of those effects require parcel sales, rents and household data.

## Evidence to collect after construction

The next checkpoints are permits, financing documents, construction completion, tenant relocation records, executed leases and the occupancy of commercial space. Those records can test whether residents remained and whether rents followed stated limits.

The supported conclusion is that public money enabled acquisition for a redevelopment purpose. Claims about rising values, new foot traffic and an investable corridor have been removed because they were predictions rather than reported results.

articles.title: CMHA Opens 82-Home Senior Community in Grove City
articles.excerpt: Cobblestone Manor opened as CMHA’s first Grove City development, providing 82 income-restricted senior apartments at a reported cost of $28.6 million.
articles.body:
Cobblestone Manor opened in April 2026 as the Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority’s first development in Grove City. The completed $28.6 million community contains 82 apartments for older residents with income restrictions; it should not be described as a completed $125 million project.

## What opened

The [CMHA project announcement](https://cmhanet.com/media/press%20releases/2024/CMHA_Cobblestone%20Manor_Press%20Release_8-13-24_FINAL.pdf) identifies Cobblestone Manor as an 82-unit senior community at 1050 Lamplighter Drive. CMHA put the development cost at $28.6 million and described it as its first Grove City development.

[WOSU’s opening report](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-04-20/columbus-metropolitan-housing-authority-opens-its-first-development-in-grove-city) confirmed that the complex opened on April 20, 2026. It reported a fitness center, community room, library, computer room and paved walking trail.

## Who the apartments serve

WOSU reported that about three-quarters of the apartments were reserved for people with annual incomes near $20,000, while the balance would serve residents earning up to approximately $55,000. Those are eligibility descriptions from the opening coverage, not current vacancy or waiting-list data.

The project adds a specific type of housing: income-restricted apartments for older adults. It does not measure the full need for senior housing in Grove City or establish how many eligible residents obtained homes.

## Correcting the $125 million framing

The earlier CREN headline paired the completed complex with a $125 million housing push. [Hoodline’s account](https://hoodline.com/2026/04/cmha-drops-125-million-bet-on-grove-city-housing-crunch/) assembled that larger figure from several proposed acquisitions, preservation efforts and future developments.

Those separate projects were at different stages and did not constitute one approved or completed Cobblestone Manor investment. CREN therefore removed the $125 million figure from the headline and treats future CMHA work as a separate reporting assignment.

## What remains unknown

The available sources do not provide current occupancy, waiting-list length, operating subsidy per apartment or resident outcomes. Amenities and eligibility rules alone cannot establish whether the supply meets demand.

Income restrictions also require continuing compliance after opening. A ribbon-cutting confirms that the physical development reached completion, but it does not substitute for later reporting on leasing, maintenance and whether eligible residents can access the apartments.

The next useful records will be CMHA occupancy reporting, compliance documents for the income restrictions and public approvals for any additional Grove City sites. Those records can distinguish completed apartments from financing authorizations and early proposals.

articles.excerpt: Bishop Elementary was dedicated in August 2025, not 2026. Dublin families should use current district tools instead of treating school assignments as fixed.

Bishop Elementary was dedicated in August 2025 and is already operating as Dublin City Schools’ newest elementary building. CREN’s earlier story incorrectly presented the dedication as a 2026 opening and tied the school to home-value gains without evidence.

## The dedication happened in 2025

The [current Bishop Elementary site](https://bishop.dublinschools.net/) identifies the school as the district’s newest elementary building. A [CityScene account](https://www.cityscenecolumbus.com/communities/dublinlife/a-letter-from-your-superintendent/) published by the district superintendent shows the ribbon cutting occurred on August 11, 2025.

The previous CREN article moved that event forward by a year. Its August 2026 opening language was therefore not a preview; it was a stale event presented as new.

## School assignment requires an address check

Dublin City Schools publishes separate maps for the [2026–2027 school year](https://www.dublinschools.net/about/district-maps) and says a mailing address or Dublin ZIP code does not itself establish district assignment. Families should use the official address-level locator.

The district’s [redistricting FAQ](https://www.dublinschools.net/redistricting-information/frequently-asked-questions) says another set of changes takes effect in the 2027–2028 school year. That makes static real-estate listing text especially unreliable for future enrollment.

## A school building does not prove a price premium

The old story claimed a new building could lift demand and values on assigned streets. CREN found no controlled sales analysis comparing affected and unaffected homes before and after the boundary change.

School facilities can matter to households, but transaction prices also reflect taxes, housing type, condition, location, interest rates and limited inventory. CREN has withdrawn the claim that Bishop’s opening itself increased property values.

## The next reliable checkpoints

Families should verify the current assignment before a lease or purchase and recheck it for the school year in which a child will enroll. The district—not a seller, listing portal or article—is the authoritative source.

Future coverage should use adopted boundary maps, enrollment reports and board records. It should not tell sellers to market a school assignment as a value gain or describe enrollment growth as proof of healthy property appreciation.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the district timeline and its address-level boundary tools as separate evidence. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Westerville Housing Gauges Disagree Because Their Methods Differ
articles.excerpt: Redfin, Zillow and a broker report use different periods, geographies and measures for Westerville, so their prices and market times cannot be merged.
articles.body:
Westerville housing sources disagree because they measure different things, not because one number necessarily proves a hotter market. Current Redfin and Zillow pages use different methods and time periods, while the nine-day figure came from a broker report with a narrower dataset.

## Redfin reports a rolling sales picture

Redfin’s [Westerville page](https://www.redfin.com/city/20634/OH/Westerville/housing-market) reported a $452,229 median sale price for the three months ending May 2026, up 5.2% year over year, with 30 median days on market. It counted 143 May sales.

That rolling window reduces some one-month mix noise but still reflects only properties included in Redfin’s geography and data feed.

## Zillow uses both an index and transaction measures

Zillow’s [Westerville page](https://www.zillow.com/home-values/76516/westerville-oh-43086/) reported a $457,533 typical home value through June 2026 and a $437,967 May median sale price. It also listed three median days to pending in June.

Zillow’s typical-value index models property-level values, while median sale price summarizes completed transactions and days to pending measures listing status. They are not substitutes for one another.

## The nine-day figure needs its dataset

The [broker report](https://www.searchcolumbushomesonline.com/blog/may-2026-westerville-real-estate-market-report/) used a $532,500 May median and nine days, but the original CREN story did not document its precise geography, property filters or whether nine days meant average time to contract.

CREN therefore cannot call Westerville a single nine-day market. The larger difference from Redfin and Zillow is a reason to disclose methods, not a reason to choose the most dramatic figure.

## How to report the next update

A useful update should name the geography, property types, aggregation period, measure and download date for every figure. It should compare like with like and explain revisions when a provider updates history.

CREN has removed commands for buyers to move fast and claims that seller timing is excellent. The supported conclusion is methodological: Westerville remained active, but no single source in this comparison describes every home or transaction.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats each provider’s geography, time window and measure rather than blending unlike indicators. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. It also gives readers a clear baseline for comparing later public records and consistent datasets.

The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Meta Prometheus Advances, but Household Bill Claims Need Evidence
articles.excerpt: Meta’s Prometheus project is tied to major power arrangements near New Albany, but CREN cannot attribute a specific household bill increase to the site.
articles.body:
Meta’s Prometheus computing project is advancing near New Albany with unusually large electricity requirements and new power arrangements. CREN found no regulator-approved calculation tying the project to a specific increase on an individual household bill, so the earlier dollar claim is withdrawn.

## The project and power agreements are real

The [City of New Albany](https://newalbanyohio.org/news/2026/01/statement-regarding-metas-nuclear-energy-projects/) says Meta’s energy agreements support grids serving the Prometheus supercluster in the business park. The [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/0eb051a9a11d96f7ce200e186ad13476) described Prometheus as a one-gigawatt cluster expected to come online in 2026.

A gigawatt rating describes power capacity or demand, not continuous household-equivalent consumption. The original conversion to hundreds of thousands of homes lacked a stated capacity factor and time basis, so CREN removed it.

## Temporary substation use has a public record

[WOSU reported](https://www.wosu.org/2025-11-26/meta-wants-to-draw-power-for-unused-new-albany-electrical-substation-built-for-intel-project?_amp=true) that AEP Ohio and Meta filed an arrangement involving a substation built for Intel. The report described a three-year service period while Intel’s project remained in development.

That arrangement helps explain how near-term service may be delivered. It does not, by itself, identify the amount allocated to residential customers or the effect on a particular bill.

## The previous bill claim mixed unrelated costs

The earlier article said an average customer could pay $36 more each month across electricity, gas and water, then connected that figure to data-center demand. CREN could not trace that combined-utility estimate to a proceeding that attributes it to Prometheus.

Electric rates, riders and infrastructure charges require regulator-approved tariffs and defined customer classes. Gas and water bills come from separate systems, so combining them obscured causation.

## What residents should watch

The useful checkpoints are PUCO case orders, AEP Ohio tariffs, interconnection milestones, the project’s operating status and disclosed energy contracts. Those records can show who pays for dedicated infrastructure and when service begins.

CREN also removed claims that the project supports home values or creates a strong investment story. Construction spending and land purchases do not prove a direction for residential prices, rents or household affordability.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the facility announcement separately from utility cost allocation and household bills. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test. The correction does not mean the broader outcome is impossible. It means the evidence reviewed here cannot yet measure that outcome or assign it to one project, institution or market signal. articles.title: Dublin Bright Road Plan Advances, but Price Effects Are Unproven
articles.excerpt: Dublin records show Bright Road Reserve advancing through review, but projected home prices do not establish gains for nearby owners or the wider market.
articles.body:
Dublin planning records show Bright Road Reserve advancing as a small luxury subdivision on a wooded site near Bright Road. The plan may add high-priced homes, but projected asking prices are not comparable sales and do not prove that nearby properties will appreciate.

## What the city record establishes

The [City of Dublin case page](https://dublinohiousa.gov/pzc/26-018/) identifies an amended final development plan reviewed in April 2026. [NBC4 reported](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/dublin/million-dollar-neighborhood-approved-for-14-acre-dublin-reserve/) that the broader concept called for 20 detached homes on roughly 14 acres, with prices described by the applicant in a luxury range.

A development-plan review is not the same as completed construction, recorded sales or occupied homes. Final plats, permits and building starts remain better evidence of delivery than a planning-stage price estimate.

## The wooded-site claim needs a baseline

The [city planning report](https://dublinohiousa.gov/alpha/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/C4_Planning-Report.pdf) described 5.6 acres of open space within the approximately 14-acre site. That figure does not mean every existing tree will remain, and it should not be converted into a broad environmental benefit without final tree-preservation, drainage and construction plans.

Public paths and an ungated layout were elements of the reviewed concept. Their final location, maintenance responsibility and construction timing should be checked against the recorded plat and approved engineering plans.

## Projected prices are not neighborhood evidence

The original article said future listings would raise nearby resale values and called the plan good news for owner equity. CREN found no paired-sales analysis, appraisal study or completed transaction data supporting that conclusion.

A new luxury sale can become one comparable for an appraiser, but relevance depends on property size, condition, lot, location and sale date. Twenty planned houses cannot establish the direction of Dublin’s entire upper-tier market before closings occur.

## What to verify next

The next useful records are the final plat, construction permits, tree and stormwater plans, and actual closed sales. Those documents can show what was built, what land remained open and whether prices matched the applicant’s early range.

Until then, Bright Road Reserve is best described as an advancing development plan. CREN has removed sales advice, equity predictions and claims that budget buyers should act early because none followed from the available planning evidence.

articles.title: Nationwide Details 148-Home Columbus Conversion at 280 North High
articles.excerpt: Nationwide Realty Investors plans 148 apartments and retained office space at 280 N. High St., with the first residents currently targeted for mid-2027.
articles.body:
Nationwide Realty Investors says it is converting most of the 18-story tower at 280 North High Street into 148 apartments while retaining office space. The announced plan, called The Centennial on High, targets initial occupancy in mid-2027 but does not yet disclose rents or a final construction schedule.

## The current program

The [developer’s February 2026 announcement](https://www.nationwiderealtyinvestors.com/portfolio/arena-district/the-centennial-on-high/) describes 148 residences across 15 floors, including a newly created penthouse level. Five apartments are planned on each residential floor, with balconies, while part of the building will continue as offices.

The project repurposes the former Two Nationwide Plaza, an 18-story office building at the meeting point of the Arena District, Short North and Gay Street District. Nationwide Realty Investors named it for Nationwide’s centennial year.

## Why the unit count changed

Earlier reporting described a larger concept. [Propmodo reported](https://propmodo.com/playbook/nationwide-is-converting-one-of-its-own-office-towers-into-apartments/) an approximately 172-unit version before the developer published the current 148-home program. The difference is a reminder that announced unit counts can change during design and construction.

The current plan includes one-, two- and three-bedroom homes, a fitness center, resident gathering space and a courtyard. These are developer-stated features, not evidence of completed construction or market demand.

## What the conversion does and does not prove

Office-to-residential conversion means adapting a commercial building for housing rather than constructing a residential tower from the ground up. The approach can reuse an existing structure, but deep floor plates, plumbing, windows and code requirements can make conversions difficult.

This project supplies a concrete local example, yet one conversion does not establish that every underused downtown office can become housing. CREN found no public feasibility study comparing the building with the rest of Columbus’s office inventory.

## What remains unknown

Nationwide has identified mid-2027 for first occupancy. The available announcement does not provide apartment rents, total development cost, affordability restrictions or a detailed construction milestone schedule.

The next useful records will be building permits, any revisions to the 148-unit plan and a leasing launch with prices. Those checkpoints will show whether the announced mixed-use conversion remains on its current scope and timetable.

articles.excerpt: Columbus approved rezoning for 419 homes at the former State Library site, but building design, demolition timing and affordability remain unresolved.
articles.body:
Columbus approved rezoning that allows a 419-unit mixed-use development at 274 East First Avenue in Italian Village. That action changes permitted use, but it does not prove that demolition or construction is scheduled, nor does it settle design, financing or affordability.

## Rezoning is complete, not the buildings

The city’s [Z26-009 record](https://portal.columbus.gov/Permits/cap/CapDetail.aspx?HideHeader=true&Module=Zoning&agencyCode=COLUMBUS&capID1=26LAC&capID2=00000&capID3=00161&type=1000) says Columbus approved rezoning for 6.94 acres and 419 dwelling units at 274 East First Avenue. The ordinance became effective on July 22, 2026.

The city action changes allowable land use; later project steps remain separate.

## The plan began as an early concept

In February, [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/multi-building-development-proposed-for-italian-village-bw1/) reported that Merus and BBCO submitted a five-building residential concept with parking. The developer described the plan as early and conceptual.

The first CREN article treated 419 apartments as certain and said the site was set to become one of the area’s largest projects. The approved density is real, but final architecture, unit mix and phasing can still change through later reviews.

## Library relocation and development are separate

[NBC4 reported](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/central-ohio-news/ohio-state-library-moving-to-make-way-for-redevelopment-project/) that library functions were moving to downtown offices and separate collection storage. Relocation can make redevelopment possible without proving when a developer will close, finance or start construction.

CREN has removed claims that the project will slow rents, raise surrounding land values or draw shops. None of those outcomes was measured in the reviewed planning or relocation records.

## The next records will define the project

Readers should watch for property transfer, demolition permits, final commission review, building permits, financing and any affordability agreement. Those records will establish whether the entitled density becomes constructed housing.

For now, the precise conclusion is that Columbus approved zoning for up to 419 homes on the site. The construction schedule and who will be able to afford the apartments remain unresolved.

## How to use this correction

This revision treats the land-use decision separately from physical delivery, design and household affordability. That approach keeps a verifiable event or measurement from carrying conclusions the underlying sources do not test.
